#3687. Drake’s Stylist Juliet Charlotte Has Seen All Your Memes

Stylist Sessions is a series of conversations in which Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, unpacks the details, strategies, and Easter eggs on red carpets with the leading stylists. Up next, Juliet Charlotte tells VF about dressing Drake and, yes, reading all your comments about his looks

If you have access to the internet, it’s likely that you’ve seen what Drake wore to celebrate his 40th birthday last weekend in New York City. The rapper opted for a pair of red Versace leather pants and a cheetah jacket, a customized Chrome Hearts jeans and a suede vest, and an archival Chanel scarf paired with gray sweats. But it was an Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed shawl from 1997—a bonafide fashion vintage holy grail—that launched a thousand memes. Drake stepped out, and the jokes poured in: he was dubbed “pumpkin spice papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle @champagnepapi, described as a Real Housewife on a girls trip to Aspen, and as someone ready for “Christian girl autumn,” another viral trend.

Drake has been the punchline in culture many times, but—online trolls be damned—he’s been dressing better than ever. Chalk that up to his new-ish stylist, New Jersey native Juliet Charlotte. The 27-year-old started her career working with Ye and his fashion brand, Yeezy, as part of his wider styling team. Now that she’s a year into working with Drake, she’s based in Toronto. She also styles the up-and-coming Canadian singer-songwriter Chxrry, whose debut album U, Me & My Ego was released earlier this year.

Charlotte is a singular kind of stylist, particularly in that she prefers to buy pieces—some new, most archival—to build archives for her clients instead of borrowing clothes that any other celebrity could wear. In her first-ever interview, she tells VF about dressing Drake, and addresses the many memes. Spoiler alert: She’s seen them and remains unfazed—she even found some of them funny.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Juliet Charlotte: I started styling five years ago now. I had just turned 21. Kanye’s team reached out to me, his GM [general manager] at the time, this guy named Laurence Chandler. They were like, “Are you a stylist? Can you come in and do some fittings with us?” I was literally a college student working a retail job, and I was like, Yes, I am a stylist. Of course I can [laughs]. It was around the time of the pandemic, when Ye was at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium and working with Demna. I walked into this room and there’s Demna and all these Balenciaga clothes and Ye. I just wanted to work. I was excited, and I just pretended that I knew what I was doing. I ended up working with him up until maybe two years ago now. I learned a lot from that experience, and then I took on new clients. I worked with [rapper and singer] Molly Santana, and now Chxrry and Drake.

Why do you think they thought you were a stylist?

I was going to school for fashion in New Jersey, and I didn’t actually know which area of fashion I wanted to enter. I just knew that I always loved clothes. When the pandemic happened, all the stores closed, so I had to find a new way to make money. I started to make angel number necklaces, and it just blew up and it was really profitable for me. Looking back, it’s kind of embarrassing, but I was young and it allowed me to buy clothes that I wanted. I would take pictures and post on my Instagram just casually. It wasn’t like I wanted to be an influencer or anything, I just wanted people to see the way I dress. It was a very casual thing, but Yeezy is very reference-based, and I guess I kept showing up on mood boards at that time. So Ye was like, let’s just get this girl in here.

I was part of a bigger team, and Ye would throw me into different roles. So it wasn’t always just styling. Sometimes I was working on e-commerce or doing campaigns, or sometimes it was Bianca [Censori]’s wardrobe. It’s really collaborative at Yeezy. There’s so many talented people that work on everything together.

I was wondering if there was a Ye or Yeezy connection, because I noticed an aesthetic throughline with your personal style. What would you say is your aesthetic, your “thing,” as a stylist?

The Yeezy background definitely helped make me this way, because I want to simplify everything and strip down everything and just be like, let’s just do the absolute best version of whatever you want to do. I’m always trying to declutter. And I really think that came from working with Ye, because he just wants to strip everything back and make it just simple but beautiful and effective.

Drake is a maximalist when it comes to his style, and I appreciate that. I don’t want to just throw my personal style on anybody that I work with. I really want to take what they love and be like, “Okay, let’s do the best version of this.” Working with him, I really just try and keep it in his world and keep it to things that excite him.

Drake out in New York City wearing vintage Hermès by Martin Margiela from 1997.

Hermès by Martin Margiela, fall-winter 1997.

Have you always been into vintage fashion? Or is it something that you’ve developed with Drake to build that into his wardrobe?

Obviously we just had that Hermès by [Martin] Margiela moment, which I really enjoyed and I thought it was fun. But I’m really interested in taking pieces, just random vintage pieces that didn’t get such a moment in the past, because that Hermès piece already had its moment on the runway. It’s fun to bring it back, but the way that I like to shop is finding vintage pieces that didn’t get a moment and reinventing them. Obviously there’s a lot of amazing designers right now, but I’m also not so into over-consumption, and just what we’ve turned into. I’d really rather shop vintage as much as I can.

Drake is someone who has such a wide range of influences and sounds. When you work on looks for him, are you trying to pull from this really wide range of inspirations and aesthetics, or are you trying to be a little more focused? Do you try to speak back to the music or do you just try to be a little more focused on just the look?

Sometimes we’re pulling inspiration from Michael Jackson or Liberace, or another artist. But, for example, we’re in Texas right now. He just bought a ranch in Texas. It’s so beautiful. When I first started working with him and I came to the ranch, I’m like, “You are a ranch owner. You’re not larping this aesthetic. You literally live it.” I was really inspired by the saddle shop that’s nearby and all these different stores because it’s two hours away from Houston. He was already wearing [Western clothing] when I met him. This is just a different variation of it. The Western stuff is heavily in his style now, loves vests. I take what I see in his everyday life and see what we lean on more. Like even this mob boss type of thing—he’s really interested in Italian culture, and I’m Italian, so that influence comes in as well.

He has had such a long and prolific career, and he is often self-referential. Do you ever reference early moments in his career?

We did just pull back in his “FOMO” video. We did a variation of the “Hotline Bling” outfit that he wore. But we really don’t draw back too much, I think because he’s just evolved so much as a person. I’ll still send him some looks and be like, “Oh, you ate this,” [laughs]. I have met him as the person that he is now and I’m like, “Okay, he just turned 40. Let’s just be elevated and grown.”

Chxrry at Paris Fashion Week in September.

Chxrry is building something really strong. What’s it like to work with both an artist that has been working in the industry for so long while also with someone who’s so green?

Chxrry and I have become best friends in the process, so we’re just figuring it out together. We’re the same age. She’s so early in her career that I’m sure she’ll have many evolutions, but for now it’s just about having fun.

With Drake, he just loves clothes and is pretty easygoing, but there’s obviously a lot more pressure that’s involved because he’s so established. It’s very different, but equally as rewarding.

I have to ask about the birthday outfits. I thought they were great, but I’m curious if you planned a birthday weekend wardrobe or if you are more casual about it?

Well, October’s a crazy month, so there’s so much stuff going on so I did a lot of preparation. We knew that we wanted to do a beautiful suit, but we actually had three other suits that fell through before that one. Last minute, our atelier had just made that tux for him, and then I got the brooch, we put on a bow tie. It all came together at the last minute, and that Chanel scarf I had just bought that morning in New York. The Hermès shawl I bought the day before we left for the trip in Canada. Everything is really just down to what he’s feeling like that night. We can do all this preparation, but that night if he’s like, “Actually, I just feel like being more chill or I just want to do this,” we just pivot, and we always figure it out.

Drake wearing gray sweats and a vintage Chanel scarf.

A Chorme Hearts cheetah jacket and Versace red leather pants.

I like that he seems to wear only things he owns, when many celebrities wear borrowed clothing. Do you also do that, or do you prefer to just buy things?

On the record [laughs], I hate pulling. I hate loaning. I hate all of that. It gives me anxiety. I hate if it was my stuff and it was out in the world and you just never know what happens. It could get messed up in travel, and there’s just wear and tear. Things just happen. I know it’s a huge part of styling, but for me, I’d rather just source the pieces myself and have them be a part of our archive and a part of our collection.

With someone like Drake, who is so big, you want there to be an archive of what he’s done and worn, otherwise it’s all lost in brands’ sample closets. I have to ask about the memes. People had so much to say about the Hermès by Margiela. As the stylist, what do you think of that?

I love a joke. I love a joke we can laugh about, but I still love the look. I don’t feel less than or like, “Oh God, it’s a meme.” I still love the look. I think it was amazing. Even when we did “FOMO” and he was wearing that leather jacket with the fur on one side, that was a women’s Saint Laurent piece. I love when men do things that are out of the box, or that isn’t just pants and a shirt. Why not wear a fringed shawl? I was into it, but I could appreciate the joke and I did think some of them were funny.

Pumpkin Spice Papi was really funny. If anything, becoming a meme nowadays adds to the look. It’s already a Halloween costume.

Yes [laughs], I’ve seen that. I was too young, but I always think that if we had the internet the way that we do now, what would people say about Michael Jackson or what would they say about Prince? I’m sure there would be so many memes. There would have to be.

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

You mentioned the Saint Laurent women’s jacket. Something that I always really liked about Drake’s style is his willingness to just go there and have fun with fashion. There’s something really cool and really refreshing about that.

It’s really just fun and it’s really just down to what we’re both happy with. And as a man, if you’re really comfortable with yourself and comfortable, and you know who you are... He gets so many opinions projected on him all the time and he just doesn’t care. He still chooses what he likes. It doesn’t change his mind. I think it’s just because he’s so confident and comfortable with who he is. It’s really refreshing to work with somebody who’s not like, “Oh no, I can’t wear that. That’s crazy,” or whatever. If anything, he’s just like, “Oh yeah, fuck it. Let’s do it.” He’s really just excited to try new things. And even the fringe shawl, we spoke about it afterwards and he was like, “Yeah, it was sick. I loved it.” There’s nothing that can change his mind.

People may not think I’m the best [stylist] or whatever, but I like it. I don’t trust anyone else’s opinion because you’re not in my shoes, so you can’t really tell me how I should do it. Drake as a person has so much fun with his life. He had a blast for his birthday weekend. He doesn’t care about comments and neither do I. We don’t sit there and read them. We’ll give a chuckle if it’s funny or share a meme, but keep it pushing. We have fun.

#3686. Final Fantasy 7 Remake And Rebirth Are Absurdly Cheap On Switch 2 Right Now

Final Fantasy VII RebirthFinal Fantasy VII RemakeSaleSwitch 2

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade and Rebirth both came to Switch 2 earlier this year and they are currently just $8 each. That is a ridiculously low price for two very good ports of two excellent RPGs.

Rebirth is normally $50 and Remake is normally $40, but until November 17, Square Enix has made the digital versions of the Switch 2 ports available for $7.50 and $8, respectively. Why is Remake priced $0.50 higher than the newer, bigger game? I have no idea. The physical versions are both game key cards as well, so you’re not missing out on anything there.

If you own a Switch 2 and haven’t yet picked these up, I’d definitely recommend it, especially ahead of Final Fantasy VII Revelation, which will close out the trilogy when it arrives in April 2027. Both games perform decently enough on Nintendo’s newer hardware, too.

Square Enix put in a lot of work to get the gorgeous games running at a solid 30fps framerate without completely downgrading the resolution to hell, though Cloud’s spiky hair still looks way better on the other consoles.

If you already own the series on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, or PC, it’s not worth picking up extra versions for the portability factor. There’s no nifty cross-save function like with Cyberpunk 2077. But for people who only have Switch 2s, these are easy pick-ups and will probably never be cheaper.

The long wait for All’s Fair’s second season is finally almost over. The Ryan Murphy legal drama is set to return on Wednesday on the 2026 TV schedule, nearly a year after Season 1 ended. Not surprisingly, the cast is making headlines ahead of the new season, and also not surprisingly, everyone is talking about the corset dress Kim Kardashian wore to the premiere. However, can we please talk about Teyana Taylor’s fit, too?

On Monday, Hulu hosted a premiere for All’s Fair Season 2, and the fashion was absolutely on point. Kardashian, as usual, turned heads as she wore a custom Ashi Studio silver strapless corset dress with a matching silver collar, per Law Roach's Instagram. She posted the look on her Instagram Story, and I am positively obsessed:

That being said, her co-star Teyana Taylor might be giving her a run for her money. The Oscar-nominated actress has also been making waves in the world of celebrity fashion, leaving no crumbs at the BET Awards over the summer by rocking a stunning burgundy Stephanie Rolland gown. Now, once again, she proved that she’s a fashion icon at the All’s Fair premiere with a daring low-rise ensemble:

The look is from Nicholas Oakwell Couture, per Women’s Wear Daily. Between the corset sheer top, the large bow over the black pants, and the bolero jacket, the entire ensemble is incredible. You never know what you’re going to get when it comes to Taylor, and she definitely made that point clear with this look. Of course, Kardashian looked great as well; however, the One Battle After Another actress definitely has my vote for best dressed.

However, I have to say that Kardashian and Taylor’s friendship makes this pair of outfits even better. The Rip actress previously opened up about her friendship with the reality star, pointing out that they were already friends before All's Fair. However, she said that doing this series together “really brought [them] closer.” She continued, “We really went into the show friends and finished out the show as sisters.”

Now, fans will be seeing more of that friendship in the upcoming second season of All’s Fair. Kardashian will return as Allura Grant, while Taylor will once again be playing Milan in the Hulu hit. In the new season, there will be plenty more scandals, secrets, and stilettos, as new allegiances are formed, friendships are tested, and a “shocking revelation threatens the very existence” of Grant, Ronson & Greene.

Meanwhile, since All’s Fair has pulled off some incredible fashion in the show, it’s understandable that the cast would want to do the same IRL. Now, I need Teyana Taylor to do another red carpet, because I can only imagine what she and her stylists have planned next. And the same goes for Kim K.

Now, to see the two women in All's Fair, you can stream Season 2 this Wednesday, November 4, with a Hulu subscription.

#3684. Why Your Smartwatch Size Really Does Matter

“Is my watch too big?” is a constant question on forums dedicated to smartwatches and fitness trackers of all kinds. (Some, but fewer, wonder if their watch is too small.) Personally, I don’t much care how a watch looks, but I’ve noticed that size can make a big difference in how accurately a watch functions. If your watch is too big, your numbers may be off.

Watches measure heart rate through an optical sensor on the back of the watch. (That’s what you see glowing green back there.) The heart rate sensor detects how that light reflects off the blood vessels in your skin. To get a proper reading, it needs to be snug against your skin, ideally in a way that blocks out ambient light.

If the sensor loses contact with your skin, or if too much light sneaks in, heart rate readings may be inaccurate. If a watch fits you well to start with, you can generally get an accurate heart rate by simply making sure the watch is snug during workouts.

But if a watch is too big, it can move around, letting light in. When you run, if a watch is bouncing around, the sensor may detect a flash of light with every footstep. This can lead to your watch reporting a heart rate that is the same as your cadence (footsteps per minute), which is sometimes called “cadence lock.” Some runners will cover their watch with a sleeve (especially in cold weather) to minimize this possibility.

No matter how you wear it, a big watch on a small wrist is likely to have a lot more difficulty than one that fits properly. Very small devices can have a similar problem: The device isn’t large enough or can’t be tightened enough to block light. This isn’t usually a problem with wristwatches, but it may explain why smart rings tend to be so poor at daytime heart rate tracking.

Now, is this a real-life concern, or just a theoretical quibble? I wasn’t sure, until I took the Forerunner 265 and 265S for a run at the same time. These are the same watch, with the same heart rate sensor, differing only in size. You can read about my results here, but the graph tells the story pretty well: The smaller 265S (42 mm) captured my heart rate more accurately than the 265 (46 mm).

If heart rate accuracy were the only issue, I would tell you to get the smallest watch you can find. It wouldn’t even look weird; before smartwatches became popular, wristwatches were often much smaller than a person’s wrist. (Watch old movies and you’ll see some tiny watches, even on people who don’t have tiny wrists.)

But watches are big and seem to be getting bigger. A bigger screen means numbers, text, and icons are easier to read. This is great news if your vision isn’t the best anymore, or if you use the watch while exercising and want to be able to see what’s on your screen with a quick glance.

Bigger watches can provide bigger screens, but also bigger batteries and more room for other internals. This is probably at least partly why more “premium” watches come in bigger sizes. That said, it’s hard for me to distinguish when a watch is huge because it needs room to pack in its hardware features, versus when the company is making the watch bigger so it will seem fancier and thus justify a higher price.

And this brings me to something I need to rant about. Smartwatch and fitness watch companies know that watch size matters: They often offer two sizes for at least some of their models. The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in 42 or 46 millimeters, while the Garmin Forerunner 570 comes in 42 or 47 millimeters, to give a couple of examples.

But when it comes to premium models, those options often disappear. The Garmin Forerunner 970, far more feature-rich than the 570, only comes in a 47-millimeter size, matching the larger size of the 570 but without a smaller option. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only comes in a 49-millimeter size, which is even larger than the larger size of the Series 12. I’m about to start testing a Hyrox feature that only comes on Amazfit’s Balance 3 or Balance Ultra watches; those watches are 51 and 52 millimeters, respectively. This is getting ridiculous.

As a woman reporting on tech, I can’t ignore the way gender plays into this. According to ANSUR II, a U.S. Army study, women have an average wrist size of 154 millimeters (about 6.1 inches), and men have an average wrist size of 176 mm (about 6.9 inches). My wrists are right around 6 inches, making me very average for a woman.

When companies make two sizes of watch, the smaller size usually fits the average woman’s wrist fairly well, and the larger size is a better fit for men’s wrists. This isn’t a perfect match, of course, since plenty of women may fit or prefer the larger size, and vice versa. I’m glad the companies market these as “small” and “large” or just by the numerical size.

But as a person with six-inch wrists, I can’t wear a large watch without dealing with bouncing, rubbing, and potentially inaccurate data. I’m no twig; I’m perfectly average for my half of the population. But those larger watches just aren’t going to be as accurate for me as they are for the average man. I noticed a similar phenomenon when I tested the heart rate tracking in Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds: They barely worked for me, but did fine when I tried them on a man with larger ears.

There's also an uncomfortable intersection between this gender dynamic and the way watch companies use size as a signifier of how fancy a watch is supposed to be. While Garmin only offers the 970 in a large size (47 mm), they only offer the cheaper 70 and 170 in smaller sizes (both 43 mm). Garmin’s Venu 4 comes in both 41 and 45 millimeter sizes, but the cheaper Vivoactive 6 is only available in 42. Having a small wrist can save you money, but it still shuts you off from some of the more premium options out there.

For my work reviewing and testing watches for Lifehacker, I’ve worn smartwatches ranging from around 40 millimeters (an older Apple Watch) up to 48 millimeters (a tie between the Kospet Tank and the Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro). I love a watch in the 40-42 millimeter range; I can tolerate one around 46 millimeters if it’s lightweight enough that it doesn’t bounce too much; and I really have a hard time with anything larger.

Those bigger watches are hard to snug up sufficiently for a workout; get them tight enough not to bounce, and they’ll feel like you’re nearly cutting off your circulation. After a long run with a big, heavy watch, I’ve sometimes gotten red, irritated spots on my wrist from the inevitable friction. You may not be able to judge how badly a watch will fit when it's still in the box, but I do have a rule of thumb for when you try it on.

To judge visually, I find it helps to put a watch on your wrist, rest your arm on a table, and look directly down at it. If the lugs of the watch extend past your wrist, it’s too big. You want the watch to fit on your wrist, not overhang the sides.

And if you prefer a watch size that isn’t going to be the most accurate for heart rate, remember that you can always pair a chest strap to a watch that supports it, or to your phone if you don’t have a compatible watch. If you prefer a larger watch for more readable text or maps, or if you want a premium feature that doesn’t come in smaller sizes, a chest strap may be the way to get the best of both worlds.

#3683. Devs Are Blaming A Flood Of AI Slop On Steam For Delaying Their Games

November is, to put it lightly, nuts for video games. World of Warcraft: Forever launches tomorrow. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be out just a few hours after that. And a short two weeks after that, the juggernaut arrives: GTA 6. So as you might imagine, dozens of indie games are trying to get their releases out now, before these heavy hitters show up and suck all the air out of the room, monopolizing the time of content creators and players who might otherwise pay attention to smaller projects. But the folks behind a lot of those indie games are now worried they might be forced to launch right in the middle of that AAA maelstrom, thanks to what they believe to be a major bottleneck going on internally at Valve; one they think is caused by a flood of AI slop games.

Throughout October, multiple indies have posted on social media suggesting that their approvals process on Steam was taking longer than usual. Normally, Valve says it expects a 3-5 day waiting period when a developer submits a game for approval to appear on the Steam store. Valve then might get back to the developer with any issues it has, and it’s another few days to review again. Once Valve considers any such issues resolved, the game can then be published on the storefront. For all this, Valve specifically advises developers, “you’ll want to submit your page for review at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”

Except recently, seven business days hasn’t cut it. Throughout October, a number of indie developers have posted on social platforms sharing that their reviews are taking two or three weeks or more to complete for no discernible reason.

There’s Caravarn Carnage: Fruity Road, for instance, which finally made it through Steam approvals on November 1 after submitting on October 16:

Hi @Steamworks, my games build has been stuck in review since October 16, beyond the usual 3-5 business days. I've contacted support but haven't received an update on the build review.

Ashen Legacy submitted on October 15, and was finally approved on November 1, coming in hot ahead of a planned November 6 release date:

Oh my god! My first submission was rejected, and Iâve already had to wait over two weeks. The scariest thing right now isnât the threat of AI-generated game clonesâitâs the wait for Steamâs review process. Itâs a race to see whose game gets approved first, and with my scheduledâ¦ pic.twitter.com/rgbgwK8PVE

— Ashen Legacy | Wishlist on Steam (@VerStudiovn) October 31, 2026

Lacey’s Flash Games was recently forced into a delay; it finally came out on Halloween, four days late:

And Wheel Make It was forced to launch three weeks late:

Wheel Make It has been unintentionally delayed while we're waiting on @Steam's approval.

The game was submitted for review 2 weeks ago, and was rejected because they couldn't figure out how to access local co-op (you literally just share a keyboard…)

The re-review has beenâ¦ pic.twitter.com/jLvB6QHZvK

— 2 Left Thumbs (@2_left_thumbs) October 12, 2026

Here’s a statement from Mira, one of the developers of the similarly-in-limbo Cubic Earth, provided to Kotaku:

We’re a small team, and we’ve spent a long time building up to getting our debut Early Access title, Cubic Earth, out into the world. Having it derailed last minute has been incredibly disheartening. Despite our best effort to follow Valve’s established processes and adherence to their stated timelines, our game now has no known launch window.

We’ve received a number of player complaints and questions across the Steam Community and YouTube, wondering why the game did not launch at the stated time. To make matters worse, organic traffic to our store page from Steam features has dropped off completely, and what was shaping up to be a promising Early Access launch now feels more like an anxiety inducing nightmare.

We’re hoping that this can be resolved as painlessly as possible, and trying to keep our eyes on the future!

Earlier today, I spoke at length to another impacted developer: Alfred Kamon, director of Studio Daimon, which is making Food Devils. Food Devils was supposed to launch today. It won’t be doing that, though, because it’s still awaiting Steam approval after being submitted way back on October 12.

Kamon says he first started to wonder if something was wrong about a week after the submission, with Valve still silent. On October 24, he followed Steam’s published advice for what to do if response was too slow: he submitted a support ticket. On the 26th, Valve responded with a concern about sexual content in the game, to which Kamon immediately replied in an attempt to resolve the issue. Now, seven days after that, he’s still waiting for a reply. Valve also responded to his support ticket, essentially telling him to wait for the review team to get back to him. (Kotaku has seen all of these messages between Kamon and Valve).

Kamon tells me that from his perspective, Studio Daimon did everything right in order to launch on time. Even with Valve having an issue with content, he says that in the past such problems have only taken 2-3 days to resolve, and he had prepared for that. He had not prepared for three weeks of waiting…and counting. He can’t even provide full game keys to reviewers until approvals are done (beta keys can and have gone out).

“Just before the release, everyone is crunching a lot just to finish everything, to do QA, to polish and to prepare all the content,” he said. “So everyone in the team maybe even stayed up late or even during weekends. It was very, very hard. And despite everything, I think it’s sad because everyone made so many sacrifices to be here now today, and we still couldn’t make it.”

What’s really ironic is that Food Devils‘ original release date was actually supposed to be November 5, but 24 hours before the team planned to announce it, Ocarina of Time planted its flag that same day. So the team moved it up. “Oh, no, we are not releasing on the same day as Zelda,” Kamon said. Of course, now there’s a solid chance they might.

I asked Kamon if it made sense to hold the game even longer, maybe into early December. After all, following Ocarina of Time is GTA 6. It’s a terrible month to release a small indie game, and Food Devils was originally getting in just barely under the wire. But Kamon tells me that’s not an option.

Studio Daimon is a small studio: just nine people, based in Italy, working on Food Devils for the last four years. It’s made one other game before, Path of the Midnight Sun, and it’s not exactly rolling in cash. Kamon tells me that the studio really needs the money from sales of Food Devils before the end of the year, and Steam pays out on a one-month delay. If Food Devils can’t launch soon, the studio might be in trouble financially.

Why is all this happening? We reached out to the company for comment and were directed to a blog post from today about the situation. In it, Valve acknowledges that it has seen “a significant increase in submissions for store page and build review in recent months,” noting later that the process is taking “up to 12 business days.” It goes on to say that most of that time is spent re-reviewing games that have issues at submission, and that in addition to adjusting its internal processes to help match the heavier load, Valve is also adding a number of items to its release checklist for developers that it says will help cut down on the number of submissions it needs to send back for adjustments.

What the blog post doesn’t mention is the role of generative AI, which many developers are theorizing is playing an outsized role in the massive wave of submissions. As of mid-October, more games have been released on Steam in 2026 than in all of 2025, with two and a half months to go. And in October alone, around 4,000 games were released on the platform, with nearly 50 percent of them disclosing some use of generative AI in development. That’s a lot of games coming through very, very fast, the speed aided by the ability of generative AI to churn out game-shaped things quickly. Developers suspect that, given these numbers, Valve is struggling to keep up with the sudden influx of submissions, and smaller studios without the clout to ask Valve to expedite their games are suffering for it. But without more specific word from Valve, no one can prove that’s what’s really happening.

The thing is, ValveÂ hasÂ acknowledged that the platform has some issue with AI slop. It finally made a statement last week, after over 8,000 demos flooded Steam Next Fest last month, alongside a report that a developer was extorted by someone threatening to make an AI clone of their project, as well as several developers admitting publicly that they hesitated to release game demos for fear of having their games cloned. But that statement was just that people at Valve didn’t want to be “gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

Valve’s Marc Wilkinson also said, “We are fully aware of the situation, and a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve this problem.” But as much as one might appreciate how difficult it may be to figure out how to regulate AI, at the moment, a number of developers are actively suffering with no clear path to relief.

At this point, all Kamon wants is for Food Devils to be approved as soon as possible. He did say it would be nice to get some increased visibility on Steam to make up for this situation, since his release plans have now been all messed up through no fault of his own. And he wishes Valve would be transparent about how long the review process will take.

“I can also sympathize with those who have to review all these games,” he says. “But as a dev, at least I would like some honesty in the UI when you submit a game. Tell us it may take weeks. Just don’t promise us three to five days because then we make plans around the release date. We create hype. We announce everything. People are happy that the game is releasing and in the end, it doesn’t.”

#3682. 10 Hacks Ever Siri AI User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

If you're like me, you've spent years ignoring most of Siri's functionality. Sure, it's great for setting timers, making calls, and sending a text. But that's kind of it—Apple's promise of an "always-on" digital assistant never truly delivered.

But that's finally changed with the recent launch of Siri AI. Fifteen years after debuting the app on the iPhone 4S and four years after the release of ChatGPT, Apple has taken the time to build out its own private Apple Foundation Models (with little help from Google) that work both on-device and on Apple's servers to give quick responses to your queries. Siri AI's answers are short, to the point, and actually useful. However, the conversational side isn't the only new thing about Siri AI. In fact, once you scratch the surface, you'll find Siri AI features embedded across the entire iOS and macOS ecosystem. Here's how to get the most out of Apple's new, enhanced digital assistant.

Siri AI is already tuned for brevity. Compared to Gemini or Claude, its responses are short and to the point. But still, if you ask something with your voice, it responds using voice as well. I personally prefer to quickly read through Siri responses. If you’re like me, you can enable a hidden setting that makes sure that Siri always answers silently, no matter if you’re writing to it or using your voice. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and switch to the Silent Response option.

On the other hand, if you prefer to listen to Siri's responses, it's worth it to spend some time fine-tuning them. If you have an iPhone that’s under two years old, you have access to a more expressive Siri voice. Siri AI has an Expressive Voice feature that works on iPhone 17 Pro and higher, iPhone Air, and Macs with an M3 processor or higher (at least 12GB RAM).

To find this feature, go to Settings > Siri > Voice. Here, you can change the Pace to make Siri faster or slower. The big feature is the Expressivity slider; you can use it to make Siri sound brighter and more enthusiastic, rather than flat. You also have several voice options at the top (color-coded).

Visual Intelligence is deeply integrated into iOS 27 and macOS 27, and it turns anything on your screen into a source that Siri AI can act upon. It can search anything on your screen, and even take action on things it finds out. You can highlight any text on an iPhone, tap and hold, and choose the Ask Siri option. On the Mac, Ask Siri is the first option in the right-click menu. Choose a file, select text, and get started talking to Siri.

But it goes further. Just pull up Siri AI on your iPhone or Mac and start asking questions about what you’re seeing on screen. If you’re seeing a photo of a cafe on Instagram, ask where it is, or ask Siri to open it in Maps. If you’re watching a scene from a movie or a TV show, ask Siri where it’s from.

Clean Up was part of Apple Intelligence features in iOS 18, but it wasn’t great. It used on-device models to remove objects, and the results were lacking. Now that Apple runs its own Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute, it can securely process images on its servers, and the Clean Up process is much better. It now removes objects from photos very reliably, and even accounts for shadows. But to use this, you have to make sure to use the High Quality feature (instead of the default Auto mode).

Tap the Edit button in a photo, go to Tools > Clean Up, and from the top, switch to the High Quality option. Now brush over or tap an object you want to remove. Then, tap Clean Up and wait for a while until Apple’s servers complete the process. Tap Done to save the changes.

One of the most tedious parts of using the Calendar app is manually entering multiple events from a complicated schedule—say, for a season's worth of your kid’s soccer practices, or your college course's weekly lecture schedule. With Visual Intelligence in iOS 27, this is now table stakes: You can point your iPhone camera towards a schedule or take a screenshot of one, then tap the Add to Calendar button. Siri will recognize all the events, and you’ll get an option to add them to the calendar individually or all at once.

Siri AI's Mail integration is a hidden gem. Once your iPhone or Mac is done indexing your local data from Mail, you can use Siri AI to triage and manage your Mail without even opening the Mail app. In my testing, it works really well, especially because Siri AI understands the context of an email. This means you don't need to remember the exact details about the sender or the subject. You can just ask something like, "Find all emails about my flights from last week and send them to my accountant." You can also ask it to do things for you. For example, you can say, "Archive all the emails from Walmart from last month," and it will give you a one-button option to do just that.

When you start using the new Siri AI more often, you'll realize that it asks for confirmation way too often. For things like deleting mail, that's useful. But for sending messages, less so. There is a hidden setting that removes the extra step when it comes to sending messages via Siri. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and enable Automatically Send Messages.

After the Siri AI upgrade in iOS 27, I find myself using the Camera Control often, and you should try it too. Just press and hold the Camera Control button to launch the camera's Siri mode. Point towards anything you want to find out more about and tap the big Siri icon. In a second or two, you will get the Siri response at the top, along with relevant actions based on what you're looking at. This feature is genuinely useful, and if you don't like using the Camera Control (or don't have access to it on your iPhone), you can also add the Siri AI shortcut to the lock screen, Control Center, or the Action button.

While Shortcuts has been one of Apple's most powerful features, it's also one of the hardest to use. Making an automation requires setting up steps, selecting variables, and thinking about chronology, and more. With Siri AI, Apple is trying to reduce that burden. And when it comes to simpler stuff that an everyday iPhone user needs, it works.

For example, you can open Shortcuts, create a new shortcut, and use the Describe a shortcut feature to talk about a Shortcut you want to build in natural language. You can ask Siri to create a daily morning Shortcut that shows you the day's weather, upcoming calendar events, and the to-do list for the day. You can also ask it to create a Shortcut that converts images in batches and creates new notes with a pre-made template.

While Apple is now using its own Apple Foundation Models for the new Siri AI, ChatGPT isn’t technically gone. If you have a complex question, or if Siri AI’s answer isn’t doing the trick, you can still summon ChatGPT from the Siri AI app (no need to go to the ChatGPT app for this). Tap on the text field in the Siri app, choose the Ask option and then switch to the ChatGPT service. Siri AI is quite intelligent at routing, so if ChatGPT can’t answer, it will route you back to Siri AI’s own models.

#3681. Game Pass Is About To Get One Of My Favorite Minimalist Strategy Games

The first wave of Xbox Game Pass additions for November 2026 has been revealed, and there are a whopping 12 games joining the Ultimate tier of the Netflix-like subscription service for the first time. It’s hard to choose a headliner, so I’ll highlight one of my favorite minimalist strategy games of the past few years: Thronefall.

Imagine what you love about a 2D medieval management sim like Kingdom Two Crowns, apply it to a top-down map, and add a lot more combat. You control a general who spends money on various buildings to generate resources and troops. Each round, you face a wave of enemies and then pick up the pieces once the sun rises again. It reduces the economy balancing and army micro-ing of a regular RTS down into its most basic but sublime elements. The graphics and music are excellent too.

Hereâs everything joining Xbox Game Pass in wave 1 for November 2026:

Other games you should have on your radar are Void/Breaker, a new FPS roguelite with destructible environments that’s been getting some decent reviews. There’s also Warhammer Survivors, the upcoming Warhammer-themed spin on everyone’s favorite bullet heaven auto-shooter. John Carpenterâs Toxic Commando is decent enough for fans of the horde shooter genre, and if you had kids and took them to see the Paw Patrol dinosaur movie this summer, you’re in luck: Paw Patrol: Dino World is now free to play with Game Pass.Â

Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 and Wreckfest are both leaving on November 15. Winter Burrow, a cozy survival game and a favorite in my household, will also be gone. But there’s still time to finish 1000xResist, a 2024 sci-fi visual novel that was one of that year’s best games.
