#3680. Darializa Avila Chevalier Explains the DSA

In June, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic nominee for Congress in the 13th District of New York, burst onto the national stage when she won her primary against five-term incumbent Representative Adriano Espaillat. Along with several other candidates this cycle, Chevalier became emblematic of a new swell of progressivism in America. Almost immediately, she came under fire for inflammatory posts she had made on the internet—about defunding the police, abolishing prisons, and Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. She has what many would characterize as some pretty radical views.

Chevalier comes from the world of academia—she’s a PhD candidate, a longtime grassroots organizer, and a member of the New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. But we don’t live in a theoretical world, and it seems to me that ideological purism often gets in the way of getting real things done. So, ahead of next week’s midterms, I wanted to know whether she stands by some of her most divisive statements and how she plans to govern once the race is over and she (presumably) takes office. And I really wanted to know who Chevalier is as a person. I sat down with her on October 26 for a conversation about how she views protests, being recruited to run for office, being compared to AOC, why President Donald Trump likes Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and more.

Mark Guiducci: Candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, welcome to the show.

Darializa Avila Chevalier: Thanks so much for having me.

Thanks for being here. Darializa, you are the Democratic candidate and presumptive winner for Congress in the 13th District of New York. You’re also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, one of many candidates this election cycle who represents a swelling progressive movement. Your national profile is growing.

You were photographed by Annie Leibovitz for our New Establishment Issue, and today I wanna talk to you about how you situate yourself in the political landscape and the leftist surge that we’re seeing right now. And I also wanna talk to you about you. So let’s start a little bit with your background.

New York is your home now, of course, but you were born in Florida and briefly lived in the Dominican Republic and in Venezuela before settling in Tallahassee, I think, as a teenager. And, you know, looking back at your childhood, I wanna know, what was the moment that you had your first political inkling?

Yeah. I mean, I moved around so much as a kid—not only around all those different places, but also within those different places, right? Because my mom was a working-class single mom. My dad wasn’t very involved, but he was also very working-class and, you know, he’s a truck driver. My mom’s a caseworker, worked multiple jobs, and it was not always easy.

And I think my first moment where I realized, Oh, we’re, like, very working-class, if not working-poor, was when I was driving to school with my mom one morning and we had to stop for gas, and my mom said to me, “Crouch down and look for coins,” because we weren’t sure whether we had enough to get gas to get to school.

And we crouched down; I think we barely got to a dollar, and I went into the, the gas station and I gave the man at the counter the dollar, and he looked at me, looked at my mom—who was waiting and looking into the gas station, watching me—and looked back down and said, “I put $5 on the pump.” And I think that was the first time, and I was small. I was still in elementary school at this point that I realized, Oh, this is not something that people normally experience, right? And we were literally relying on the kindness of a stranger that day.

When would you say that you were able to start putting language to that? You know, a five-year-old or a six-year-old probably doesn’t know that they’re working-class.

They know the situation, they know the emotions, but when were you able to start putting the language to it? ’Cause I think that’s an important piece to the politics, you know?

Yeah, I think, you know, as I got older, I was definitely aware that class was a thing.

I think I didn’t call it class, right, until I started reading more about, you know, people’s experiences. I think even in our society, we confuse what working-class means often, right? And we think about ourselves; everyone wants to be middle-class, right? And even folks who are really struggling, like they’re one paycheck away from losing everything, seeing themselves as middle-class [is] a point of dignity, right?

No one wants to see themselves as struggling so much that they could lose everything, but that is the reality for most Americans in this country. And once I was reading more, you know, just progressive, leftist, socialist literature, right, that was talking about these things in a very concrete way and giving language to it—I was reading folks like Baldwin and Du Bois and Angela Davis, right?

And they were really talking about these experiences in ways that really resonated.

Yeah, high school I was reading Baldwin; I was reading, you know, more class-conscious literature. And college, I guess, it was really where, like, things started to get a concrete definition for me, right?

I realized I just really wanted language for my experience, for the experience of my community, and, you know, I really felt really immersed in that world of literature and theory.

So you went to college at Columbia. You’re a New York transplant. How do you think your experience as a non-native New Yorker—I also didn’t grow up here—how do you think it influences your relationship to the city that you’re about to represent?

Yeah, I mean, I love the city so much because it made me the woman that I am. You know, I came and I was 18, but I also grew up coming here often because my mom’s side of the family was here, and New York always felt like the place where I could be all parts of myself. And having lived here since I was, you know, a teenager and 18 and growing into myself, I learned that I love organizing here, right?

I became politically active, and I became active in my community here. And, you know, if you ask me where my roots are, it’s here at this point, because this is where most of the people I love are.

I understand that. I moved here the day after college, and—

I get it. You were just saying your organizing started here.

And that really started when you were an undergraduate at Columbia as part of the Students for Justice in Palestine. I’m curious what you thought that movement was missing when you came across it and what you thought you could bring to it.

Yeah. Well, I actually started organizing earlier than that.

I was—well, in college, but before I joined Students for Justice in Palestine. I was organizing around ending sexual violence on campus. Emma Sulkowicz’s name is coming up a lot now because of the case at Cornell, but I was at school at the same time as her. And this was something that we, on campus, were really starting to build around and organize around to get the university to make meaningful change.

And I think, you know, unfortunately, clearly from what we’ve seen in the last few months, a lot has not changed on college campuses for a lot of people. But that was the work that we were already doing. And I was also organizing with the Black Students Organization, which takes its name because it was an organizing organization, whereas, you know, at other universities, it’s usually the Black Student Union.

We were actually invested in organizing Black students on our campus. And I joined SJP after having gone to Palestine. I’d spent a summer there in the West Bank. And having firsthand experience for, you know, just witnessing the apartheid system there, and—

That was 2014. And I was there as tensions were rising in the West Bank.

And the day after, or within a few days of getting home to the US, you know, Israel began bombing Gaza, and it was a very dark experience. I don’t have another word for it. I just felt so disempowered to be at home scrolling through the names and images of the people who had been slaughtered in Gaza, and people who look so much like the people I had just left behind in the West Bank.

And I think that was where I first started to really take an interest in the notion of power.

Because I’d never felt so powerless in my life.

You attended the pro-Palestine rally on October 8, 2023. What was your thinking in attending that event, and how do you think about it now? Do you regret that?

You know, I have always believed that protests are about power. Again, like, I think power itself is a morally neutral thing. It is about whether or not you can change the conditions around you, right? And so empowering communities to be able to change those circumstances is something I think about all the time.

Like, what are the conditions that you’re thinking, That’s the day to go?

Yes, and so, you know, as someone who’s an American citizen, as someone who pays my taxpayer money, the thing that I have power over in this cycle of violence is where my government uses my tax dollar in this cycle, and the party that we pay our tax dollars to and that we support and arm is the Israeli government, right?

And, you know, are there folks who say things you disagree with at any protest? Yes, of course. The same is true for many elected officials who attended the Israel Day Parade with Israeli officials who have openly called for the genocide of Palestinians, right? And I would hope that they have vehemently disavowed that, right?

But when it comes to advocating for the human rights and human dignity of Palestinians, there seems to be a double standard, right? Where we can’t express our outrage at our tax dollars being used in a way that denies people their human rights and their dignity, particularly when so many people in our communities are being denied those resources, right? Whether it’s in funding schools, whether it’s in addressing childhood poverty.

And I really deeply believe that we are responsible for having a power analysis when we engage in any kind of protest, right?

I think the people that you mentioned, especially public officials, should have to answer the question that you just posed to them.

But specifically on the October 8, you would do it—like, you would go back again on October 8, 2023, to that protest?

I would, because that same day, what I was thinking about was my experience in 2014, where I had sat in my bed and felt powerless, right? And knew in 2023 what was coming was Israel’s response would lead to more and more death.

And that same day, hundreds of people had already been killed, right, in Gaza. And to me, when we mourn human life, we have to mourn human life and prevent more loss of life.

I’m thinking about, on October 7, 2023, people who have done Birthright trips to Israel or have visited in some way and are scrolling through faces and names of people they knew. How do you feel your experience differs from theirs?

I think where, again, asking a question of, where are we positioned to interrupt cycles of violence? I think losing someone you care about is something that, universally, we can all empathize with, right? It is something that is tragic and heartbreaking and is hard to wrap our heads around. If in that moment I could’ve called up the president to yell at Netanyahu, to tell him to stop dropping the bombs, or if I could have, you know, called whoever at any point in the cycle of violence, of course you’d wanna do that.

That’s not a power I have. The power I have is to organize my community into creating that societal shift.

But do you see how those experiences are similar?

Again, the experience of losing somebody, I think that is a universal, like, experience of loss and trauma and pain and grief. Where I see things are different is, again, around a question of power.

Do you have the power to create a world where there is less grief, right? And I think if we look at things institutionally, our government currently is investing in continuing grief for a certain group of people.

Today you are no longer just an organizer. You are poised to be an elected official. When you were younger, did you ever think that you’d be running for office?

Can you describe the moment that you decided to run?

I was recruited to run by Justice Democrats, and I—you know, it’s an organization that takes community nominations, and they told me that someone from the community had nominated me, and that they had spoken to other members of the community and really were excited about this idea.

And I was like, All right, well, I’m just gonna take some time to think about it, ’cause this wasn’t something that I’d thought to do. And I had many conversations with other organizers, with members of my community, with folks who I was like, Oh, they’ll definitely tell me this is a bad idea. And to my surprise, everyone was like, “No, this is a great idea, but it really is up to you.”

This is the same organization that found AOC. How did they find you, and how did you start that relationship?

Yeah, I mean, I’ve been organizing for a really, really long time. And we actually had spoken with them about running somebody else, and a few months later, I get an email, and they told me that folks had reached out to them about me.

And the first question I asked was, “Why me?” And I was like, “And do you know—”

Well, I was like, “And do you know that, like, I have been very vocal,” right, “on a lot of issues?” And they said that’s why. Because they really just wanted someone who felt firm in their convictions and on their view of what this country can and should be for working people across this country.

And I had to really sit with that because it was not an easy decision to make, and so that’s why it took me so long to give them a yes.

How did you win? Because beyond grassroots organizing, moving out an incumbent like Adriano Espaillat in Harlem is no mean feat.

In the clearest possible terms, how do you think you did it?

And it was bringing groups together and building a coalition that knocked over 155,000 doors, that talked to their neighbors even when it was not an easy conversation. And it was, you know, organizing all of the members of our coalition into this larger vision, because not everyone was sold at first.

You have been using this word organizing. What is organizing?

So organizing is coming together with others in your community or who share your same understanding of what the problem is, right? And coming together to address that issue. It is about fundamentally shifting power away from the concentrated few toward the many, right?

So when we think about, for example, housing organizing or tenant organizing, right?

It is about tenants coming together, right, to build power among themselves to change the conditions in their building, whether that is because the tiles on the floor are actually dangerous for the grandma who might trip on them, right?

Or the leaks that are making it so that you are having to endure black mold and just deeply undignified conditions.

And coming together to build the power to have these repairs actually happen.

What does that look like on the day-to-day? Like, what are some things that I might not understand is organizing that you—you know, things that you did in your campaign that I might not understand as organizing, but that were effective?

I think a lot of people, they think there’s, like, this wow or flashy thing that happens in organizing that is what makes it like all of a sudden the power has shifted, but really, it is deeply unsexy work. It is the boring phone calls. It is the meetings that could’ve been an email.

It is the thing that, you know, just brings people together and [makes them] feel connected on a human level to build the trust necessary to move toward something else.

And what’s the role of the DSA in that? In that organizing and in that coalition, how did the DSA influence, impact, your race specifically?

Yeah. Well, I mean, DSA is such an incredible organization.

It is a member-based organization, so if you’re part of the DSA, it’s because you love organizing and you love being in that work, and you share this vision of a socialist, or democratic socialist, country. And once they were excited about this race, right, we knew we could win because we all of a sudden had an army of folks who were ready to knock on doors, were ready to talk about a politic that works for working people.

When you say “they” about the DSA, who’s they? I mean, because is it, like, Megan Romer, the co-chair of the national chapter? Is this the mayor?

Well, I’m a member of the New York City chapter of DSA, which is, you know, affiliated but separate from the national DSA. And I think maybe we take a step back and explain what DSA even is.

That’s perfect. Yes. Let’s do that. I had Ta-Nehisi Coates in this chair a few weeks ago, and the conversation went there, and even he was asking, “What is the DSA?”

Well, to Comrade Coates, I can explain that a little bit more.

It is a member-based organization that is focused on building people power in a democratic way.

And so if you share the values of a socialist, which, to us, is making sure that the wealth that working people produce is also wealth that working people can benefit from and enjoy in our society, then, you know, you can come organize with us to make sure that we’re building that world. And when I talk about socialism, I think sometimes people get stuck in the theory of it and don’t understand what that concretely means.

Sure. It’s a tough brand in America sometimes.

Yeah. And I think most of the most popular policies we’ve ever had in this country’s history, including now, are themselves socialist policies. So thinking, for example, of Social Security or Medicare, right? These are incredibly popular policies, to the point where we’re always fighting to defend them, right?

And we should be fighting to expand them. We should be fighting for more socialist policies that make the lives of working people better.

It is not a party. It is an organization.

I mean, many of us are members or are part of the Democratic Party, right? We’re registered as Democrats, but it is—

Yes. And I’m the Democratic nominee. But the DSA is just an organization. It is an organizing organization, right? And organizing, again, is really about shifting power away from a concentrated few toward the many.

The national chapter of the DSA has a published platform that includes aims like abolishing the presidency—

Abolishing the Senate, replacing the Supreme Court, open borders. How do you—do you agree with that? Or how do you address that with people who read that and are frightened?

Mm-hmm. I mean, again, I’m a member of the New York City chapter.

There are some of those things that I really just don’t agree with, like I don’t agree with abolishing the presidency, for example. But I do think that the beautiful thing about DSA is that it is truly a democratic organization. So as a New York City chapter member, right, I can participate in all of the democratic decisions that happen within our chapter.

And anytime we make a decision as a chapter, we are voting on it, right? And the beautiful thing is, if you have an idea for how to shift politics or policies to work for working people, inside the chapter, you can introduce that, right? You can introduce a resolution. And so—

So what I’m hearing is that it’s not—it’s more of an approach.

It’s not one specific policy or goal in mind, or even one specific worldview; that it’s flexible depending on—

Yeah. I mean, there is a huge diversity of thought within DSA, right? And even between national and the New York City chapter, there’s diversity. There’s, like, sometimes disagreement, right?

And that is what democracy is, right? And I think democracy is a practice, it’s an exercise, and it’s something we have to do often, right?

You have often been compared to AOC, also a New York DSA member. You’ve been called the next AOC; AOC but to the left. She recently endorsed you. What’s your relationship like?

It’s a positive relationship. She is someone who has really laid a path for so many people to be able to come into Congress as a working person. And, you know, I have a lot of respect for the congresswoman, and I’m really excited to see what she might do next.

What do you think are the key differences between the two of you?

Yeah. And, again, I think I’m my own person, right? So—

I think, as someone who comes from a different area of organizing but largely agrees with, you know, the vision that she came into Congress with, I think it’s exciting to be able to come in with a new perspective of where we can grow things even further, right?

President Trump has been recently praising AOC. He said—sort of begrudgingly, he said he doesn’t mind her so much, which is funny coming from the leader of the MAGA movement. And, of course, Mayor Mamdani and Trump have had very public meetings, cordial meetings at the White House and then Gracie Mansion.

I am also very fascinated by this. And I think part of it is that he’s a New Yorker, right? And I think that’s something for New Yorkers to also contend with, right? But I think he just also is someone who understands popularity, right? And I don’t mean popularity as like—

Yeah, he likes a winner, and I think he likes it when people are actually willing to stand on what they believe and not just, you know, kiss up to him.

Who do you think gets more from that relationship, him or them? That’s interesting. Specifically Mamdani.

You know, I think it has been really fascinating to watch the way that they’re cognizant of the power disparity.

He’s the president of the United States. That is just the political reality, unfortunately, for all of us, right? But to watch, you know, the mayor and to watch the congresswoman in the way that they interact and really move strategically to make sure that New Yorkers benefit from every interaction that they have with the president has been…

Honestly, I’m taking notes. Because I’m like, eventually, right, that will be something that I’ll have to do.

Yeah. It makes me think of something else too, which is, like, you know, so much of campaigning, certainly organizing, is about principles and ideology, and there’s a purity to that.

When you’re governing, you have to work with people, whether it’s centrist Democrats or even Republicans, and that often means compromise. How do you think about that? Are you prepared to compromise, or do you sort of—are you prepared to compromise?

I think that juxtaposition is funny and interesting because, even in a campaign, you’re organizing with people who you might not always agree with on everything, and that doesn’t mean that you compromise your ideology, that you compromise your vision of the world, that you compromise your principles, right?

I deeply believe that we have to be uncompromising in our principles and willing to move on strategy. Because if we are set on strategy, then what does that mean for our principles? Where are we bending there?

Can you give an example of where you’d compromise, or an example of AOC or someone else who has had to make compromise that you’d be okay with?

You know, I’ll actually point to myself, and that is that I’m running for office. I never thought that I would run for office. I’ve always seen myself as a grassroots organizer, and when I realized we had a strategic opening to meaningfully transform politics in this country, I said, Okay, let’s do this.

Let’s use this vehicle that I had for many years not really—like, that was not my world of organizing, right?

As much as I saw it as valuable, it just wasn’t where I was. But I stepped into it because I saw it as a really important vehicle for how we shift our politics more largely. And after winning, right, people told us that that could only happen in New York, and a week later, Melat Kiros won in Denver.

And then after that, 103 Democrats voted to stop sending arms to Israel. So we’ve already transformed the politics of what’s considered acceptable politics within the electoral world.

Sure. I was gonna say, when you get to Congress, do you see your role as someone that is there to make laws or to move the Overton window to the left so that the laws that are made are closer to what you and your compatriots are after?

Yeah. I think it’s both and. I mean, I think, like, if we are only ever talking about our values, but we’re not shifting the policies, then the world around us doesn’t actually change. And I think about—I mean, we’ll just continue down this example of the issue of the genocide, right?

We can talk about our values.We can convince an entire country of people. We’ve convinced the entire Democratic base on this issue, and yet we still have elected officials who are voting against the interests of their base, right? The material conditions have not changed, right? And that’s only going to happen when we have policy that also shifts with it.

And so that’s why it’s important that we are being, you know, good colleagues, right? And we’re talking to folks, finding those points where we do have something in common, and organizing our colleagues to see reason as well, right? Because it’s—yes, sometimes we have to, like, see reason of why something is difficult for them.

That’s what I was gonna say. Are you ready to see reason?

Yeah. And they have to also see that, like, their Democratic base wants them to move on these issues.

How much time have you spent with your future Republican colleagues?

Well, actually, I haven’t spoken to many, but I’ve spoken to, you know, folks across the spectrum on the Democratic Party at this point.

Have you met any Republican congresspeople?

Not actual members, but I’ve met plenty of Republicans.

Oh, plenty. I mean, I grew up also in Florida.

So there are plenty of Republicans there.

Who’s the Republican that you’ll reach out to first when you get to Congress?

Yeah. No, I mean, I’ll say this. I think that there are no two people who agree on every single issue, even as aligned as you might be, right?

And you’d be surprised how people who think very differently can still find a point of commonality and can build trust.

Exactly, and so that is what organizing is.

Earlier this month, ICE agents attempted to arrest 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Bronx.

They shot him in the neck while he was in the car with his five-year-old son in the back seat. As you pointed out in the aftermath of this incident, the shooter, an ICE agent, hasn’t been identified or charged with a crime. Can you talk me through what you think should happen now?

Yeah. I think there should be a full investigation into what happened.

I think Oscar should be released and returned to his family, and so that he could get medical care. He still has the bullet in his body and is losing hearing and feeling in his face. And, you know, I think we need to abolish ICE. I don’t see a world in which an institution that is a rogue militia, that is walking around in crowded streets with no uniform, no identification, masked, and shooting into cars—seven bullets into a car that had a five-year-old child in it—while people were returning home from school and work, is an agency that has any business operating in our country.

We’ve seen so many instances of communities and families being torn apart because of ICE’s actions, and the only reason that it exists at this point is to serve as Trump’s cudgel for fascism.

If the shooter in question was apprehended, what should happen to them?

I mean, they should be prosecuted, obviously.

But I also think—I don’t have faith in that because what we’re looking at is the institution that would oversee that is Trump’s, right? It’s Trump’s DOJ. And so I think what the solution here—

Yeah, I mean, this is attempted manslaughter at best.

It’s attempted murder, right? This was, like, ICE shooting at somebody in broad daylight.

I see a bit of a contradiction between wanting the shooter apprehended and your stance on prison abolition, and where’s the shooter going, if not to jail?

Mm-hmm. You know, abolition is a process and a vision, right?

It is the idea that we are constructing a world where a shooting like that doesn’t happen to begin with. And so when I talk about abolishing ICE, the point is that we are taking away the condition for this to ever happen again. We are taking these arms off the street. We are taking these people away from the power to do that to our communities, right?

And we are reinvesting those resources into things that actually make our communities more safe. Abolition is also the view that we should be proactive in safety and not reactive. Because right now we’re talking about an incident that already happened, where a man was shot, right? The world that we’re trying to build is one where that isn’t something that can come to pass.

I understand that, and I think that is a worthy vision, and to advocate for broad systemic reform to prevent murder is something I think a lot of people can get behind. But that’s a future goal, and I’m just curious about now. Now that you’re gonna become a lawmaker, do you believe that someone who is convicted of murder with intent should be physically confined to protect the public?

But that is what happens in the day-to-day.

And I know that because I’ve worked at a public defender’s office. I’ve seen this happen, right? What I argue, as someone who deeply cares about ending violence in our communities, is that if we don’t begin the process now of building this world where we are proactive in preventing violence instead of reactive once the violence has already happened, then we’re never going to get to that world.

I’m pushing you on this because I think people see this as radical. What you’re saying is an idealistic vision of the future that is worthy. I think most people, many people would think [it’s] a worthy vision.

But they’re concerned about that specific idea now. It feels radical.

Well, again, it’s not something that happens overnight. We’re not gonna depopulate and close Rikers tomorrow, even though the law, right, is that we are supposed to close Rikers, and we’re supposed to do that, like, now, right? But we need to also, of course, do that in a way that actually makes sense and functions for a society, right?

Where are these people gonna go? Do they even have homes to go back to, right? And I think what that is signaling is that we have a larger structural issue that has prioritized incarcerating people over taking care of communities, right? You know, I once worked with a client who would seek to get arrested because it was the only place he could take his bipolar medication.

That is a failure of our medical system, that is a failure of our housing system, and that is also a public-safety issue.

No question. But that ICE agent, in a perfect world where the DOJ behaves as they should, is going to prison.

In a perfect world, ICE wouldn’t exist, is my point, right?

And as a sociologist, we create our world.

We create the infrastructure and the structures that encourage people to behave in particular ways.

Have you ever heard the Tom Wolfe quote? He said, “A Democrat is a Republican who’s been through the criminal justice system, and a Republican is a Democrat who’s been mugged.” [Editor’s note: Wolfe’s quote is, “If a conservative is a liberal who’s been mugged, a liberal is a conservative who’s been arrested,” which builds upon the neoconservative aphorism “a conservative is a liberal who has been mugged.”]

It’s good. Let’s look forward. It’s January 3, 2027, and according to all prediction models, you’re gonna be taking office that day. What are your immediate priorities? Where do you begin?

So our platform was deeply important to our district, and we know that because not only after knocking doors did the folks say, like, “These are the issues that matter to us,” but also because I’d spent a year knocking on doors for the mayor and knowing that those were the issues that our community cares about.

So addressing childhood poverty, investing in our babies and not bombs, signing on to the Block the Bombs Act to stop the genocide, making sure that we are fighting to abolish ICE, and making sure that we’re winning housing for all so that everyone in our district has dignified housing.

You know, I have questions about impeachment. We’ve impeached him twice, and he seems to want impeachment, and I really want meaningful accountability.

And I’m looking at what is actually going to bring that about.

So instead, are you hauling administration officials and others into Congress after investigations? Is that a more meaningful approach?

I think hauling everyone who had any role in any of this corruption into Congress to answer to the American public, that’s what I think was a more meaningful approach, yeah.

So you haven’t committed to backing Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker, but you recently met with him. When it comes to deciding if you will cast your vote for him, what are you weighing? What are your considerations, the pros and cons?

I think this would be a really historic vote, and this would be a very historic moment—not just for myself, as it’ll set the tone for the kind of representative I’ll be for my district, but also for this country, where we’re talking about having the first Black Speaker, right?

And for the city, where we’re talking about bringing the Speakership to New York. I want that to mean something to the people of my district, to New Yorkers, to Black folks across the country, right? And so the things that I’m thinking about are, will we have a Speaker that’s gonna back and support getting the John Lewis Voting Rights Act across the finish line?

Are we gonna have a Speaker that is gonna push for “Medicare for All,” that’s going to push for blocking the bombs, for any number of policies, right, that matter to the people of this district? We have the most public housing units in the country in the city. Are we gonna have a Speaker who’s going to fight for investing in public housing?

Those are the things that keep the people of the city up at night, and I think that they should matter to our Speaker.

What commitment do you need from him for you to give your thumbs-up?

I think commitments on moving on all of these issues, right?

And actually bringing more power to Congress to take on Trump, right?

Reminding ourselves that Congress has the power of the purse. Trump can’t make all these threats around cuts to funding. It’s Congress, right, that has the final say on that.

Mainstream Democrat, pro-Israel, staunchly pro-Israel, is a congressman in your neighboring district. Do you know him?

I’m interested because you will have, when it comes to public housing, immigration, there are lots of issues where your—the fates of your districts are tied together.

So I’m interested to know if you plan on collaborating with him.

I mean, again, on things that I think both of our districts will benefit from. His district and my district, by many measures, are the two poorest districts in this country. I think there’s a lot that we need to deliver, right? And, you know, I’ve been meeting with members across the New York delegation and working to build those relationships, so I’m sure Congressman Torres and I will be talking very soon.

Would you support a primary to challenge him based on your disagreement on Israel?

I’m still working to get across the finish line on my race.

Okay. All right. So I wanna end by talking about the future. You and your colleagues in the DSA have presented a pretty transformational vision for the future of this country.

Do you think that’s achievable through incremental change, or do you believe a systemic overhaul, something monumental and dramatic in the moment, is necessary?

I think both. I think there are many things that we can be striving toward in a step-by-step manner, and then there are things where I think we have the opening now to really move forward on.

I think “Medicare for All” would be monumental. It would completely transform our society and benefit everyone in this country, right? And I think there is so much hunger and appetite for it across the ideological spectrum. And I think if we do the work to make sure that in the next two to four years we have the power to actually pass it—

That would be a monumental overnight shift for so many people, right? But we have to do the day-to-day work, right? That doesn’t just happen.

If you were to vote right now, who are you looking at for the presidency in 2028?

Well, you know, a lot of folks haven’t announced whether or not they’d run.

I don’t know. I mean, I think Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would make a great president, but I also don’t know what her final decision is on that matter. But if she decides to run, I think she’d be great.

So, Darializa, the Proust Questionnaire is the longtime back page of Vanity Fair.

It lists a number of probing questions by Marcel Proust, and I’d like to put a few of them to you. What is your greatest extravagance?

All over. Thai, pizza, soul food. I just order a lot.

This was one of the things that I talked to Justice Democrats about. I said, “I, you know, I can’t lie. I don’t know if politics is for me,” and they laughed and they were like, “That’s actually a good thing.” So…

Oh, I mean, I think Trump is too easy of one, but we’ll go with that.

Netanyahu. There we go. Both of them. Maybe they’re tied.

What do you consider your greatest achievement?

Honestly, this campaign has been just the biggest honor of my lifetime. And to know that we have had thousands of people come out to support and volunteer and be activated in their communities again, that all of our coalitions saw growth in their membership—that, to me, has been my greatest achievement so far.

Candidate Chevalier, thank you very much.

#3679. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

The late actor was struggling while playing McSteamy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Grey's Anatomy is one of the most legendary medical dramas of all time, and we're currently in its whopping 23rd season on ABC (and streaming with a Hulu subscription). The beloved medical drama is till going strong, but many fans like to look back at its glory days. Late actor Eric Dane famously played Mark Sloane/ McSteamy during that time, and excerpts from his posthumous memoir got honest about his struggles during that time.

McSteamy is one of the most beloved Grey's character of all time, in no small part thanks to the charisma and heart that Dane brought to the role. In his recently released memoir My Book of Days (via EW) he wrote about an injury and reliance on painkillers resulted in him deteriorating during his time at Seattle Grace Hospital. He wrote:

My body goes to shit. I drop to 170, my face caves in, my eyes cloud, I look gaunt; shit, I look like a drug addict. You can tell. I can tell. My attitude on set changes. I’m no longer bubbly, the fun guy, a ringleader in laughs. I don’t act out. I don’t throw tantrums or chairs. I go the other way. I bring everything inside. I dissolve.

What a heartbreaking recollection. While Grey's fans were still head over heels in love with Sloan, Dane was having a private struggle with his health and substances that was making his job difficult. Rather than acting out he felt himself "dissolving", and not letting it impact this coworkers. Indeed, Grey's Anatomy stars wrote tributes to the late actor following his tragic death in February.

Later in his memoir, the Euphoria star does mention that his coworkers noticed the change in him. He wrote about the dynamic he felt at the time, in a section which reads:

I can’t help it. I feel other members of the cast looking at me. They’re my friends. My work family. No. My family. They don’t judge me. They don’t look angry. They look concerned. They look sad.

It's tough to hear how Eric Dane was struggling during this time, and how he was being so private about it while bringing McSteamy to life. He didn't want to bother his co-workers and chosen family, but they noticed that something was going on. That includes the one and only Shonda Rhimes, who did offer to help the Last Ship actor. As he wrote:

I tell her I’m dealing with it. I lie to her. I lie to myself. I suck it up. Fight through it. I don’t want to be Shonda’s burden. I don’t want to be a problem. But I am. I am a problem.

Clearly Eric Dane took the time to reflect on his years on Grey's Anatomy, and the struggles he was dealing with at the time. In his book he was able to speak honestly about his issues, and take responsibility for being a "problem." It's a powerful testament, one that might help inspire readers who are dealing with similar issues.

New episodes of Grey's Anatomy air Thursdays on ABC as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Folks who want to re-watch Dane's iconic tenure as McSteamy can do so on both Hulu and Netflix. Although after hearing about his experience, it might hit differently.

#3677. 'Elsinore' Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman on 'Fleabag', Auditions, and Acting Through Illness

Olivia Colman and Andrew Scott’s friendship pre-dates Fleabag by a decade, though Colman wouldn’t know it. “Was it in the garden for the wedding of Fleabag? Was that the first scene we [did together]?” she asks as the pair sits down in London.

“Oh darling, we met about 10 years before,” says Scott with a laugh. “We did a radio play, which you never remember.”

Colman giggles, and insists she does. It was a BBC Radio 4 adaptation of Harold Pinter's classic play Betrayal, which aired in 2012.

“The big thing that you have to do when you’re playing a radio play is not make the paper make any sound,” says Scott, revealing that another actor once told him a trick to keeping his script silent: “You scrunch it right up, and then you unscrunch it so it’s rigid…so even if you move them, they’re never going to [make a sound].”

The pair have a natural chemistry, which isn’t a surprise after seeing their work on Fleabag. Colman played Godmother, a passive-aggressive, vulgar villain who ate up every scene she was in. And Scott, of course, played the “hot priest” in the second season, the charming and slightly unruly clergy member that became a sensation.

This year, they reunited in the much more dramatic Elsinore, a moving drama about Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Oscar winner Colman plays Charleson’s doctor, Margaret Johnson, who discourages him from taking on the strenuous role because of the threat it poses to his health.

An exploration of art, ambition, and mortality, Elsinore is centered on a career-best performance from Scott, who had previously played Hamlet (150 times!) onstage in London in 2017.

Earlier this month, Scott and Colman looked back at their favorite Fleabag memories, the way Elsinore brings out comedy within the tragedy, and their best tricks for acing auditions.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Vanity Fair: What was the first scene you did together on Fleabag?

Olivia Colman: Was that the wedding or was it the dinner party?

Andrew Scott: No, I will never forget it. I had to say that I was pulling out of the wedding and we were in the house and I'd say, you were like, “Oh no, that's absolutely, it's perfectly fine.” And you see me out. And there had to be a door slam and the camera stays in the living room and you just hear the door slam and then we hear you saying—

Scott: Exactly. But I wasn't able to leave because of sound. So I had to crouch down. And then you were, “What a cunt!” And I remember thinking, Hold it together. Do not laugh because I'm going to ruin it. I was in the room and I couldn't laugh. And it was so funny.

Colman: And we had the dinner and the wedding.

Scott: I remember so much about that dinner scene because you'd just come back from Venice, and you just won that big fancy prize. All of these had to be filmed on the weekends.

Colman: Yes, because I was doing The Crown Monday to Friday.

Colman: That's why I can't remember anything. That's in my defense. There was one month, was it September? Where I didn’t have a single day off.

Elsinore opens in theaters beginning Nov. 20.

How did you each get involved with Fleabag?

Colman: Phoebe [Waller-Bridge] and I were doing a play, and she was writing a lot and she'd written Fleabag and she was doing a crowdfunder to get it to Edinburgh. And [English actor] Kevin McNally and I were two of the people who sponsored it to go to Edinburgh. Then I think before [the festival], they did a little read-through of it somewhere. I saw it. Then I also said, just shamelessly, “Can I be in it? Or can I be in anything that you write?”

Scott: So you gave money for the original Edinburgh show? Wow! I never knew that. You must feel so proud of that.

Colman: I’m pretty thrilled with myself, yes. But also just trying to buy Phoebe's friendship.

Scott: A perfect way to buy friendship. That's how you got mine and I'm still getting those direct deposits every month.

Scott: Phoebe and I had done a play at the Soho Theatre about 10 years before Fleabag. And so the first [season] had come out and everybody loved it. And then she called me and said, "I'm thinking of writing this other character. Can we have a sort of talk about it?" We hadn't seen each other in a few years, and we ended up having this incredible walk around Soho and talking about love. And she had this idea of this priest and we talked about religion and what that means. And I remember bringing her into this place in Soho and it's on St. Martin’s Lane, which is the Quaker meeting hall. Have you ever been in there?

Scott: You know that scene where we go into the Quaker meeting hall? Anyway, I brought her into this place and I said, "This is where I come to sort of chill out sometimes and you can go into some really silent room in the middle of St. Martin's Lane." And so we sat in there for about two hours and we just talked about love and life. And then she incorporated it into the story. I sort of signed up to it with no script. So the day before the read-through I was like, "Oh my God, this is incredible." She's so brilliant that she just incorporates things and that amazing mind is always at work.

Olivia, when the “hot priest” situation happened, what was it like seeing Andrew, your friend, suddenly catapulted into this sensational online narrative?

Colman: Well, I remember my girlfriends just going, "Oh my God, the hot priest! I'm having awful thoughts about him!” And I loved it. I thought it was hilarious. All my women friends, just thinking filthy thoughts about you.

Scott: People do get very feral. It's the priest thing. It's the collar.

Colman: It's the taboo. It's the transgression of it.

Scott: Who would have thunk it? I knew that it was kind of funny and sexy and actually very soulful, that relationship between those two characters, but you never think it's going to be…

Colman: I was so cross with Phoebe when I first read it though, and the ending that they weren't together. Why can't you make a happy ending? I want to re-watch it all now.

Scott: We should have a little Fleabag party. That would be so fun.

Colman: Fleabag holiday. Oh my God, let's get a nice big house in a countryside. I want to have dogs and just watch Fleabag every night.

What do you remember about shooting that dinner scene together?

Colman: It took two days to film that scene. And it felt like, “I can imagine film students are going to study this one day.” It's so brilliantly written.

Scott: And I remember at the time I had a 103-degree temperature. I was so sick. But it's that amazing thing about when you're acting, you sort of forget about it.

Colman: I don't want to make this about me, but I had pneumonia when filming Wicker.

Scott: Did you really? How long did you have it for?

Colman: I can't remember. I started to sort of get better as they sort of fell in love, weirdly. Otherwise, I don't think I could have done the marriage dance thing. But it is amazing how you just—and maybe we're sort of a bit old-school, but maybe it's silly.

Scott: Probably it is a little bit silly. You just do those things…

Colman: The fear that you're going to get replaced. Still in the back of my head that someone else will take the job.

Scott: Absolutely. And in a way, it might be a little bit foolish. I had to have a sort of affect having a weird panic attack in [his one-man stage adaptation of Uncle] Vanya, and towards the last two weeks, I was like, "This isn't really stopping." Because I think your brain knows, but your body doesn't know and you sort of continue. It is a sort of corny, nuts thing to do for your life.

Colman: This rather beautifully ties in with Elsinore, doesn't it?

Scott: You're acting and you sort of forget about it for a little while. And in some ways, on a much, much more serious scale, Ian Charleson was really suffering with illness, and he went on and he did this heroic, Olympian part. And then he would just collapse at the end.

Scott: Yeah, six weeks later. I suppose it's about quality and quantity, right? Dr. Johnson basically said, "You can have more time. If you just give yourself a bit more time, then there might be some developments in the treatment. But if you play this part, it's going to mess up your immune system and it's going to mess you up. It could be fatal." And that's their big conflict. And then bit by bit, it's about art and what it means and how we use our time. And eventually—

Colman: They had come to an understanding.

Andrew, how did performing Hamlet onstage back in 2017 inform your performance as Ian Charleson playing Hamlet?

Scott: It was kind of difficult because all the scripts leave my head almost immediately. So I had to relearn Hamlet.

Colman: Do you find, when you're auditioning, the audition scene is the hardest one to film if you get the job?

Scott: Oh my God, totally. Because you're like, “You liked that. Can I do it again?” Because you feel like that must have been what they liked because otherwise I wouldn't be here. You're so right. Did you like auditioning?

Colman: Partly because I really enjoyed forcing them to like me. I'd go in and they'd go, "What the fuck? She's not right for this." I go, "I'm going to win you over. I'm going to do it." And so there was a job where I was playing a mom to some really tough lads and I really enjoyed it and they went, "Oh." Now with everyone taping, I wouldn't get the work I got if I had to do tape. I had to be in the room to win people over.

Scott: And also, I think what's difficult is that if you're putting yourself on tape, you present what you think that your instinct is. But if someone goes, "Oh, actually no, I think a person is much less friendly or more generous or whatever." You go, “ok,” because acting is so much about going, “I can do it a different way.”

Colman: It’s great for people who are far away and can't afford to get the train fare, but I think it's tough for actors now.

Scott: I remember auditioning for Sherlock and exactly the same experience as you had where I think they were like, "Who is this tiny little fella that's coming in?” And I remember thinking, "I'm going to frighten you. I'm going to frighten you." I remember I sort of shouted in the audition and I could tell they were like, "He's a bit creepy actually."

Do you always know when you’ve gotten the part?

Scott: No, you never know after an audition, do you? You sort of have an instinct.

Colman: Occasionally I knew that I didn't get it. I used to do a little thing: I'd go, "Do you want me to leave the script?" And if they went, "Yes, that'd be great. Thank you," I knew I hadn't got it.

Do you prefer dramatic parts or comedic ones, or is there even a difference in your approach?

Scott: If we were to meet for dinner, I don't think we'd go, “We'll do the sad bit. We'll do the funny bit.” I think you've got to be prepared for all the colors. You know what I mean? That is why you are truly exceptional. I don't think you can be a really great, great actor to my mind without having a terrific sense of humor. And that's just what you have. You just have that interest in the lightness of human beings. I don't love overly serious acting, just because I don't think it's real to human beings.

Colman: I think the funny has to be based in realism and if you're trying to lay on funny, play funny. It's not funny. But you are naturally funny and you're naturally feeling and giving.

Scott: I think that's why even though we had some serious scenes to do, but also we should say that the screenplay was just massively funny. And they have a sort of antagonistic relationship and I always think antagonism is a funny thing to play. It's a great fun thing to do. And then they gradually sort of warm to each other.

Olivia, what’s your approach to awards acceptance speeches? Because some have gone viral, like your shoutouts to Lady Gaga, or calling your Favourite costars Emma Stone and Rachel Weisz “my bitches.” What goes through your head in those moments?

Colman: No idea. I can't remember any of it. The Oscars, it's like a wedding day. I remember my dad saying, "There'll be moments, just stop and just look at it. Take it all in. Look at all the faces. Who's there?" And that was amazing advice. And on my wedding day I remembered it. And it was before phones and things—that magic of theater— when it's gone, it's gone. And so that was rather beautiful. But the Oscars was such a head fuck because it’s such a huge occasion. You just sort of can't believe that's happened, and you wake up the next day and go, can't remember any of it.

Scott: I think it's a testament to you because you come on and you're just completely yourself and what's completely yourself is just completely adorable and sincere. That speech is just so incredibly sincere and it's fun and it's also ridiculous, but also meaningful.

Colman: It means so much. And that's why in the buildup when people talk about it, I really understand how it's, “Please don't, please don't” because you can't help but sort of dream about it. And then it happens and then you wish you'd paid more attention.

What role of each other’s would you have loved to try to take on?

Scott: I don't want to do anything that you've done. I'd just be shitter.

Colman: I want to be in more of the stuff that you've done. I want to be in scenes with you.

Scott: Would you do a play? Do you feel you just don't really want to do a play?

Colman: I think until my youngest [child] has left home, I find going out to work just as everyone's getting cozy heartbreaking.

Scott: It's so hard. Or even in the summer when everyone's like, “Oh, we might go to a beer garden,” you think—

Scott: I'm going in the dark. I’m going to scream in the dark.

Colman: The camaraderie is extraordinary. I love that. I miss that. I miss rehearsals, but I might not go back to it until I know my kids are all grown.

Is this something that you’d want to see each other do in the future?

Colman: Well, we talk about doing a little thing together about houses.

Scott: We think we should have a reality show about houses and beach walks. We might not have a huge viewership.

Colman: We walk around and we go, “I wouldn’t put that there.” We'd be a bit bitchy going around people's houses. We thought that'd be fun. Probably no one will see it.

Scott: Nobody would watch that. They’d think, “What awful, horrible people.”

#3675. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. She wore a mask because she was suffering too much. She was completely unable to cope with her depression, but she had been an abused child. She was looking for someone to save her.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

Since Patrick Stewart's death became public knowledge nearly a week ago, many across social media have been taking the time to honor the late actor. Also, a number celebrities have been honoring Stewart, including more than a few of his Star Trek cohorts. On that note, John de Lancie is now adding his voice to the many who've been sharing their memories of the Jean-Luc Picard portrayer. The beloved Q actor paid a fitting tribute to his former co-star and dropped the perfect reference tied to Picard and Q's past tussles.

While he wasn't a main character, John de Lancie's Q became one of Star Trek: The Next Generation's most memorable foes. After many adventures over the years, including Picard, De Lancie posted the following message about Stewart on Facebook:

For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard’s side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn. Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him. The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing. Goodbye, Patrick. You touched so many. See you out there, Mon Capitaine.

That "mon Capitaine" brought a tear to my eye when I read it, and reminded me of some of my favorite TNG episodes. While Q and Picard's relationship ran hot and cold, I could always sense that it was always love coming from the former's end. Of course, he was certainly a jerk, putting Picard through some wtf-worthy scenarios, but I always appreciated that there was some mutual love between them at the end of Picard's second season.

I'm A Star Trek Fan, But I'd Never Heard This Cool Story About Patrick Stewart Showing Up On Jeremy Clarkson's Set

For those who haven't streamed Picard Season 2 with a Paramount+ subscription, the storyline ends with Picard's realization that Q has constructed the entire scenario he's put them through in order to help him overcome past trauma. Q then reveals to Picard that he is dying, and the two share a hug before Q sets the timeline right again.

It was emotional for me, even if it was potentially retconned when Picard Season 3 had Q return in a post-credits scene. Fans have, however, theorized that everything from the Q species exists outside of time. Therefore, his death doesn't have to be linear.

Personally, I think Q is not above faking his own death just for the thrill of pulling one over on Picard. The fact of the matter is, we'll likely never know now that Patrick Stewart is gone, though I'm sure he won't be the last to play Picard. Star Trek hasn't been afraid to recast iconic characters, though I think it'll be a challenge for someone to follow in Stewart's footsteps and play the role.

Patrick Stewart's death comes amid the celebration of Star Trek's 60th anniversary, which has been rife with bad news. As far as the franchise itself goes, there is a movie in development, but no TV shows are actively in the works as far as the general public knows. Stewart's passing certainly feels like a gut punch to the fandom and the former actors, many of whom held out hope for positive news before the year's end.

Tributes continue to pour in for Patrick Stewart, and I'm continuing to love every eulogy and story that is shared. Both Star Trek: The Next Generation and Picard are available to stream on Paramount+, so anyone who is missing the great Captain should head over there and watch some classic episodes.

#3671. Gang Of Dragon Won’t Be The First Game From Nagoshi Studio. It Won’t Be Any Game At All

Nagoshi Studio, the studio formed by Yakuza creator Toshiro Nagoshi at NetEase, has been shut down before it even released its first game. According to Gematsu, shareholders officially dissolved the developer on October 31 via a resolution later published in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

Under Nagoshi, the studio worked on Gang of Dragon, a new game that looked similar to the veteran developer's work on Sega's Yakuza and Like a Dragon series at Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio. Work on the game continued over the years, and a trailer was shown at The Game Awards last year, but in March, reports said NetEase had pulled its funding for the project. The official Gang of Dragon YouTube channel also went down for a brief time in April, and in May, the game's website was whacked.

So why did the studio shut down? Exact details on the reasoning behind its closure haven't been revealed yet, but in March, Bloomberg reported that Nagoshi was seeking another $44 million to get Gang of Dragon across the finish line, a figure NetEase may have decided wasn't worth investing in further.

Meanwhile, Nagoshi's former home, RGG Studio, has released multiple games since he left. Nagoshi's final credits with Sega were for Lost Judgment, Super Monkey Ball Banana Mania, and Virtua Fighter 5: Ultimate Showdown; since then, RGG Studio has released five games in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon franchise. These include prequels, sequels, and remakes: Like a Dragon: Ishin, Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, Gaiden: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, and Yakuza Kiwami 3 & Dark Ties.

Next year will see the launch of Stranger Than Heaven, described as a distant prequel to Like a Dragon that spans 50 years.

#3669. GoFundMe Launched for Late TV Producer Matt Wright's Family After His Death

Matt Wright’s family is being supported after the former Ellen DeGeneres Show producer’s sudden death.

“In an unfathomable tragedy, Matt Wright passed away Oct 30th while working remotely in Los Angeles,” a GoFundMe message read. “His husband, father, sister and niece are in New York, desperate to be reunited for a proper goodbye. We’re asking for all of his friends, who Matt loved so fully, to help the family at this time.”

The note continued, “As many of you know, Matt & Justin were both laid off this summer. And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear.”

The GoFundMe has raised more than $75,000 at time of publication, surpassing its initial $50,000 goal. Ellen DeGeneres, for her part, donated $5,000.

“If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it, or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor,” the description read. “Please donate what you can and share this with anyone who’s been in the orbit of Matt’s huge heart. And when you’re at dinner and see a sunset, know that Matt is looking down, loving you, but wildly disappointed in what you ordered.”

The GoFundMe explained that Matt’s sister, Mandy, would be receiving the funds and making sure they are going toward “getting Matt to Justin & Matt’s family,” as well as New York funeral costs and Los Angeles memorial costs. Any further funds raised would be “set up in a trust for Matt’s pride & joy — his niece Sami.”

Wright, who worked as an executive producer on the daytime talk show, was remembered by DeGeneres, 68, as an “amazing guy” who made her laugh.

“We’re going to miss him. He is, and always will be, the glue to our entire family at The Ellen Show,” she said in a Monday, November 2, Instagram video, before adding, “I don’t know what I’m saying. Anyway, and to Justin, his husband, and to his family, I’m so sorry. Because we lost a good guy. He was a good guy.”

After working on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, Wright also helped launch The Jennifer Hudson Show in 2022. Jennifer Hudson shared that she was “so saddened” by Wright’s death.

“He was just back to visit on Thursday for our Halloween show!” she wrote via Instagram, alongside photos of the pair. “He made such a huge impact on so many people in this industry and beyond! My heart goes out to his family and loved ones. Rest in peace, Matt! 💜.”
