#3650. Which of Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s Kids Have Changed Their Last Names?

Four of Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s six children have taken steps to remove “Pitt” from their names.

After Jolie filed for divorce from Pitt in September 2016 citing “irreconcilable differences,” Maddox, Zahara, Shiloh and Vivienne have each distanced themselves — publicly or legally — from their famous father by changing their last names. (Jolie and Pitt also share sons Pax and Knox, who have not publicly revealed the same change.)

“[Brad] feels most hurt out of everything that happened with Angie that his children don’t want a public association with his last name,” a source exclusively told Us Weekly in May 2026. “It’s been very difficult.”

Pitt and Jolie ultimately finalized their divorce in December 2024, though the F1 actor still remains estranged from several of his children.

Scroll down to see which of Pitt and Jolie’s kids have changed their last names:

Pitt and Jolie’s daughter Shiloh filed a motion to change her last name on her 18th birthday in May 2024. In court documents obtained by Us, Shiloh requested to drop Pitt and simply go by Shiloh Jolie. Her petition was granted three months later without a hearing.

“[Shiloh] hired her own lawyer and paid for it herself,” a source told Us in June 2024.

A second insider added that Pitt was “devastated by this choice,” explaining, “To him, it was more than a change of name — it was a symbol of a deeper estrangement that has been brewing for years.”

Zahara filed her own petition with the Superior Court of California to legally become Zahara Jolie in April 2026, which was processed that June.

Weeks earlier, she was called “Zahara Marley Jolie” during her Spelman College graduation. Zahara introduced herself the same way in 2023 when joining the Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority, chanting, “My name is Zahara Marley Jolie. Coming all the way from the Golden State in the city that is full of angels, Los Angeles, California. … I am this line’s No. 7.”

A source, meanwhile, dispelled the narrative that Pitt was wounded by Zahara’s decision.

“The children are now adults and make their own decisions,” the insider told Us. “It’s really horrible that [Pitt] has tried to paint himself as a victim. When will people start asking real questions about what happened to the kids?”

In September 2026, Us obtained court documents confirming that a Los Angeles judge officially signed off on Zahara’s request to change her name from “Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie.”

Judge Virginia Keeny wrote in her ruling, “There being no objections, the petition for change of name is granted. The Decree is signed and filed. The Petitioner’s name is changed from Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie.”

The hearing was held at the Los Angeles Superior Court’s Stanley Mosk Courthouse, though Zahara was represented virtually by her lawyer Peter Kenneth Levine. (Page Six was the first to report the news.)

Maddox filed his own paperwork in May 2026 to legally become Maddox Chivan Jolie, using his middle name in place of Pitt, Us confirmed. (Jolie adopted Maddox before meeting Pitt, though the actor later became his legal father.)

Months earlier, Maddox was credited simply as “Maddox Jolie” in the end credits of Jolie’s film Couture, where he served as an assistant director.

Vivienne was credited as a production assistant on the Broadway show The Outsiders, which her mother produced, with the Playbill listing her name as Vivienne Jolie.

Us confirmed in July 2026 that Vivienne also filed to drop “Pitt” from her surname. A judge granted her request that November, allowing her to legally change her name to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie.

#3649. GTA 6 Buying Guide: Get Ready For Sticker Shock

Rockstar's GTA 6 finally releases on November 19, and if you're looking to play the game, you'll also need a console--and those are more expensive than ever. Here's a quick buying guide to help you understand what you need and how much the items will cost. 

A console

First, you'll need a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S console. The least expensive option for buying a new system outright is the Xbox Series S, which costs $500. Unfortunately, that's $200 more expensive than the system cost at launch in 2020--there are a number macroeconomic and AI factors that drove prices up significantly.

A new Xbox Series X, meanwhile, costs $750 for a system with no disc drive, or $800 for a console with a disc drive. GTA 6 is not available on a disc, but having a disc drive may still be important to you for other games and media like DVDs and Blu-rays. 

Switching to PlayStation, the least expensive system on Sony's side is the $600 digital edition, scaling up to $900 for a PS5 Pro (with a disc drive). PS5 Pro, as the most powerful of these options, is likely to provide the best experience from a technical and graphical standpoint, although the gameplay itself should be identical across all platforms.

These are all prices for brand-new units, but Sony offers certified refurbished PS5 consoles starting at $500. A certified refurbished Xbox Series S, meanwhile, goes for $400. These are the prices from Sony and Microsoft directly, but you can find secondhand consoles at a variety of other retailers, along with places like eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and Craigslist. As usual, check your local or preferred retailer to see the latest prices.

New and certified refurbished consoles come with everything you need--including the system, controller, and power cords. You will need a TV or monitor, but the odds are good that if you're looking to play GTA 6, you probably already have one. 

People on platforms outside PlayStation and Xbox are out of luck, as GTA 6 has not been announced for Switch 2 or PC. A PC edition is expected to release in early 2027, but there is no word on a Switch 2 version. 

The game

To play GTA 6 you will need to buy GTA 6. The game's standard edition goes for $80, with its Ultimate Edition selling for $100. As mentioned, the game is not available on a disc. That being said, retailers are selling the $80 edition in stores, though you only get a code in the box. The $100 edition appears to be exclusive to digital storefronts.

The $100 Ultimate Edition includes loads of extras, including a variety of cosmetics and even in-game shops that people who buy the $80 edition cannot access. Since GTA 6 is a digital-exclusive game, there is no reason to worry about units selling out, but if you do want to preorder, you get the Vintage Vice City Pack and a free month of GTA+.

GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013--adjusted for inflation, that's about $85 today.

You will also need an internet connection to install GTA 6, since it's a digital only game. It's a beefy one, too, weighing in at a reported 201GB. Thankfully, preloading begins on November 12, a full week before the game launches. That means you'll be able to begin downloading it early in the hopes of being ready to go on November 19.

November 12 is also when GTA 6's code-in-a-box copies will be available to buy at physical stores. You're not getting a week of early access, though, as the game does not unlock fully until November 19.

Do you need PS Plus or Game Pass?

GTA 6 is a strictly single-player game, and as such, you likely will not need PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass to play. Rockstar has yet to confirm this, however. 

Rockstar is surely going to release a new version of GTA Online at some point--some believe that will happen in early 2027. And at that point, you'll likely need a membership. But for launch, there is no online or multiplayer support, so we don't think a subscription to PS Plus or Game Pass would be required. 

Why no disc?

Neither Rockstar nor studio owner Take-Two have provided a reason for GTA 6 being a digital exclusive, but the answer seems pretty obvious: It's all about money. Rockstar makes more money from digital game sales, and having no disc eliminates the secondhand market. 

“A disc can be resold or rented a hundred times, and Rockstar earns nothing after that first sale," Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics said. 

The code-in-a-box strategy for physical games has been around for a long time already, and while people might complain online about the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6, the game is going to sell phenomenally no matter what, Mat Piscatella of Circana says.

Beyond these factors, consumer spending patterns have trended increasingly toward digital since the early 2010s. GTA 6 is such a large game in terms of its file size, so making it digital-exclusive also saves Rockstar and Take-Two money by not needing to print a second disc, if one was ever needed.

Hallmark has produced a slew of popular TV shows over the years including When Calls The Heart to Chesapeake Shores, The Good Witch and The Way Home. Over the past couple of years, the network added a little more greenery to the Christmas schedule with Mistletoe Murders, a holiday series with a little bit of whodunnit flair.The show is back for another round amidst Hallmark's (extremely) popular holiday programming this year, with more intrigue, murder, fun fashion and guest stars than ever before.

A few months ago, I was able to visit the set of Mistletoe Murders in the hot, hot heat of the Toronto summer –yes, filming holiday content in the summer is not for the faint of heart. Ahead of the Season 3 premiere hitting the Hallmark schedule on Thursday, November 5th, I learned a lot about series leads Sarah Drew and Peter Mooney, as well as the big guest stars heading to our TVs this season. Without further ado, let’s talk about the mystery and mayhem coming down the pipeline.

There are a slew of famous names coming to Mistletoe Murders this season, but chief among them is Hallmark regular Holly Robinson Peete. She joins the series as a psychiatrist named Dr. Russo who is helping out a patient in Fletcher's Grove. Peete told CinemaBlend this is her second time playing a psychiatrist after having done so in a sitcom called For Your Love years ago. She’s also no stranger to a good murder mystery, having starred in the popular Morning Show Mysteries series for Hallmark prior.

Her character this time around will be yet another character making Emily “uncomfortable” after the show picks up 11 months after the drama's explosive Season 2 finale. We know very little about Robinson or her character's motivations so far, but she told CinemaBlend fans should prep for some "good drama."

She’s very smart and extremely inquisitive and intuitive. She has a sense about people where she can find out something about yourself that you don’t even know. So that’s like a superpower for her. She’s warm and friendly, but she’s also very sharp and she can see through lies and manipulation very very quickly. The cool thing about the character is that, even though she’s dealing with some of her patients of whom she’s very protective, with Emily she recognizes things that even Emily doesn’t yet. And I think that makes Emily uncomfortable. Which makes for good drama.

When we pick up in Season 3, time has passed in Fletcher’s Grove and some things have changed, including the addition of Peete’s character. There’s no word on whether or not this series is getting renewed for Season 4 yet, but Ms. Peete told CinemaBlend she was watching the show before getting cast, and she’d be game to do more should it continue.

I was a fan of the show, and so when they came to me and said, ‘Hey we’d like you to come on a couple of episodes.’ And then hopefully if we get a Season 4 I’ll be back. We’ll see.

It’s not just Holly Robinson Peete making a splash this season, either.

Alongside Peete, the show has landed more notable guest stars, some of whom had prior Hallmark connections. Showrunner Ken Cuperus told me they were lucky enough to land an absolute Canadian icon for a murder mystery involving Santa’s workshop. They hit up veteran actor Patrick McKenna to join the Season 3 cast, and series lead Peter Mooney was pretty over the moon about it, telling me about the Santa-adjacent episode the team was filming when I was able to head to the set.

It’s really, really nice. Patrick McKenna’s in this episode, he’s Santa. He really is Santa. It’s alarming to see him. I knew him growing up from the The Red Green Show, which is an iconic piece of Canadian television. I loved him growing up.

I always love it when Hallmark holiday content dives into a good Santa theme, and this should be no exception, but I'm also pumped longtime Hallmark fans will get a reunion. Yes, Good Witch's Catherine Bell will be guest starring opposite Kylee Evans, who is already a regular on the show. That's not the end to the Good Witch connections, either. Mooney is actually married to Sarah Power, who was a mainstay on Good Witch during its run!

These connections across Hallmark run deep, and Mooney told me how cool it's been to be a part of that.

You know, the longer I’m in this Hallmark community, the more I realize it’s actually a pretty right community. You get to like overlap with people. Catherine Bell is amazing. My wife is Sarah Power and she was on a series with Catherine Bell for 7+ years. Our daughter was born during that series, so I’d be on set with a little baby Bjorn trying to get out of the way.

If you've wondered why you see so many familiar faces, Hallmark does employ a lot of Canadian stars, and works with a lot of the same people over and over again. It sounds like it works out great for everyone involved.

I’ve been enamored with Emily’s casual but well-tailored Mistletoe wardrobe since Season 1. I was surprised to find out a lot of her looks are high end but thrifted, and the wardrobe team also has to factor in some wild non-clothing items. Think: Ice packs in coats and more. The team is thrifty and crafty, and if you talk to series lead Sarah Drew, they keep her very happy.

On set, I learned that in Season 3 Emily isn’t going to get a statement dress this year given the context of the mysteries she is solving and the storylines this season (boo), but Sarah Drew did tell me Hallmark has yielded her enough coats to last many lifetimes (yay).

I have so many Christmas coats and jeans. I’m set for life. Too many clothes. Turns out, when I go home, I don’t actually want to dress like Emily. Like she looks really cute because she has [wardrobe] tucking her shirt in before every take. When I’m living my life, it’s like a t-shirt that hits the top of the jeans, so no tucking required.

The best news for the actress? The team is always great about sourcing her favorite brand of jeans (also yay).

I pretty much only wear Mother. I’ve gotten now, so, picky about it. Every time I do a new project they’re like, ‘What kind of jeans?’ I’m like, I only wear Mother. They fit me really well, and often they’ll let me take them home so I have many Mother jeans.

As I mentioned before, the fashion is paramount for keeping things cool, particularly when Mistletoe Murders must film in the summer, as happened this year. They'll be more on that and other stories from the set to come, so stay tuned to CinemaBlend, and be sure to check out Season 3 when it hits the fall 2026 TV schedule on November 5th at 8 p.m. ET, with episodes streaming the next day for those with a Hallmark+ subscription.

#3647. Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers

Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game sold 10 million copies over its first three days. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, meanwhile, sold 10 million copies in three days as well.

If you’re looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items.

“S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired combat puts you in the middle of a Chinese action movie,” Richard Wakeling wrote in GameSpot’s Phantom Blade Zero review.

#3646. Man Arrested in Girlfriend's Death Years After Body Found Burned in Field

A man has been arrested in connection to the cold case murder of his 20-year-old girlfriend, whose body was found burned and “extremely decomposed” in a Texas field nearly seven years ago.

Joey Emiliano Tovar-Vargas has been charged with tampering with evidence in the death of Meagan Gonzales, according to authorities.

“What we can prove at this point is that he disposed of her body,” Bexar County Sheriff Javier Salazar said during a Saturday, October 31, news conference.

Tovar-Vargas, 24, was arrested at his San Antonio home Saturday evening, according to Salazar.

Gonzales was last seen alive on November 11, 2019, when she was with Tovar-Vargas inside her truck on November 11, 2019.

Gonzales’ family members reported her missing four days later, after they couldn’t reach her, per the San Antonio Express-News. Her relatives told investigators Tovar-Vargas was her boyfriend.

Within a few weeks, Gonzales’ pickup truck was discovered December 2, 2019, with traces of blood in the truck bed, according to authorities. The blood was ultimately linked to Gonzales’ DNA.

The next day, Gonzales’ burned body was discovered in a field, wrapped in a blanket, in southwest Bexar County, Salazar said.

The blanket had a “distinctive pattern that factors into the case,” Salazar noted.

Tovar-Vargas had been considered a suspect during the early investigation into Gonzales’ death, but the case went cold after Salazar said investigators exhausted initial investigative leads.

In 2025, cold case investigators revisited the case using new technology and uncovered evidence linking Tovar-Vargas to Gonzales’ murder, Salazar said.

Phone records placed Tovar-Vargas near where Gonzales’ personal items were found discarded, as well as where her truck was abandoned, according to authorities.

Investigators also found searches in his cellphone, such as “how long do fingerprints last” and searches on “how to delete social media,” Salazar said.

Photos on Tovar-Vargas’ phone the blanket that had been wrapped around Gonzales’ body, according to Salazar. The images uncovered by investigators showed the blanket inside Tovar-Vargas’ home.

“Although we’re not yet there to the point where we’re able to charge him with murder, we would ask anybody with information to give us a call,” Salazar said of Tovar-Vargas during the news conference.

Tovar-Vargas is accused of asking a witness in the case to help move a body.

Information on whether he had retained legal counsel wasn’t immediately available.

Following Tovar-Vargas’ arrest, Gonzales’ father, Eddie Gonzales, told CBS affiliate KENS-TV that he visited an altar for his daughter.

“I told her, ‘Meagan, it looks like you’re getting your justice that I promised you,'” Eddie said. “Meagan, I hope you get some rest now, as I’m getting it.”

#3645. When Is Resident Evil Coming To Home Video? It Could Be Very Soon

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie crushed it at the box office, banking more than $400 million globally to become the most successful entry in the series ever. When will the film be available to watch at home, though?

According to Fandango, the home video release is set for November 3. That's apparently when people can buy the movie outright or rent it digitally, with a physical edition for Blu-ray coming at some point later. It will also presumably come to streaming at some point, and it should hit Netflix given the multi-billion-dollar Pay-1 deal the two companies have in place.

While we wait, Netflix just announced that director Paul W.S. Anderson's original Resident Evil, along with its follow-up, Resident Evil: Apocalypse, are now available to stream.

They join the other Resident Evil movies already on Netflix, including Resident Evil: Afterlife, Resident Evil: Retribution, Resident Evil: Extinction, and Resident Evil: The Final Chapter. The 2022 Resident Evil TV show is also currently streaming on Netflix.

While the new Resident Evil movie may be coming to home video on November 3, it's also staying in theaters. In fact, it was just announced that the movie is returning to IMAX and other premium large format (PLF) screens.

Cregger, who co-wrote and directed the new Resident Evil movie, recently discussed the backlash from the hardcore gamer community. He said he should have known better that fans of the games wouldn't embrace him and his ideas. After the movie came out and got great reviews and made tons of money, Cregger said he felt "gratified."

#3643. Former Xbox Exec Shares Her Side Of The Story After Mysterious Depature

Helen Chiang, the veteran Xbox staffer who got promoted in July and left the company amid mysterious circumstances just recently, has shared her side of the story--but her response doesn't close the book on this saga.

In a LinkedIn post titled "Clarity is Kindess," which itself is a reference to her former boss (and Xbox CEO) Asha Sharma's much-ridiculed and cringey mantra, said it's "not accurate" that she was "fired for a policy violation" as multiple reports said.

Chiang said she will not "turn this into a play-by-play" and reveal the specifics, but she wanted to speak out to dispel rumors. "What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize."

She went on to "set the record straight" by claiming she did not leak confidential company information to the press as some had speculated. "I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job," she said, adding that this includes having no contact with any journalist who reached out to her before today to ask for her side of the story.

Chiang went on to say she did not leave Xbox to join a competitor. "You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build," she said

"Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here," she said.  

That may all be true, but it's also unquestionable that people regularly spend lengthy periods of their career at one company, in high-level positions, and then move to other companies.

Third, Chiang said she "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity."

"I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record," she said.

Chiang added that she did not leave Xbox because she was "passed over for a bigger role." She said that since having children, she became more "intentional about how I define ambition and success." She said she has purposefully not sought out bigger roles or jobs with more responsibilities; she said she hadn't interviewed for a job since 2011.

"My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact," she said, adding that she did not ask to become Xbox's first-ever COO.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.

#3642. You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.

Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.

The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety. The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.

Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.

#3641. GOG Wants To Bring Back Physical PC Games, But There’s A Catch

While PlayStation 5 console owners are preparing for a discless future, PC gamers have been living in all-digital world for decades now. The advent of Steam and cheaper broadband internet helped end physical PC game sales in the early 2000s, but GOG is dreaming up a future where these games can thrive once again--if it can get past a few obstacles that stand in its way.

Speaking to GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, GOG's senior business development and partnerships manager, laid out a dream scenario in which a consumer can browse GOG, select a game, and have a physical copy delivered to their home. "Ideally, my dream would be to be able to buy physical versions of those games on GOG," Paczynski said. "You go to your shelf on GOG, you click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario."

While that sounds ideal, it's easier said than done, as Paczynski noted that selling physical goods is a logistical challenge when compared to running a digital storefront. Physical media requires organizing storage, delivery, and additional publisher approvals, but Paczynski hopes to see it realized one day.

It's worth noting that the GOG Preservation Program did recently create high-resolution scans for five classic games--Myst, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Star Trek: 25th Anniversary, and Armikrog--and turned them into 3D models that you can view on your PC--as well as printable files for anyone looking for a papercraft project. It's similar to the work done by another site, Big Box Collection, which offers a far larger library of classic PC boxes to admire in 3D.

GOG isn't the only company nostalgic for the big boxes of a bygone era; several sites have popped up in recent years to offer curated collections of physical PC and console games. From Limited Run Games to Special Reserve Games, there's still an appetite for owning something with a tangible quality.

#3640. Tomi Adeyemi Does Not Want to Talk About the Children of Blood and Bone Movie

“You are a once in a generation talent,” says Tomi Adeyemi, tears in her eyes. The author is not paying me a compliment; she is reading a line from one of her numerous fan letters.

Adeyemi is a New York Times bestselling writer, a feat she accomplished at twenty-four with her 2018 fantasy debut novel Children of Blood and Bone—the first in her Legacy of Orïsha trilogy, which marries old-fashioned American YA with West African mythology. Her new novel, The Siren—released in September—follows Emery, a freshman at Dartmouth desperate to find her place as she undertakes a series of trials to join the titular group of powerful girls on campus.

This is Adeyemi’s first time since childhood not writing fantasy; maybe her first time period, since she says the first book she ever wrote was a Parent Trap fan fiction. But it’s also an attempt to move past the widely successful young-adult fantasy with which she made her name—as well as the drama surrounding the film adaptation of Adeyemi’s debut novel, an experience she has called the worst thing she ever lived through.

In now-deleted TikToks, Adeyemi said that she’s distancing herself from the film, she won’t watch it, and that she blocked one of its leads, Amandla Stenberg, on social media. Sources indicated to VF this summer that Adeyemi got more creative control over the film than most first-time authors do, including a co-screenwriting credit; they also noted that she's switched talent agencies multiple times since striking an initial deal with ICM. “There must be something [going on] because she’s burned every bridge,” one insider who works in the book-to-film space said.

When we meet, Adeyemi says that she doesn’t want to talk about that.

Instead, she talks about how she used to exclusively write fantasy because the world wasn’t safe enough for her to write anything else. Now, though, she no longer feels like she has to hide behind magic. “I’ve become someone who can inhabit it fully,” she says. “When you allow a woman to grow her claws, I am more akin to a jungle cat than I am a house plant.” She breaks into a chorus of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” adding a Jackson 5-esque run: “Da-da-da, oh, baby, yeah-yeah.” She tells me that sometimes, when she connects with certain people—like me—she just can’t help herself from singing. “The stars, the moon!” she belts—lines from Florence + the Machine’s “Cosmic Love.”

Adeyemi’s a musical person. She saw Florence play at Lollapalooza: “Somehow, Florence wielded her magic so I was able to get to the very front row, and she’s singing to me. I’m like, Look at this wild woman, howling to the moon.” This reminds her of a scene from her new book: when Roux, the girl Emery idolizes, is introduced. Adeyemi writes Roux dancing on a table, kicking glasses, alive and wild. Emery wants to be like that; so does Adeyemi. She explains this before singing some more: “You woke up like that, you woke up like that.”

Adeyemi’s admiration for Roux is almost tangible. She smiles dreamily when she speaks about her creation, leaving you to wonder if there was a specific person this character was based on.

Though Adeyemi started working on The Siren in 2020, she says the novel’s published version was written entirely last year. She’s gotten used to trying, and trying again; while applying for fiction writing classes in college, Adeyemi says, she was rejected five semesters in a row. One professor actually told her he couldn’t teach her to write, an anecdote she’s happy to relate now: “Hello! So many bestsellers later.” She spent four and a half years writing her first, unpublished novel, which she says was rejected 63 times. Only then did she write Children of Blood and Bone.

Adeyemi says she writes to free herself—and while one can’t be sure exactly what she had to free herself from last year, the film adaptation of Blood and Bone was shot in 2025. That’s also when Adeyemi allegedly fell out with Stenberg. And while they’re spelled differently, it’s notable that Roux—The Siren’s charismatic villain—has the same name as one of Stenberg’s most popular characters, Rue in the first Hunger Games movie.

Female authors are often asked, unfairly, whether they are writing their own lives into a story. Yet it’s also impossible to ignore the parallels between Emery and Adeyemi herself. Both are Ivy-educated writers and self-proclaimed outsiders. Adeyemi also doesn’t shy from comparisons between herself and her most recent main character: she says that all authors write themselves, because doing so is a vehicle for understanding. Reading The Siren is like stepping into her consciousness.

So is interviewing her. Adeyemi has a tendency to go off on tangents about astrology, tarots, mystical energy. “Do you remember how it felt when the entire universe came alive? All these spindles, nerve endings rise,” she asks me at one point, holding out her arms. “If you could feel the stars and taste the wind?”

The novel is wrapped up in themes of belonging, identity, and loneliness—a narrative Adeyemi tells me she relates to. “I think if you don’t belong to yourself, you don’t belong anywhere,” she says—though Adeyemi also thinks that her Aquarius placements mean people like her will never fit in, because they are not designed to. Take “our most iconic Aquarius rising, Audrey Hepburn,” or SZA, who famously wears fairy wings onstage and on red carpets. “How painful must it have been when you were on land?” Adeyemi asks her fellow Aquarius rhetorically. “How painful must it have been to learn how to fly? How painful is it for the butterflies inside before they become their butterflies?”

Adeyemi herself appears on the cover of The Siren—something that “has never been done before,” she says. “But a lot of what I do has never been done before. I remember choosing the image because I saw the darkness, that power in Emery. I’ve never seen that look in anyone else’s eye.”

There was a time where having her books adapted for the screen felt like the epitome of Adeyemi’s work. The author no longer feels that way: “I am the epitome of my work,” she says. And as she said on those now-deleted TikToks, she really would rather not talk about the film adaptation of her first novel at all.

We avoid the topic during our initial conversation. When our time runs out, though, Adeyemi tells me she’d like to talk more at a later date. When I do eventually speak to Adeyemi again—and ask about the Blood and Bone film—she shuts down physically. Her smile drops; the question throws off the energy of the conversation, almost like a betrayal has occurred. I ask another question, and Adeyemi tells me that she is getting a call. She turns off her camera, and I sit in silence for seven minutes.

Eventually, Adeyemi returns and asks if I am still there. She tells me, “The Siren is number three, New York Times.” She’s feeling the hot flash version of goosebumps, she says, like she just finished a marathon.

Adeyemi says that all of this—her career, her work, her writing process—was inspired by extreme fear. She speaks about it in the second person: “An agonizing understanding that you’ve been taught to work so hard to build a better life, [but] you might not get to build that life. It could be snapped away from you like that. I live in that terror.” She’s gone through her own trials: not just the long journey to publishing Blood and Bone, but the internet’s scrutiny over the comments she made about the Blood and Bone adaptation. “I’m exceptionally proud of who I am today,” she says, though “life is terrifying.”

In our first conversation, Adeyemi had said The Siren might be her last book—that she might be finished with writing altogether. “You can depart from all these previous eras of your life with a gentle sort of ruthlessness,” she said, “and then tomorrow can actually be a new day.” Now, she seems reenergized by the idea of work, telling me that she’s met children’s literacy organizations that try to inspire kids with the work of James Baldwin, Octavia Butler, and herself. “I’m proud of writing this from a really hard time and place,” she says, “and I wanna continue Emery’s journey.”

I ask her what changed between that interview and this one. Her smile freezes; she laughs awkwardly before hesitantly replying, “I think it’s interesting talking to you in the summer and then talking to you post this tour. I don’t know how the piece will end up, since you’re getting two very distinct cross sections.”

She takes another beat. “So that quote felt more… there was more of a resonance the first time we spoke. As I’m sitting here with you now, I just have a vision of myself writing deeply.”

The time between our talks seems to have given her space for deep reflection. I remind Adeyemi what she’d told me about feeling more like a jungle cat than a houseplant, and ask if she felt she had to be a jungle cat during her journey with the Blood and Bone film. “I think all women have to be in tune with their power. I think Black women have to be in tune with their power, dark-skinned Black women especially,” she answers. “There’s a sense of gravity that wouldn’t have been there without knowing what it is to step into my power and voice. You owe it to yourself to feel safe, and if you’re the only one there to defend yourself, you have to have the claws.”

As the film’s January release inches closer, one has to wonder if Adeyemi has a desire to retract her claws—and her statements about the movie. Or at least whether everything that’s transpired has changed her relationship with her debut novel. “I think my relationship with myself has changed more than anything,” Adeyemi answers. When narrating the audiobook for The Siren, she noticed that Emery doesn’t recognize her own genius. That broke Adeyemi’s heart, because the character’s insecurities came from a personal place. The difference between her character and her own feelings also shows Adeyemi’s own growth: “You don’t feel that way anymore,” she told herself.

When asked whether she might try to make another movie someday—or adapt The Siren—she answers firmly: “I’ve already done that journey. It’s a lot of work, but it’s not work that is for myself. When you commit to doing something on screen, it’s more about everyone else on the other side of that screen. I think because I have such a directorial and cinematic approach to my writing, I do value having experienced everything.” Selling the rights to your novel means essentially giving it away to other people, she says. That was extremely difficult for her. “I don’t need anyone in this world.”

Maybe Adeyemi’s film future lies instead in front of the camera. She did film a cameo in Blood and Bone, and one in the second Devil Wears Prada film: “At the beginning of the year, I thought, Oh, I would like to try acting,” she laughs now. “By the end of the year, I had a cameo across from Viola Davis and another across from Meryl Streep.” In the future, she’d be interested in voice acting and animation. Or live-action—but maybe only if, say, Jon Chu asked her to star in a Bollywood rom-com with Dev Patel.

“SASUKE!” She yells the name of a Naruto character in a high-pitched voice, then adds in her normal voice, “I’m clearly a very animated person.”

Liberty Mutual has gone too far with its latest ad campaign, and people are taking to the streets to protest it. While the general public often rallies behind commercials featuring popular actors or funny mascots, dozens gathered outside the headquarters of the insurance company to protest the existence of "Liberty Biberty." I'm sad I missed this protest, but I'm totally down to show up for the next one.

Led by YouTuber DimesAreTasty, people recently gathered in Boston in front of the Liberty Mutual headquarters to protest Liberty Biberty. Looks like the heat is officially off Limu Emu and Doug, because consumers decided they have bigger fish to fry.

In the words of the protest organizer himself, Liberty Biberty is a "nasty little pest" that was created by Liberty Mutual to "make the world worse." While his original video was directed specifically at how the new creature is a disgrace to all corporate mascots, the protest itself seemed to consist of people who were annoyed by seeing ads for the company while they watched sports or streamed shows with a Prime subscription.

The protest was only one day and only attracted dozens of people, and legitimate outlets like ABC News and others came out to cover the event. Unfortunately, I think the negative attention will only give Liberty Mutual more incentive to use the character, and maybe this all builds to a wild Super Bowl halftime ad. We shall see!

Liberty Biberty originally started as a joke in an older Liberty Mutual commercial, which featured an actor trying to say "Liberty Mutual" and instead saying "Liberty Biberty" instead. That character went on to do more commercials, with a running gag that he couldn't correctly say Liberty Mutual.

32 A-List Celebrities Who Have Appeared In TV Commercials

This gag evolved into a creature, which Liberty Mutual officially rolled out in July. The yellow fur ball was a puppet created in collaboration with the Jim Henson Workshop, so yes, I think that makes it a muppet. It's unlikely it'll be remembered as one of the best Muppets, but possibly the first to have a protest against it.

There is a part of me that suspects that Liberty Biberty was made in part to be annoying. The more people are making videos and content online about how much they hate the Liberty Mutual mascot, the more the company gets its name out there. It's not like having an annoying mascot is going to do much to impact the company's legacy and how it sells insurance. Heck, this might be the most I've talked about insurance all year, so if that was the play by the marketing team, kudos to them for pulling it off.

The Liberty Biberty ads will continue as the 2026 TV schedule rolls on. I'll be interested to see if any future ads address the backlash to the mascot, or if they'll phase out the mascot entirely after this negative attention.

#3638. Borderlands Franchise Hits 100 Million Sales As Gearbox Hints At What’s Next

The Borderlands franchise has reached a new sales milestone, as developer Gearbox Software announced that Borderlands 4 had pushed the series over the 100 million units sold mark. Celebrating the achievement, the studio also took time to reveal what's next for Borderlands 4 as it enters its second year, as well as plans it's busy cooking up for the IP.

"We just wrapped our Year 1 roadmap, and the team is cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year," Gearbox wrote in a blog post, adding that weekly activity refreshes and Community Challenges will continue in the game. So what's next for Borderlands? Gearbox says that it's "a bigger look at the franchise as a whole," and it's also listening to fans to gauge which characters they want to spend more time with.

Don't expect Gearbox to drop a Borderlands 5 announcement anytime soon, as the developer said it needs time and space to work on future projects. "Big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we’ll talk more when the time is right," Gearbox added. Thirteen months ago, Gearbox Software boss Randy Pitchford had predicted that Borderlands 4 would continue to sell millions of copies and would help the franchise cross the 100 million units sold line eventually. "We will break 100 million units with this launch, easily, all in, with the franchise," Pitchford said at the time.

To put that in perspective, the Borderlands franchise had sold 94 million units through August 2025, meaning Borderlands 4 would move at least 6 million copies. Historically, Borderlands 2 is the franchise's top seller, with 31 million units sold, while Borderlands 3 is second with 23 million sales to date. It's worth noting that these games have also gone on sale regularly--with Borderlands 3 once being sold for just $3 on PC via Steam--and Borderlands 4 has also received a few discounts since launch. Gearbox and publisher Take-Two Interactive haven't revealed sales figures for Borderlands 4 yet, so it's hard to know where it currently fits on the Borderlands sales chart.

The game didn't have a smooth launch either, as various technical hurdles required multiple rounds of patching, and the oft-delayed Switch 2 edition was eventually paused so that Gearbox could focus on the PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S editions of the game.

And then, of course, the one time we do it live, my prosthetic gets caught in her fringe,” Frech, 21, exclusively told Us after the Monday, November 2, Disney Night episode. “I literally … my heart dropped to the floor.”

Karagach, 33, jumped in to add, “You still nailed it. You nailed it.”

During the pair’s samba to “Under the Sea” from The Little Mermaid, the fringe on Karagach’s costume briefly got tangled in Frech’s prosthetic before unwrapping itself. While Karagach said she had “no idea” that it had gotten caught at the moment, Frech was internally worried about the situation.

“I was like, ‘Oh my gosh.’ I was like, ‘Oh my gosh.’ I was like, ‘Oh my gosh,’” the Paralympian, who was born without most of his left leg and hand, recalled, while Karagach added of her own reaction, “This is like resistance training. … The fact that it just unwrapped on its own is insane.”

Despite the wardrobe malfunction, Karagach and Frech ultimately received a 37 out of 40 from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli and guest judge Cynthia Erivo.

“She’s such a massive icon, and she’s so knowledgeable in performance. So to have her here and say those things was out of a dream,” Karagach said of Erivo, 39, while Frech added, “Yeah, I completely agree.”

He continued, “I mean, she will go down as one of the most legendary guest judges, and she brought that energy. Everything she said, you could feel it. Her critiques and her comments are so valuable, period. So when she says something so positive about us, it means so much.”

The pair also received a perfect 40 out of 40 for their group dance number to High School Musical’s “We’re All in This Together.” Frech shared that he had “the best time” working with the group led by team captain Connor Wood.

“Getting to be around such talented dancers, such amazing human beings, we had a blast in the rehearsal studio. Literally so much fun, and we worked really well together,” he said. “And this dance was a fun dance. Our team dance was literally a fun dance. I was having a blast doing it.”

He continued, “They adjusted the choreography for me and put me in positions where I was comfortable. I just appreciate that so much. That consideration, that team chemistry, that’s what helped us go out there and put together a dance that we were all so proud of.”

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

#3636. Remedy’s Big Bet On Control Resonant Appears To Be Paying Off

Following the September release of Control Resonant, business is boomin' for developer Remedy Entertainment. The studio reported that its third-quarter revenue surged 226% to €39.6 million / $44.3 million after the game's release, following the financial review period on October 15, a feat CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon called "a defining milestone" for Remedy.

In terms of operating profit, Remedy said it made €0.6 million / $670,794, and while that may not sound like much, it's still better than the €16.4 million / $18.3 million loss the studio posted in the same quarter last year. Control Resonant has sold over 1 million units, making it Remedy's fastest-selling title to date, with most sales coming from the US. The game has also been popular in the US and the UK, and Remedy says that half of the players were new to the franchise.

"Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy," Gaudechon said, adding that the developer is looking to get the game into the hands of more people. Control Resonant's predecessor, Control, also saw increased sales, and that financial runway will help Remedy as it continues working on other projects, like its Max Payne 1 & 2 remake. Gaudechon also noted that Control Resonant is currently on 2.4 million wishlists, which could provide a "substantial potential audience" for the future.

"Excellent player reviews, penetration in all our target markets and a substantial outstanding wishlist base give a solid foundation for the game’s longer-term sales potential, supported by both organic visibility as well as our targeted marketing activities," said Gaudechon. As for the other games in the Remedy catalog, Gaudechon said that most people are playing FBC: Firebreak through subscription services like Game Pass or PlayStation Plus, and in its second year, it is making less money. The Alan Wake franchise had a quieter quarter, but the Alan Wake 2 capitalized development costs were fully depreciated during Q3.

For more on Control Resonant, read up on how different it is from its predecessor, why you have to watch out for scary buses, and the cool little details lurking in the background.

#3635. Substack’s Cofounder Might Not Know How to Save the Media—But He Knows How to Outplay It

As recently as a few years ago, Substack was struggling to shed the perception that it was radioactive. “Substack Has a Nazi Problem,” read the headline of a 2023 Atlantic story that surfaced “scores of white-supremacist, neo-Confederate, and explicitly Nazi newsletters” on the platform, which was, in some instances, taking its standard 10% profit from them. Over 200 Substack writers wrote an open letter opposing the company’s hands-off approach to content moderation, and several high-profile writers and publications migrated to competitors.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Charli xcx publish there—Kylie Jenner has said she’d like to—as do new media phenomena like Feed Me and The Free Press. The platform has significant footholds in fashion, AI, politics, literature, celebrity gossip, and most everything in between. In the opening pages of his book, How to Save the Media, McKenzie recalls drinking whiskey at the Chelsea Hotel alongside former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown, who now publishes the popular Fresh Hell newsletter on Substack. The United Kingdom–born Brown, like McKenzie, came to America from abroad, only to rise to the highest rungs of its media world, and she seemed now to see him as a peer.

“You’re a New Zealander, aren’t you?” she asked McKenzie. “There’s something to being an outsider.”

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, speaking from the Toni Morrison Conference Room at Substack’s San Francisco headquarters, McKenzie appeared uncomfortable with the idea that his book, liberally sprinkled with such encounters with the cream of the Substack crop, amounted to a victory lap. He was, despite a generally mild manner and steadfast earnestness, relentlessly on message. “I’m always going to be like a broken record coming back to the importance of direct relationships,” McKenzie acknowledged. It’s the Substack theory of fixing an ailing media ecosystem: replacing the ad-based chaos sown by the internet with a more nourishing connection between writer and reader, and having consumers pay for the media they want to see in the world rather than subject themselves to the whims of an attention economy controlled by big social media companies. McKenzie admitted his book’s title was a provocation, but “for me, it’s backing up the gospel that I’m trying to preach.”

Still, we could agree that something about the controversies that dogged the platform in recent years now seems quaint—that Substack has achieved some fundamental conquest. Instead of reactively responding to the “Nazi problem,” the company chose to stick with its hands-off approach to content moderation, and the outcry dissipated: Substack remains the go-to home for your established journalists striking out on their own (Jim Acosta, Nate Silver) as well as your upstart media operations repurposing the expertise once best associated with legacy outlets (The Bulwark, The Ankler). I suggested to McKenzie that the platform today is akin to Instagram or Grindr: a tech company, yes, but also an undeniable element of the fabric of contemporary life.

From a writer’s perspective, one knock-on effect of the Substack boom has been the rising cachet around writing itself, despite the spree of recent news stories declaring the end of reading. There are so many—too many?—personal essayists and gift guide impresarios emerging seemingly out of nowhere. (“I’m not snobby about that,” McKenzie said. “I think everyone should try to write and no one should be discouraged through peer pressure from writing.”) And then there is the ever-increasing atomization across media, with political discourse splaying out across countless newsletters that are only intermittently in conversation with one another. Is this new cacophony strictly better than the ones we encountered on Facebook and Twitter? Part of the reason the open letter concerning Nazi Substack newsletters didn’t stick, perhaps, was that no one is reading the same things anyway.

McKenzie is currently chipping away at Anna Karenina. “I honestly think writing is good and reading is good,” he said, echoing the kind of unadorned aphorisms he sometimes issues on X. As far as the purported literacy emergency, he says, “I don’t see many centuries of progress on this fundamental communication form being undone overnight.” Our “cultural crisis,” McKenzie thinks, has more to do with the distribution mechanisms of writing, and “is intrinsically tied to the state of the media system.”

After departing small-town New Zealand to pursue a career in journalism, McKenzie, 44, tried his hand at tech reporting in Hong Kong and San Francisco. Later, while working at the messaging app Kik, he and the company’s chief technology officer Chris Best hatched their plan to reroute the flow of publishing profits away from social media companies and toward writers. (Best is Substack’s CEO, while McKenzie works as its “chief writing officer” and heads up the company’s partnerships and talent acquisition efforts.)

“We had more direct relationships in the traditional media system,” McKenzie said, referring to, for example, a subscription to a print newspaper. “But then it got broken by the internet and replaced by something that corroded the direct relationships and gave all the power to Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg instead.”

As it happens, one of the touchstones in McKenzie’s own writing career is his dust-up with Musk. He worked for a time in communications at Tesla, and Musk, McKenzie writes, threatened to sue to block a book that he wrote about the company after leaving. (Insane Mode was published in 2018. After this story was published, Musk, whom I’d reached out to for comment prior to publication, told me, “Hamish grossly and deliberately violated his Tesla NDA. No one should ever trust Hamish ‘Oathbreaker’ McKenzie. Total piece of shit.” McKenzie responded on X, writing, “Can I use this as a blurb for the book?”) Later, McKenzie and Best would turn down acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X.

It was a choice they made, in McKenzie’s telling, to preserve the company’s independence—to prevent the Substack ecosystem from going the same way as those social platforms, which tend to leave their consumers more exhausted and frustrated than enlightened. I proposed to McKenzie that the company’s endurance in the face of its detractors has something to do with the shifting shape of online discourse, and that Substack itself has had a key role in making the tools of mass censure weaker in the age of media fragmentation. “I wonder if a lesson we are all learning,” he suggested, “is that the heavy-handed censorship approach can often backfire.”

“Did it do any good to kick Trump off Twitter and Facebook for two years?” he asked.

In How to Save the Media, McKenzie reflects on an evening he spent at the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles in 2021. He was there to support Bari Weiss, who had struck out on Substack after leaving The New York Times about a year earlier. The schism would go on to shape the future of journalism from the newsletter economy all the way up to the highest echelons of Hollywood and television news after Weiss was appointed editor in chief of CBS News last year. (Of the common criticisms that Weiss has made the network overly Trump-friendly and lacks the requisite TV experience for the role, McKenzie says, “I think for the most part, the media industry is experiencing Bari Weiss as a media gossip story. And I think the more interesting story is the structural story and what it suggests about what’s possible in this emerging media economy. So I’m mostly watching from that perspective and I still think it’s too early to draw grand conclusions about what’s happened so far.”) In her resignation letter from the Times, Weiss wrote that Twitter had become the paper’s “ultimate editor.” On Substack, she built The Free Press, an outlet that has largely defined itself in opposition to what it sees as mainstream media orthodoxies.

That night, the Los Angeles Press Club was honoring Weiss. McKenzie took the accolade, he writes, “as validation of the nascent direct-relationships model”: Despite the ongoing and widespread opposition to her politics, Weiss had identified a journalistic niche that required no traditional media backing. Yet, The Free Press ultimately brought Weiss back to the legacy press—the new Substack class has its eye on some of the old media rewards, to the extent that they remain available.The night served as a sign, McKenzie writes, that “independence can still deliver prestige.”

“I don’t think what we’re going through here,” he told me, “is a moment of change where all the benefits from the old things have to be thrown out.”

#3634. South Of Midnight Director Says He Would Not Have Funded The Game

Xbox funded and published 2025's South of Midnight, a highly acclaimed action-adventure game set in the American Deep South. The game's creative director, David Sears, said he believes South of Midnight is a "generational" game that he hopes people discover and play for a long time and one that he thought would help elevate the "prestige" of Xbox.

At the same time, Sears said he wasn't sure Microsoft's spending spree under the previous leaders Phil Spencer and Sarah Bond--which is how Sears' studio Compulsion got the funding to make South of Midnight--was going to work out long term.

"I literally told people, I was like, 'Yeah, wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say, someday, 'The money tap ... we're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream," he told Ben Hanson on MinnMax.

Microsoft spent billions and billions of dollars to buy studios and franchises to help get Xbox Game Pass off the ground. The bet did not work out, and now Spencer and Bond are out. The new Xbox CEO is Asha Sharma, and one of her first moves was to cut costs dramatically with layoffs, studio divestures--including Compulsion--and game cancellations. Sharma also talked about how Game Pass needs to evolve into something that's "more enticing to a broader range of customers.”

Asked directly if he had been in control of the Xbox funding at the time, would Sears have stopped writing checks for games like South of Midnight? "Yeah, probably," he answered (via Kotaku).

"I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable," Sears said.

A lot of people said Microsoft's spending on Xbox Game Pass was unsustainable and ultimately going to lead to pain and turmoil. Raphael Colantonio, the co-founder of Arkane, said Game Pass is unsustainable and "increasingly damaging" to the industry. Game Pass has been propped up by Microsoft's "infinite money," Colantonio said.

Raccoon Logic studio head Alex Hutchinson spoke out about Game Pass devaluing games earlier this year after his game Revenge of the Savage Planet was a day-one title on Xbox Game Pass. Conversely, Rebellion touted the launch of Atomfall on Game Pass as a huge success for the company.

With Microsoft's big bets not panning out in the way the company envisioned, the Xbox business struggled, and the ensuing Xbox "reset" has been painful for the people, teams, and fans of Xbox. Sears said hindsight is 20/20, but he always had a feeling that things just weren't right and that the bottom could fall out one day in terms of Xbox's spending spree.

"Of course it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time ... I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like ... 'For now,'" he said. "And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Sears went on to say the Microsoft of today is "much more humane" than the company was in the '90s and 2000s, something he said is "remarkable and commendable."

Sears said it's a good thing that Microsoft is allowing studios it wants to let go of get spun out instead of shutting them down outright. Compulsion, for its part, was among the studios that got spun out, and is now operating independently and seeking new projects and funding sources.

South of Midnight originally launched for Xbox and PC in April 2025, later coming to PS5 and Switch 2 in March 2026. Now that Compulsion is independent, buying the game supports the studio directly, and not Xbox.

Throughout all of the downturns at Xbox, Microsoft continues to make gigantic sums of money, in part because Xbox represents just a tiny sliver of the company's overall business. For the latest quarter, Microsoft made $92.3 billion in revenue (up 19%) and a profit of $36.6 billion (up 32%). Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Sharma for gutting the Xbox business so heavily.

#3632. The Jewelry at the Center of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall’s On-Set Romance

In many photographs from the 1950s, Lauren Bacall appears alongside Humphrey Bogart with a small golden object between her lips. Curiously, it is a small gold whistle hanging from a bracelet. Not exactly the kind of accessory one would expect to find in a Hollywood star’s jewelry box. Yet, for Bacall, that particular piece held a very special meaning. Bogart himself gave it to her, inspired by a line the actor delivered in the film where the two met and fell in love.

In 1944, Bacall was just 19 years old when she made her film debut alongside Bogart in To Have and Have Not, directed by Howard Hawks. Bogart, 44 at the time, was already one of Hollywood’s most famous actors. On set, their relationship developed into something more than professional. They fell in love, and in May 1945, got married.

It was here that the origin story of the unusual bracelet began, with a line from Bacall that became one of old Hollywood’s most memorable: “You do know how to whistle, don’t you Steve? You just put your lips together and blow.” The scene, a candid moment of trust between the two characters, was a standout in the film, and it was this line that inspired the idea for the bracelet.

The result was a 14-karat-gold bracelet with a small pendant whistle, also made of gold and fully functional. The piece has a rather minimalist look, with smooth, polished surfaces and no particular decorations, except for a few personal engravings.

On one side of the tag are the words “Betty Bacall,” a reference to the actor’s original name, Betty Joan Perske, and on the other, “The Whistler.” On the whistle itself, the initials “B&B”—for Bogart and Bacall—are engraved, along with the number “21,” the meaning of which is still a mystery.

Bacall wore the bracelet in her daily life, carrying with her that small memento of the film that marked the beginning of her relationship with Bogart. In 1954, during a television interview with journalist Edward R. Murrow, the actor herself revealed the meaning of the whistle, explaining its connection to the famous line from To Have and Have Not.

Decades later, in September 2023, the bracelet made headlines again, when it was auctioned by Julien’s Auctions. The initial estimate ranged from $100,000 to $200,000, and on September 8, it sold for $158,750—a substantial sum for a small gold whistle. Though, considering who it belonged to—and especially who gave it to her—it’s not all that surprising.

Originally published in Vanity Fair Italy.

#3631. Buying GTA 6 Could Save You $5,000, Or At Least This Guy Thinks So

Self-made millionaire Mark Tilbury has shared some advice for how buying GTA 6 can actually save you $5,000. Just don't take this too seriously.

Here's how he arrived at that number: If the game costs $100 (for the Ultimate Edition) and it takes 80 hours to complete, that works out to $1.25/hour of "fun." After adding on side missions and simply exploring GTA 6's map, investing in the game seems like an even better deal at just 50 cents of fun per hour.

If you play for four hours every evening, that's 50 nights of entertainment. Tilbury said people should compare this to a night out where they could easily spend $100 in a night.

"That's why buying GTA 6 actually saves you $5,000," Tilbury says.

Even if it's not a full $100, Tilbury is spot-on that going out to do most things today costs a pretty penny. So staying in to play GTA 6 may indeed "save" you some money you might have spent elsewhere. You may also play a lot of GTA 6 and continue to go out and spend money on other things.

His math also might be conservative, as people are no doubt going to play GTA 6 for far more than 50 days, especially when GTA Online 2.0 releases in 2027, as expected.

Clearly, though, Tilbury is being cheeky here and created the clip for virality and for people to send to their friends and partners to justify how much they are going to play GTA 6.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and a PC edition is expected to be released in 2027.

It's still early days for Warner Bros' new DC universe headed James Gunn and Peter Safran, but we just got one exciting update on one of the upcoming DC movies on the way. Dynamic Duo will officially star Mason Thames as Dick Grayson/Robin. It's perfect casting, especially since the actor once told us himself how much the character means to him.

In a new interview with Collider, Safran confirmed Thames casting, which has been rumored for awhile. Here's what he said about the 19-year-old from How To Train Your Dragon and The Black Phone movies earning the role.

We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios, and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did. And he came in, and auditioned the shit out of it, and was awesome. He's a wonderful young actor, but boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we’ve got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan.

When Mason Thames stopped by San Diego Comic-Con's suite back in July, he gushed with us about his deep love for the character. As he shared with us at the time:

I'm a big comic book nerd... Spider-Man's always been No. 1, but I love Robin, specifically Dick Grayson's Robin. I've loved his comic books. I have about a million of them. It's just fun to see his journey from him being first Robin to becoming Nightwing, to becoming kind of the symbol of what Batman wishes Batman was. And, he's always kind of been the best of him.

This new role for Mason Thames is absolutely deserved because he truly knows his stuff. In between chatting with him, I could see how genuinely stoked he was to be at his first San Diego Comic Con. He was asking me about all the tips to best enjoy the experience, and was hyped to walk the floor and get the full SDCC experience. He really and truly is one of us. Here's the video:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

DC's Dynamic Duo movie is set to have Thames' Dick Grayson working together with another Robin iteration, Jason Todd. Grayson grew up in a family of circus performers, but had to watch his parents fall to their deaths while trying to be complete one trick (after the act was sabotaged). He becomes Batman's first sidekick. Jason Todd, on the other hand, is a character who grew up on the streets of Gotham to a petty thief and a drug addict for parents before being taken in by Batman.

When the movie was announced it on X in October 2024, Gunn revealed it'd be "a mix of animation, puppetry, and CGI," making it a rather unique take on the characters. While Thames is presumably just taking on the voice role for Robin in this movie, Gunn has previously said this in 2023, per IGN:

And what we're doing with the DCU is we are having animation tied directly into live-action television and movies and games all intertwined within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this as well as in other things.

While we should keep in mind these comments are on the older side, Mason Thames looks absolutely ready to play Robin as is in live-action. And, I hope Dynamic Duo is the start of a long journey of the actor playing the role across a variety of mediums.

It's also worth nothing the movie is also produced by Matt Reeves, who's been the filmmaker behind The Batman films with Robert Pattinson. I wonder if we could see a version of his Dick Grayson in his universe? Dynamic Duo is set to hit theaters on September 22, 2028 following the release of Man of Tomorrow and The Batman: Part II next year. Congrats to Mason Thames on manifesting a dream role of his!

#3629. GTA 6 Preloading: Start Date And What To Know About Digital And Physical Copies

After years of development and multiple delays, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally launching on November 19, and you can now actually preorder the game. The $80 game arrives on November 19, but you can actually preload it a week earlier, which is nice for the countless people who no doubt want to begin playing the second they can.

Here's everything you need to know about GTA 6 preloading.

GTA 6 preload schedule

GTA 6 players who preorder a digital copy of GTA 6 can begin preloading on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time in your respective time zone. This is to "ensure they are able to play at launch," Rockstar said, adding that code-in-box versions for both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles should be available from retailers starting November 12.

The game's physical edition will be available to buy on November 12 "to support preloading," Rockstar said. So if you walk into a GameStop or Walmart on November 12 and see a copy of GTA 6 on the shelves to buy, you can do so, but the game itself won't unlock until November 19.

GTA 6 file size

GTA 6 is going to be massive, as Rockstar has confirmed the game will require up to 212GB of storage capacity, depending on your device.

GTA 6 launch times

GTA 6 launches on November 19, but when exactly? We don't know yet, as Rockstar has not yet shared that information. Keep checking back with GameSpot for the latest on GTA 6's launch times and more.

#3628. Tatyana Ali Hints at How She Chose Her 'DWTS' Group Dance Team

Tatyana Ali is explaining her thought process behind selecting her group dance members on Dancing With the Stars’ Disney Night.

“Tatyana… as the lowest scored person why wouldn’t you choose at least ONE of the stars with a dance background for your team ? 😭,” one user wrote via Threads, while another added, “Maybe I’m reading too much into it but she strikes me as someone who is very intentional about who she shares space with. And I think who she picked was a reflection of that 🤷🏽‍♀️.”

The former Fresh Prince of Bel-Air star, 47, then chimed in to agree with the user’s assessment, writing, “Very much so.”

Ali and fellow season 35 contestant Connor Wood were crowned the team captains of the two group dances for the Monday, November 2, episode due to having the lowest combined total of judges scores.

Ali first selected Maura Higgins before then picking Amber Glenn and Julia Stiles to join her team. The group then performed a freestyle to Zootopia 2’s “Zoo” with cohost Alfonso Ribeiro.

Wood, meanwhile, chose Ezra Frech, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Dewan for his group dance freestyle to High School Musical’s “We Are All In This Together” with cohost Julianne Hough. Team Wildcats earned a perfect 40 out of 40 from the judges.

“This is the most amazing team,” Ali said in the package of the Monday episode, adding in a confessional, “Being captain is a lot of responsibility.”

In keeping with their “Slaytopia” team name, Ali and her group ultimately slayed their performance and earned a 36 out of 40 from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough, Bruno Tonioli and guest judge Cynthia Erivo.

The score was then added to each pair’s individual tally from the first round of the episode. Ali and partner Jan Ravnik had previously performed a contemporary to “Easy As Life” from Aida and earned a 33 out of 40.

“Jan had me do things that when I first came here I couldn’t have done. And I just wanted to do his work justice because it’s so beautiful,” Ali said in the skybox after the performance, to which Ravnik replied, “And she did.”

The pair were ultimately safe from elimination, with Stiles and partner Ezra Sosa saying goodbye to the ballroom. Ali and Ravnik’s dance style and song have yet to be revealed for next week’s Grammy Night.

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

#3627. One Popular PC Game Storefront Has Had Enough Of AI Slop, And It’s Taking Action

Indie game storefront Itch.io has announced it removed "a couple terabytes of AI slop" and has begun taking steps to combat the deluge of AI-created games appearing on the platform. "Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI-generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI-generated models," Itch wrote in a social media post.

The platform had already noted that the number of game pages being created per day had doubled from 3,000 to 6,000 over the last two months, with reports of users flooding the game uploads page with dozens of AI-created game spams. Going forward, Itch says that these sorts of bulk uploads will result in that spam being de-indexed, and filtering for generative AI disclosure will be added more sections of the site, including the search results page.

This doesn't mean Itch is outright banning AI-generated content, but it is taking a harder line against people who spam the site with it. In its official terms and conditions, Itch states that if the use of AI in a game is "clearly stated" and if "it adds substantial value" to the user experience, then that's okay. But if you're uploading something iterative, that'll be against the platform's rules.

Essentially, if you don't want to see AI-built games when you search Itch, the new filter will keep them out of your search results. This is a far stronger response than Valve's, as Steam's approach to AI slop has been very hands-off so far. While Valve has vaguely suggested it's considering how to address the influx of AI spam following the disastrous October edition of Next Fest, its response to developers fearful of AI-cloned projects has left much to be desired.

According to several developers, AI slop is a much bigger problem than Steam realizes.

Valve said that developers should focus on building a community and more unique features into their games to help stand out, which does nothing to address the issue of their projects being cloned the second they share progress online--although one of the big drivers behind cloned games, Anthropic's Claude, may have had its copycat abilities throttled recently.
