#3528. ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama

“The Intertwining” director Akira Yamamoto was mentored by Kiyoshi Kurosawa, and it shows. Yamamoto is one of many Japanese filmmakers to study under the legendary director of “Cure” and “Tokyo Sonata,” who was a professor at Tokyo University of the Arts from 2005 to 2023. And although he’s not Kurosawa’s most famous pupil — that would be “All of a Sudden”‘s Ryusuke Hamaguchi, whose style is also an influence here — he has clearly taken many lessons on composition and timing from his former teacher. To this end, Yamamoto’s latest feature takes a politically charged family drama and laces it with restrained, but palpable psychological tension, creating a film whose quietest moments are also its most uneasy ones. Related Stories Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

Yamamoto’s primary tactic for creating this tension is the long take. Shots in this film frequently linger just a few seconds longer than they’re “supposed” to, reflecting the pauses in dialogue scenes where characters choose their words before they speak. Many filmmakers who utilize this tactic like to punctuate these moments with bursts of sudden violence, but aside from the elderly woman collapsing on a city bus who serves as a catalyst for the film’s plot — filmed in a very Kurosawa-esque long shot, by the way — Yamamoto contains himself here, too.

The struggle in “The Intertwining” is all psychological, as the two women who respond to the medical emergency — both medical students, as it turns out — begin to realize that they have a lot in common. Ji-hyun (Jiyoung) is a fifth-year Korean exchange student, although she’s frequently mistaken for Japanese — as Nakano (Karata Erika) notes with surprise when they formally introduce themselves afterwards. They exchange numbers and hang out a few times, eventually figuring out that not only are their parents both in the hospitality business, but they were born at the same clinic around the same time.

Ji-hyun’s parents briefly lived in Tokyo before going back to their home country, discouraged by the discrimination against Koreans that’s still pervasive in Japan today. This becomes extremely important later on as Nakano, who’s never felt at home in her family, decides to test her DNA against those of her parents and brother after learning about DNA sequencing in class. Nakano is both shocked and relieved to discover that the parents she grew up with are not her biological mother and father, and her new friend Ji-hyun supports her as she tries to process these feelings. Then a nurse at the clinic gives Nakano an envelope containing the names of her real parents.

As it turns out, it’s not a coincidence at all that Ji-hyun and Nakano’s parents both sought treatment at the same fertility clinic. Ji-hyun and Nakano were both the product of IVF, and their embryos were implanted in their respective mothers on the same day. Except the doctor made a mistake, meaning that Nakano is actually Korean, and Ji-hyun — who’s also faced prejudice for her ethnicity while living in Japan — is actually Japanese. The scene where the clinic’s current head tries to explain what went wrong more than 20 years ago contains another of the movie’s rare outbursts, as Nakano’s father angrily confronts the doctor for “putting a Korean embryo into [his] wife.” In his mind, this is the worst betrayal of them all, and the way he prioritizes his family’s honor over his daughter’s happiness is one of the reasons why Nakano feels no guilt about leaving him behind.

Ji-hyun, on the other hand, loves her family very much. She does not want to become Japanese, and the political undertones of their respective identity crises are one of the film’s most crackling unspoken undercurrents. Ji-hyun pities Nakano, but maintains boundaries between them even after the two go to South Korea to visit Ji-hyun’s warm and supportive family at their picturesque restaurant by the sea. By this point, the bubble of unspoken words between these two women is straining with tension. But Yamamoto is too subtle, and too savvy, of a director to let it burst.

Instead, we’re left with some challenging questions about identity, and what makes a person who they truly are. Although it’s the central conflict, the mix-up at the clinic is not the only outrageous coincidence in this movie, and “The Intertwining” could have been even stronger with a slightly tighter narrative focus. Still, it’s a testament to Yamamoto’s filmmaking that these feel less like plot contrivances and more like the invisible reverberations of fate.

“The Intertwining” does require patience and active engagement, both of which are made possible by committed, but controlled performances from Jiyoung and Karata, who also starred in Hamaguchi’s “Asako I & II.” One could easily imagine the premise of this movie as the stuff of Sirkian melodrama. But Yamamoto asks his leads to internalize these big emotions rather than externalize them through his filmmaking, and the controlled intensity shown by all three key players is key to what makes “The Intertwining” work.

“The Intertwining” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Marshall’s Monitor III ANC headphones have the kind of design that makes you want to show them off. The textured earcups and gold logo lean fully into the amp-inspired look, and at $199.99 (down from $379.99 at launch), they’re finally priced in a way that feels competitive. It's their lowest price ever, according to price trackers.

These are over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, and they’re clearly aimed at people cross-shopping Bose and Sony. The difference is that Marshall is selling a vibe along with the sound. The build feels sturdy, and small details like replaceable ear cushions and a swappable silicone headband strap suggest they’re made to last longer than most. They fold down neatly into a compact hard case (included), but they’re not water-resistant, so they’re better suited for travel and home listening than sweaty workouts.

Living with them day to day is mostly smooth. The small gold joystick handles volume and track controls in a way that feels intuitive after a few minutes. There’s a separate button to toggle noise cancellation and transparency, plus a customizable shortcut button you can set up in the Marshall app. The app itself is simple, with a five-band EQ and a few presets, though it’s not especially deep if you like fine-tuning every frequency. Bluetooth 5.3 keeps connections stable, but you’re limited to AAC and SBC codecs, so there’s no hi-res audio support. You also can’t charge and listen through a traditional 3.5mm cable at the same time, since the single USB-C port handles both charging and wired playback.

Battery life is where these headphones truly stand out. Up to 70 hours with ANC on is more than enough for long trips, and turning ANC off stretches that to an almost excessive 100 hours. As for sound, they deliver strong bass and crisp highs, with enough punch to make hip-hop and electronic tracks feel lively. Noise cancellation reduces plane engine rumble and city noise well, but it does not match leaders like Bose in blocking midrange chatter, notes this PCMag review.

#3526. Where The Rings Of Power Fits Into The Middle-earth Timeline

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power explores a different point in Middle-earth history than past screen adaptations of Tolkien's work. While Frodo's story in The Lord of the Rings is at the foundation of the overall franchise, it is set at the tail end of a timeline over 60,000 years long. The Rings of Power is also set in this timeline, but several thousand years before the One Ring ever fell into the hands of Hobbits. Understanding precisely how all this fits together gets a little more complicated since Prime Video has made some changes to Tolkien's Middle-earth timeline.

The events of The Rings of Power are based on the various works that Tolkien constructed to outline the lore of The Lord of the Rings. This includes the appendices of The Return of the King, as well as posthumously published books like The Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales of Numenor and Middle-earth. The stories within begin at the very beginning of time and the creation of the universe and span all the way through tens of thousands of years, through the First, Second, and Third Ages of Middle-earth. Prime Video's The Rings of Power is set somewhere in the middle of all this.

The Rings of Power is set during the Second Age of Middle-earth, a period in Tolkien's timeline that spanned 3,441 years. It followed the First Age, an approximately 6,000-year period, and preceded the Third Age, a 3,021-year period. Since Prime Video's series is predominantly about Sauron's Rings of Power, and these were created in the year SA 1500, this is approximately when The Rings of Power season 1 and season 2 are set. This means the events of the series take place about 7,500 years after the start of the First Age and 4,959 years before Frodo leaves the Shire in The Lord of the Rings.

The beginning of Rings of Power season 1 featured moments from the First Age, when the Dark Lord Morgoth was the central antagonist of Middle-earth.

While Sauron made his Rings of Power in SA 1500, the timeline for Rings of Power is a little more complicated than just this. For example, Isildur, the future king of Gondor, isn't born until SA 3209, over a thousand years after Sauron's deception at Eregion. Prime Video condensed the timeline, making Isildur a young man when Sauron forges the Rings of Power in season 2. This was necessary because it would have been difficult to cover the stories of the mortals and immortals of Middle-earth at the same time.

Rings of Power has also done things out of order. Sauron's story is the foundation of the series, and Rings of Power season 1 covered his actions between about SA 50 and SA 1500. However, Pharazôn taking power and the downfall of Numenor didn't happen until around SA 3261 and SA 3319, both events that have been teased to be on the way in Rings of Power.

Second Age Events Relevant To Rings Of Power Seasons 1 & 2

Future seasons of Rings of Power are sure to dive into the Last Alliance of Elves and Men, which forms in SA 3430, as well as the Battle of Dagorlad, which is when Sauron is destroyed and the One Ring claimed by Isildur. This will likely happen sometime near the end of the Prime Video series, but it's certainly possible that Rings of Power will take things forward into the Third Age of Middle-earth.

The Third Age kicks off right after Sauron's downfall, and this period in Middle-earth's timeline sees a lot of important development for the characters of The Rings of Power. Isildur becomes king of Gondor, Elrond marries Celebrian (Galadriel's daughter), and Gandalf the Gray makes his official arrival in Middle-earth (though Rings of Power has moved that up with the Stranger). It's certainly possible that Rings of Power will carry on into this period, exploring Isildur's decline to the One Ring and the dwindling of Sauron's remaining Rings of Power in Middle-earth. Only time will tell.

#3525. The Wendy’s JRPG Is a Searing Anti-Capitalist Screed About Humans Making Real Art

'Wendy's should not have a game that's this good'

The resistance against the AI art apocalypse is being televised in a marketing campaign about burgers.

Over the past year, Wendy’s — yes, the same Wendy’s known for its square burgers, thick milkshakes, and unlikely stewardship of a mid-tier donut chain — has made waves through a series of unconventional creative partnerships. Amid slumps in sales and attention, Wendy’s has turned to popular artistic mediums, like music and video games, to try and reverse course.

The buzziest Wendy’s-affiliated project was the post-hardcore EP Songs to Listen to in a Wendy’s Parking Lot, which featured six tracks written by musicians from bands with legit emo cred, like Anberlin, Blessthefall, Silverstein, and Winona Fighter. Look, I am as sorry as you are to hand anything to Big Corporate, but all six tracks are straight bangers. (Just listen to “She Said She Didn’t Want Fries” and try to tell me you didn’t have that on repeat in a Wendy’s parking lot in 2008.) On the heels of that album release is the classic JRPG riff WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. Like Songs to Listen to, it boasts a similar unmistakable authenticity.

“Wendy’s should not have a game that’s this good,” Stephane Cotichini, founder and game director at 81Monkeys, the studio behind WendyQuest, told Polygon in a video call. (For the record, 81Monkeys was not named after the viral 2025 news story about meth dealers attempting to smuggle 81 monkeys across the Thailand-Cambodia border. Pure coincidence. “Somebody forwarded me the article the day it broke and I was, like, ‘Seriously? How?!’” Cotichini said. “Of all the numbers of monkeys, it had to be our number?”)

WendyQuest started as many projects in the indie gaming world do: funding. Or, rather, a lack thereof.

For the past several years, 81Monkeys has been working on an ambitious, systems-heavy pixel art RPG called World of Anterra. Though World of Anterra was successfully funded through Kickstarter in 2022, the scope and ambition of the game continued to swell, and the team found itself rapidly running out of runway. But as any indie or even mid-sized game developer will tell you, funding in the games industry has all but evaporated since the early 2020s gold rush. Things were looking “dire,” according to Cotichini, who said he had post-Kickstarter funding conversations with 60 prospects that went nowhere. Then an email landed in his inbox through the studio’s website form.

“Normally, I would have ignored the email, but because he said they're fans of the game, I was like, ‘Oh, I'll hear them out.’ So I get on a call and I find out it was Wendy's. And when I found out what the game was, I instantly knew we were the right team,” Cotichini said.

Within a week, 81Monkeys signed the deal for WendyQuest, allowing the studio to continue working on World of Anterra. 81Monkeys split its team 50/50 to work on both games.

The Wendy’s people apparently had the general picture and the overarching creative vision for WendyQuest, but the team at 81Monkeys still had its work cut out for it in turning it into a viable video game. They revised the battle system away from purely turn-based combat to a more active one. This echoes one of the studio’s core principles: Nostalgia has to feel contemporary, otherwise it’s just going to feel dated. Cotichini also acknowledged that while the original script had strong ideas (the Wendy’s marketing team is known for its witty social media posts), it didn’t quite click for a video game, where the writing isn’t just about telling a narrative but also about making a world feel real and lived-in.

Ultimately, writers at 81Monkeys rewrote “99%” of the script, according to Cotichini. Everything still had to fly by corporate for brand-safety reasons, but there are some unmistakable nods to the competition: The logo for WendyQuest’s villain, Dr. Mechborg, is a giant golden “M.” “Sure, sure, serving billions is great,” MechBorg says in his introductory villain proselytizing that’s mandatory for most every JRPG. “But it’s time I make billions.” He then directs his army to “cut corners.”

I’ve played a little bit of WendyQuest, and to quote the kids, it slaps. Beyond its immediate 16-bit-era vibes, the combat system is the main draw. The system is built around a gauge that rapidly fills up at the bottom of the screen. You have to press the attack button as close to full as possible; tap too early and you’ll deal less damage or miss your attack, but if you get it right, you’ll deal maximum damage. It’s a nice touch that keeps WendyQuest from feeling like yet another Final Fantasy clone. The game is pretty funny, too; its jokes-per-minute ratio is on par with TV shows like Veep or 30 Rock. Cotichini is right: Wendy’s should not have a game that’s this good.

“Initially, they weren't gonna credit us,” Cotichini said. “I mean, that's the nature of this type of agreement, right? We're just a silent partner, we'll make this game, and then they launch it.”

But he pushed back. In late 2023, when the project initially began development, AI was out in the wild, though not yet the industry-demolishing force it is today. AI grows more unpopular every year, but gaming audiences in particular react with visceral repudiation; even a trailer that features AI-generated assets can prompt a major company to reverse on a dime and issue a public apology.

“You want people to know that it was 100% human-made by an actual indie studio,” Cotichini said.

That ethos is reflected in a line of bolded text front and center on the Steam pages for both WendyQuest and World of Anterra: “100% human made.”

“Part of why World of Anterra is as good as it is, and I know the world hasn't played it yet, neither have you, but it's because of the time it took to bring it to life. It's because of the struggle it took. All of that comes across in the product that ends up being created, and I think that's essential. So the more AI is used to make a game, the worse the game becomes,” Cotichini said. “Because the more you speed up that process, the less opportunity you have to improve it.”

Earlier in World of Anterra’s development, 81Monkeys dabbled with AI for project management and efficiency, but found that despite promises peddled by the likes of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the tools actually increased costs and decreased productivity. They also found that generative AI offered solutions for problems that already had solutions. Cotichini floated the idea of using AI to help speed up the creation of NPCs, for instance. “They were, like, ‘Why don’t we just make a script to do that?’”

For WendyQuest, according to Cotichini, the marketing team at Wendy’s actively pushed 81Monkeys to steer clear of AI tools and workflows.

No one could claim that WendyQuest is as in-depth as, say, Final Fantasy Resonance or other big-budget RPGs capitalizing on the nostalgia trend du jour. But there’s a real richness — and more importantly, a real authenticity — to its design. This is why Songs to Listen to in a Wendy’s Parking Lot ended up resonating so much with retired scene kids. These were real songs written by legit artists who we actually listened to in Wendy’s parking lots 20 years ago. In an era where McDonald’s is using AI to create nightmare fever dream ads and implement dynamic pricing algorithms, Wendy’s investing instead in the arts stands out.

“I think that creative work in general has gotten watered down over the last couple decades,” Cotichini said. “And the reason is because it became more influenced and controlled by business interest and less by the creative. Now, I actually see a swing the other way.”

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

That might sound like an oxymoron coming from the mouth of the guy who’s making a game for a company with a $2.2 billion market cap. But really, why should it? Is the Wendy’s logo being on this thing any different than Sony’s or Microsoft’s or, hell, even Nintendo’s? (None of gaming’s three biggest companies started out as video game publishers.) Yes, it’s marketing, and yes, it is transparently transactional. But the games industry is facing down its fifth year of a dry spell for traditional funding models. That’s not changing any time soon. If a Fortune 500 company was debating how to allocate 0.5% of its 2027 marketing budget, would you rather it be spent on a month of YouTube preroll or on a year of overhead for a budding independent studio?

“The industry's really suffering right now. Things have never looked more dire,” Cotichini said. “This is the thing that I hope will come of WendyQuest. Wendy’s spends some millions of dollars in marketing every year. WendyQuest costs a fraction of that. So many brands out there do the same thing. My hope is that when people see WendyQuest — and that, actually, if a studio cares about a branded game, it can be a really good game — that more brands seek partnerships like we made with Wendy's. I think that could become an alternate funding source for so many really talented indies in the industry.”

Bruce Straley isn't all too fond of generative AI art

#3524. Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

The fall festivals have come and gone, leaving specialty sugarplums dancing in Oscar pundits’ heads, from Netflix’s Spanish favorite “La Bola Negra” to Searchlight’s hilarious “Wild Horse Nine,” which just boasted a raucous Academy screening reception.

But don’t forget the big guns, movies of scale and scope that wowed audiences earlier in the year. Some will fill the craft categories (see “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”) or dominate Best Animated Feature (see Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” which might land Taylor Swift an Oscar for Best Song). Others will wow not only cinephiles but the mainstream voters in the Academy. Their campaigners must push them back into voters’ consciousness, remind them of what they liked so much, all those months ago. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

On November 11, “Disclosure Day” Best Actress contender Emily Blunt will launch her award season push for an “Oppenheimer” follow-up Oscar nomination with a SAG Q&A in New York, followed by November 13 in LA. On November 15, she’s conducting press conferences for the Critics Choice Awards and the Golden Globes. She’ll also do rounds of press interviews. And on December 10, she’ll accept the Kirk Douglas Award for Excellence in Film from the Santa Barbara International Film Festival.

In other words, Blunt is in it to win it.

Best Shots: Truth is, Universal is pragmatically putting Blunt front and center for “Disclosure Day” for her remarkable turn as a foreign-language-spouting weatherwoman inhabited by aliens, as opposed to filmmaker Steven Spielberg or costar Josh O’Connor. Craft contenders will include five-time Oscar-winning composer John Williams, possibly up for his 55th and last Oscar nomination, two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, Editing, Sound, and VFX.

The well-reviewed March blockbuster has come roaring back, with filmmakers Phil Lord and Chris Miller doing most of the promo duties so far. The heart-tugging sci-fi epic produced by Amy Pascal is competing at the Golden Globes for comedy as “The Martian” did before it. The DVD released in May. “PHM” will re-release in IMAX and IMAX 70 theaters starting December 11.

Best Shots: Ryan Gosling is a Best Actor contender as scientist Ryland Grace — not a trained astronaut — who is in way over his head on a space mission to save the Earth but uses science to figure out the many problems that come his way. Gosling carries the movie but also interacts beautifully with not only his commanding mission director Sandra Hüller (who is competing with herself in Supporting Actress for “PHM” and “Fatherland”) but James Ortiz, who was on set as puppeteer and voice for another solo space traveler, a crablike alien named Rocky. He’s contending for Supporting Actor. (Whether the actors branch will accept him is a big question.)

Lord & Miller are in the mix for Best Director, and “The Martian” Oscar nominee Drew Goddard could be in the running again for Adapted Screenplay. The movie could land several craft categories as well, including VFX, Sound, Cinematography, Editing and Daniel Pemberton‘s Original Score, which supports the different tones of the movie, through action, comedy, and pathos.

Universal just released their robust screening and panel schedule for “The Odyssey,” with Christopher Nolan and his cast and key crew to be grilled by the likes of Guillermo del Toro and Robert Downey, Jr. as they step in front of Guild and Academy voters. Not coincidentally, the movie hits DVD, Blu-ray, and 4K Ultra HD on November 17.

Best Shots: “The Odyssey” is in front-runner position for Best Actor. Matt Damon has wisely leaned into the degree of difficulty required to play the peripatetic wily warrior Odysseus in harsh locations that helped Leonardo DiCaprio win for “The Revenant.” Damon is a wily and charming campaigner who is well-liked not only in Hollywood — he has worked with everyone — but around the world. (Check out his Criterion Closet Picks.) He won a Screenplay Oscar with Ben Affleck (“Good Will Hunting”) but has never won an Acting Oscar.

The ubiquitous Anne Hathaway (who won for “Les Mis”) is leading the Supporting Actress field for her performance as the patient Penelope. Constantly promoting a slew of movies this year as she became more and more pregnant did not hurt her cause. She’s competing with two-time nominee Samantha Morton, a Brit, as the witch Circe. Veteran American John Leguizamo, never nominated, leads the British “Odyssey” Supporting Actor contenders Rob Pattinson and Tom Holland.

Of this group, “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” will dominate the Oscar nominations, likely scoring from 10-15 each. “Sinners,” a period movie with original music, holds the record with 16.

#3523. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3522. Blumhouse’s New Hit R-Rated Horror Movie Officially Sets Digital Release Date

Blumhouse's new R-rated horror movie has been a box office smash hit, going on to gross $108 million worldwide after being made on a reported production budget between $18 and $19 million. Jessica Chastain plays the dual roles of mother Ursula Martin and an evil entity who looks like her known as Other Mommy. Ursula attempts to protect her daughter from this nefarious force in the adaptation of Josh Malerman's 2024 novel Incidents Around the House.

Now, distributor Universal Pictures has announced that Other Mommy will be available to watch on digital platforms starting on November 10, including on Prime Video and Fandango at Home. About a month and a half later, on December 29, Universal Pictures Home Entertainment will release the movie in 4K and on Blu-ray.

When purchasing the horror film at participating retailers or buying it as physical media, there will be exclusive bonus content, including deleted and alternate scenes, behind-the-scenes looks at the special effects and performances, and the cast and filmmakers discussing the subversion of horror tropes. Check out the bonus features below:

When the trailer started playing ahead of The Odyssey in July, Other Mommy quickly gained attention for the jump scare that happens when the titular character appears in a contorted position underneath a table. This set the stage for the box office success that occurred following the movie's theatrical debut on October 9.

Despite being a financial hit, the reviews have been largely negative. The film holds a 19% score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes based on 100 reviews, along with a 48% audience score based on more than 1,000 verified ratings. In ScreenRant's Other Mommy review, Josh Bate gave the movie four out of 10 stars and wrote that "the audience immediately has all the answers to the film’s story, even before they’ve met a single character . . . Nothing is scary about Other Mommy, and only the film’s very first sequence is even slightly creepy."

#3521. 'It Follows' Star Officially Addresses Her Return to Another Iconic 2010s Thriller Franchise

In a new interview, Monroe addressed the possibility of returning for a sequel

Maika Monroe has built a career as a modern scream queen. After a breakout 2014, when she starred in both It Follows and The Guest, she became a key figure in horror, continuing to revisit the genre in everything from Longlegs to Victorian Psycho. This year, both It Follows and The Guest have been a part of the horror conversation: It Follows just wrapped a sequel, wonderfully titled They Follow, while The Guest just received a quasi-sequel with Onslaught, which director Adam Wingard set in the same continuity as his previous 2014 film.

Monroe notably doesn't appear in Onslaught (there are no repeat characters), but will she ever return to The Guest universe? In a recent interview for her upcoming film, Victorian Psycho, Monroe sounded hopeful.

“I love Adam so much,” she tells Polygon. “We grabbed coffee not too long ago, and he's awesome, so I would love to work with him again, so we'll see.”

The Guest remains one of Wingard’s most beloved films (and this is the guy who directed Godzilla vs. Kong). Written by Simon Barrett and starring Monroe and Dan Stevens, the story follows a charming visitor named David (Stevens) who arrives at the Peterson family home. There, he reveals that he is an army veteran and was a close friend to their son, who died while on tour in Afghanistan. David soon integrates himself into the grieving family, coinciding with strange and violent events taking place in the town. Anna (Monroe), the family’s eldest daughter, begins to grow suspicious of his behavior and past. The Guest marked one of Stevens first freaky roles, an edge that has since become a defining aspect of his career.

Onslaught came out earlier this year and marked a reunion between Wingard and Barrett, who’ve built a long partnership throughout their careers, collaborating on films like A Horrible Way to Die, You’re Next, and the V/H/S franchise.

The film stars Adria Arjona as an army vet with PTSD, who’s forced to defend her community and her daughter against three Terminator-like army experiments who’ve escaped a nearby facility.

Onslaught also features Stevens as Dr. Hans Kammler, an aging German scientist with Nazi ties and the mastermind behind the super-soldiers stalking the protagonist. Wingard confirmed that the events of Onslaught take place near the town that’s featured in The Guest. Both films are a part of his and Barrett’s "KPG-verse," named after the shadowy organization that runs the super-soldier experiments and appears in several of their projects.

Even though Stevens plays different characters in both films, Wingard suggested there might be a connection between them. “I think he’s related to the genesis of the David character in some form [or] fashion, and I think that’s something that maybe we’ll more literally explore hopefully in future installments,” he told The Wrap.

Stevens, for his part, is happy to continue to explore that universe. “We’re definitely open to more KPG-verse. I don’t know whether a Guest 2, per se, is on the cards anytime soon, but you never know,” he told The Hollywood Reporter. “We’ve teed everything up for an Onslaught sequel as well, so watch this space.”

Whether we get a sequel to David and Anna’s stories or something new set in the same universe, the door is open. Monroe, Wingard, and Stevens all seem to agree: The world of The Guest is one they’d be happy to return to.

#3520. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

What does an audience need from its movie theater on election night?

A provocation? A distraction? Something… else? Across our semi-united, Letterboxd-loving nation, new microcinemas are opening up, old movies are selling out, and local programmers are giving film fans tons of exciting reasons to hit the box office.

Also breaking, I guess: the U.S. midterms. (Go vote!)

This election cycle, the future of Hollywood remains an open question, as does the strength of our democracy. With control of Congress at stake, voters are debating what they want their country to become — and, in many cases, what they’re afraid it already is — to spectacular and exhausting effect. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

Boarding yourself up in a movie palace like one of Joe Dante’s gremlins seems sort of reasonable under the circumstances. Thick walls, emergency snacks, and no checking your phone makes buying a movie ticket on November 3 an intriguing proposition in the U.S.

IndieWire spoke with 14 theater operators, programmers, filmmakers, educators, and authors across 12 states, including California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, and Wisconsin. Their answers offer a weirdly hopeful view of communities looking for comfort, perspective, and somewhere to be when the results come in.

At Las Vegas’ Beverly Theater at least, the connection is intentional: Reese Witherspoon and Matthew Broderick’s “Election” shares the day’s lineup with “The Devils” and “The History of Concrete.”

“We program The Beverly as a reflection of what’s happening outside our doors,” founding creative director and CXO Kip Kelly wrote. “Politics has become such an absurd spectacle that a dark comedy about a high school student council election might actually be one of the more sophisticated conversations you’ll have that day.”

Meanwhile, at Nashville’s Belcourt, a popcorn bag oversees the transfer of programming power. The theater’s monthly Staff Picks series typically falls on the first Tuesday, with a name drawn from a bag determining the employee who chooses the film. This time, someone picked “Under the Silver Lake”: the L.A. conspiracy thriller that’s paranoid enough to make anyone start connecting the deep-state dots.

“It’s totally a coincidence,” programming director Toby Leonard told IndieWire, laughing on the phone. “We realized what we had done after the fact.”

AFS Cinema programmer Lars Nilsen was similarly blunt about his Austin theater’s approach.

“We just programmed it as a regular week.” Nilsen resisted recruiting “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly” into any kind of election commentary, instead describing its Italian vision of the Old West as “the kind of dream America that Italians thought they understood about America itself.”

That said, tonight’s gathering still matters to Nilsen — even when the movie AFS is showing has nothing to do with the election itself. He pointed to the Texas organization’s addition of a third screen as a vote of confidence in people continuing to show up for one another through repertory culture.

“I think very intricately and carefully programmed cinemas are one of the places where community is being reborn,” Nilsen said. “Thank goodness.”

For Harlem’s Maysles Documentary Center, building community and considering who gets to tell that community’s story is the program’s point. Executive director Kazembe Balagun deliberately selected “BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions” for an evening that’s ordinarily devoted to watching the news.

He said he wanted to ask: “How do we imagine ourselves, represent our communities and think about power beyond the ballot box?” Plus, “I just think it’s a dope film.”

The “BLKNWS” screening is followed by a neighborly gathering echoing the center’s other events, from World Cup sidewalk screenings to group viewing for the Knicks playoff games. “I think that it’s not just what we put on the screen, but also the rooms that we create,” Balagun said. “The party afterwards is intentional because right now we live in a time where our communities are so fragmented.”

At Pennsylvania’s Gap Theatre, Spectral Cinema programmers Adrianna Gober and Dan Santelli are confronting power as an ambitious intellectual team. Their 35mm selection, Bresson’s “The Devil, Probably,” follows a young man overwhelmed by disillusionment with the institutions around him.

“The film speaks so much to the feelings of alienation and powerlessness that a lot of people are grappling with right now,” Gober wrote. She described the struggle to find meaning and control as “a tug of war between hope and despair.”

Santelli sharply cautioned against allowing that despair to become another reason to give up. “In the current political climate, it’s all too easy to fall into a feedback loop of despair and resignation, whereby the recognition of one’s apparent powerlessness becomes a justification for further inaction,” he wrote, adding he’s “less interested in offering audiences an opportunity for catharsis than one for reflection.”

That distinction runs through other programmers’ choices, too. Just look at “The Devils.”

At Minneapolis’ Trylon, John Moret chose Ken Russell’s film to cap the witchy “Evil Incantations” series after its restoration was announced at this spring’s national Programmers’ Jam in L.A., which he co-organized. The Warner Bros. Clockwork news sent a room full of repertory devotees into a frenzy months before “The Devils” mania got properly started — and Moret saw the opportunity to send his audience at Trylon from the voting booth straight into Russell’s religious nightmare back then.

Every screening has sold out since, Moret said. And personally, he often spends election night at the movies: “I think that there’s going to be plenty of people who are looking for distraction.”

Art can offer distance while leaving a lot to recognize on a deeper level, but even outrageously visual, avoidance and arthouse rarely mix. Moret praised the magical appeal of Russell and “The Devils” specifically, and said great film “should reverberate truth in a way that connects with you, but also allows you to be at a different time and place and truly put it into perspective.”

At Brookline’s Coolidge Corner Theatre, the 1971 film is sticking around for the same reason: The worshippers just keep coming. Now in its third week, “The Devils” shares the November 3 calendar with “Voting Counts: Elections in Film,” an adult film class that proved popular enough to require a second section. The program was conceived for election season, but “Network” also got its turn on Election Eve.

“We want this to be everybody’s movie house. We want our audiences to feel at home here,” Coolidge Corner artistic director Mark Anastasio told IndieWire. “There has to be a variety of programming appealing to the diverse appetites of the Boston area.”

In Milwaukee, author Matthew J. Prigge is about to discover what his favorite movie feels like in a theater.

His book event at the Oriental Theatre includes a screening of “Dog Day Afternoon,” which Prigge spent years researching for his nonfiction “Dog’s Day.” But somehow has never actually seen on the big screen. The election timing was mostly coincidental, though Prigge recognizes the relevance of Sidney Lumet’s film — about a man robbing a bank to fund his lover’s gender-affirming surgery — in 2026.

The actual robbery, the writer cautioned, has a more complicated history than its Hollywood adaptation. Still, Prigge said, “I think that the movie works just because it’s such a human story and it gets to the actual people that are involved and it makes it relatable, it makes it very raw.”

He also noted that for one evening watching the 1975 title wouldn’t be work for him: “That’s a big deal for me to see it as a communal experience. It’s been a while since I’ve been able to just sit back and enjoy it.”

For Hyperreal Film Club’s Blake Williams in Texas, finding an audience to join helped make a new city feel like home — but things are “definitely tense” in Austin, he said. After moving south from Indiana, Williams discovered the organization through its eclectic programming and eventually joined their team.

Now, he says his closest LGBTQ friends in the local film scene are considering leaving the state because they feel unsafe. His election-night offering to a community he wants to keep together? “Hardball.” After a month of Halloween horror, Williams wanted the kind of crying that comes with a good ol’ sports movie, and Keanu Reeves coaching a group of kids offers a true tale of common ground through weepy comfort.

“You kind of want to see a change in these things happen and you hope that it’ll happen, but at least film can kind of make people forget about these things,” he said. “I think it’s cool that we’re able to offer our comforts to the community to put them at ease, even if it’s just for a few hours.”

Relief means different things to different moviegoers, and at North Kansas City’s Screenland Armour, co-owner Adam Roberts is offering the new “Wild at Heart” restoration, alongside animation studio Laika’s first-run “Wildwood.” The former’s booking followed the remaster’s pre-planned release schedule, but Roberts nevertheless sees David Lynch’s dark vision of American life as an prime excuse for escapism.

“We are highly engaged in our local community and routinely show political films,” he wrote to IndieWire. “I think for patrons looking for a distraction on Election Night, there is no better place than the cinema.”

Charlotte’s Independent Picture House discussed special election programming before deciding its existing lineup already had the assignment covered, too. Creative director Jay Morong, also a senior lecturer at UNC Charlotte, pointed to “Wild at Heart,” “The Devils,” and specifically “Digger.”

“These are all movies that are addressing very specific things that are in the consciousness of the voter at this moment in time,” he said. “Let’s just roll with what we got because this is what independent and art house theaters do.” IPH’s monthly filmmaker meetup also happened to fall on election night, giving North Carolina’s indie community somewhere to discuss results that could affect their livelihoods.

“We are constantly battling against the state government and the incentives and them cutting back on budgets here,” Morong said, lamenting a decline in area film and TV productions. “So the film community is very actively involved in who is winning these state and federal elections and how they’re [using their voice] or cheerleading for the film industry in North Carolina.”

In Los Angeles, moviegoers can leave the voting booth for something that looks suspiciously like… another one? At WHAMMY, Julie Orlick’s One Person Cinema fits a chair, a television, and a viewer wearing headphones inside a five-by-three-by-six-foot room. The resemblance wasn’t intentional, but when someone pointed it out, an election-night opening felt fitting.

“We all just thought it’d be a good fun thing to do after a serious day of activities,” she said.

The premiere offering features her erotic short “DÉSIR,” and unlike an actual voting booth, this one has a peephole through which someone outside can watch the person watching.

“The only people who get to experience it are the people that go inside the room,” Orlick said. “And I think that also brings a secrecy to the film.” The experimental artist said she built the installation as a final project at UCLA, conceiving a private encounter with intimate images she wanted to keep off the internet. With WHAMMY and TAPE, she developed a residency featuring other filmmakers’ work, too.

An accompanying screening of “Les fantômes du hard” in WHAMMY’s larger microcinema rounds out an evening with considerably more erotic material than the average polling place — and you can find Orlick’s One Person Cinema inside the Echo Park microcinema all month.

Alternatively, over in Illinois, audiences at Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center can travel the globe without leaving their seats. Jia Zhangke’s “The World” — set among workers at a Beijing theme park filled with miniature global landmarks — screens as part of “Contact Zones,” a public series and lecture class taught by School of the Art Institute of Chicago professor Daniel Quiles.

“We’re given a sort of official line that we’re a polarized country or that we have arch enemies around the world,” Quiles said. “How can art give us a different way of framing these things?”

The professor’s interest in globalization’s recent past grew from questions about what retreating from it might cost. The screening film’s he’s chosen bring students, museum curators, and other moviegoers together to consider their stakes seriously: “I think by watching a film like ‘The World, ‘we might see parallels to the underclass in our own country rather than seeing China as some big bad guy.”

Finally, among respondents to IndieWire’s latest Reddit inquiry, several welcomed a few hours away from the election. Being “expressly forbidden from looking at my phone” was a selling point for one; but another, invested in a tight race, couldn’t contemplate the disconnect.

Meanwhile, others had already discharged their civic duties to make room for a different national emergency: Godzilla. “I voted early specifically so I can see Godzilla Minus Zero on Godzilla Day without having to worry about making it back to vote on time,” one kaiju fan wrote.

In Washington, D.C., another moviegoer plans to see A24’s “The Drama” at Suns Cinema.

“I didn’t realize it was election night when I bought the tickets, but I love supporting Suns any day of the year,” they wrote in an email to IndieWire. With its would-be wedding mired in finger-pointing, the popular flick from earlier this year feels well-suited to the socially charged D.C. setting — even if this moviegoer’s turnout concerns are more personal than political.

“I will hopefully be going with my crush (fingers crossed) if they respond to my texts,” they said.

#3518. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

#3517. GTA 5’s Unsolvable Mystery Broke Fans for Over a Decade, and GTA 6 Should Do It Again

Mount Chiliad spawned thousands of theories

In Grand Theft Auto 5, one landmark was visible practically no matter where you were in San Andreas: Mount Chiliad. "Claimed by the Spanish in 1769, Mount Chiliad is the highest peak in San Andreas, sitting at a height of 2,744 meters," reads a sign at the nearby Silent Probe Mountain art installation. "Taken under Mexican control in 1821, it was then, and remains in American hands since 1847."

It's more than just a mountain, though. Once the player has achieved 100% story completion, standing atop the mountain at 3 a.m. during cloudy weather reveals a UFO, hovering in the night sky. It's marked with an F.I.B. logo, aka the Federal Investigation Bureau, implying that it was created by the government. However, there's also reason to believe that the mysterious aircraft is a hoax, because it doesn't react to bullets, and raindrops nearby become pixelated.

The running theory is that it's a hologram, as opposed to the two other functional UFOs in the game, which are physical objects. They're located high in the sky above both Fort Zancudo and the Silent Probe Mountain respectively, they can both be collided with, and they emit electromagnetic pulses that cause the player's vehicle to shut down if they get too close. There's reason to believe they're both also government-controlled: the former visually looks somewhat similar to a real-life B-2 Spirit stealth bomber and, when viewed using third-party software, has two human pilots inside. The latter also has F.I.B. printed on the side, much like the UFO above Mt. Chiliad.

Players knew there was at least one secret at the top of the mountain, thanks to graffiti on the back of the observation deck that reads "come back when your story is complete." GTA Online revealed that the mountain is also home to a nuclear launch facility. But some players are convinced that Mt. Chiliad holds one final mystery that is still unsolved to this day.

Inside the tramway station near the summit, a mural depicts an abstract interpretation of the mountain itself. At the top is an eye, while the exterior of the mountain has lightning bolts emanating from it. Inside the mountain is a maze of perpendicular connecting lines. Each one connects to one of eight squares. Five of them are small, marked with an X inside. The three larger ones at the bottom of the picture show, from left to right, a UFO, a cracked egg, and a person wearing a jetpack.

One week after GTA 5 was released, on Sept. 24, 2013, fans created the Chiliad Mystery subreddit. For the last 13 years, users there have been dedicated to uncovering the secrets believed to be held within. The community worked out that the X's correspond to petroglyphs hidden around the mountain, each of which depicts a weather status required for the Mt. Chiliad UFO to appear. There's also a theory that each X also represents the roman numeral for 10, and since there are five of them, it's representative of the 50 collectible spaceship (aka UFO) parts scattered across San Andreas.

In the GTA Online mission involving the nuclear facility, the player escapes by using a jetpack. Is that what the jetpack drawing on the mural is referring to? It’s one of the mural’s lingering riddles. It's certainly plausible, if a little underwhelming, because the common belief was that unraveling the mystery would result in a permanent jetpack vehicle, usable in GTA 5’s single-player mode, not exclusive to Online. However, some think the jetpack just refers to the UFO above Fort Zancudo, because in GTA: San Andreas, the jetpack is found at the military base.

Then there's the cracked egg. This has been the biggest source of confusion for the sleuths working on the mystery, and there are a number of theories. It could refer to the Epsilon cult, as they believe the world hatched from an egg. It could also tie in to the fountain by the Maze Bank Tower in Los Santos, as the two bear a close resemblance. Or there's the most common theory, which is that it is simply a hint to the underwater UFO found in Paleto Bay, on the northern coast of San Andreas.

So with all of that in mind, there's every chance that the mural is simply one giant hint to finding each of the UFOs in GTA 5. But believing that would also mean believing that the Chiliad mystery is solved, and there's no fun in that, because it would be a seriously disappointing outcome. And for the users on the subreddit, that isn't even a possibility.

There are hundreds of loose ends and theories players have discovered. Even in the last year, they’ve posted dozens of new ideas. Here's user Alexisuwuu23, who is convinced an in-game film, "Capolavoro," holds the secret because a billboard ad for it can be found at the location where streetlights form a question mark if looked at from the observatory, and it all ties into a disappearing ladder. "Intentional, obviously," reads one reply. "Gotta be a marker or something. The hunt continues."

In September, AntelopeIcy6558 posed a theory about the eight lights on top of the Maze Bank Tower helipad. "I believe that to solve the secret, you need to shoot these eight lights in a certain order," the post reads. "Why? I believe there are eight locations around Los Santos that we need to find. Each of these locations from some angle resembles a keyhole, which is one of the main symbols of this mystery."

There are other theories that think the mystery stretches beyond GTA 5, and also includes Red Dead Redemption 2. Cancelled DLCs and datamined files have revealed a vast array of potential clues, but since those projects were never officially released, they're unlikely to ever provide a definitive answer. Then there are those who predict GTA 6 will provide a resolution.

Twelve years ago, user talkol made a post titled "pretty solid proof that the game was released without a jetpack or flyable UFO," which outlined what is still the most damning evidence we've had: there is nothing hinting at either of those vehicles in the game's files. Of course, that didn't dissuade the masses, because posts like these have been non-stop for the last 13 years.

Last year, as reported on by IGN, YouTuber Gator Keys uploaded a video titled "This is The End of the Mount Chiliad Mystery." He kicks it off by stating what many realists would agree with: "I'm not claiming I'm the first person to come to this conclusion. I'm sure many other players did in 2013, but for some reason, the Mt. Chiliad mystery remains in 2025. So there needs to be a video that puts an end to it before GTA 6 releases."

Gator Keys goes into plenty of detail in the eight-minute-long video, but to sum it up, his explanation is that the mystery is nowhere near as deep as the community had believed. The answer is essentially that the government is all-seeing and all-powerful, as represented by the F.I.B. logos on the UFOs and the eye on top of the mural. It's simply a satirical take on real life, similar to the idea of the Illuminati.

Ultimately, the "true" answer for the Chiliad mystery is irrelevant. The mystery itself spawned a thousands-strong community, with everyone cooperating and theorizing. It's reminiscent of when that kid at school promised they'd found Mew underneath a truck in Pokémon Red and Blue. Easter eggs and gaming mysteries these days are usually solved within days, thanks to datamining and the sharing of information via the internet. GTA 5, on the other hand, whether intentionally or not, gave players something to talk about for 13 years.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

There's no doubt GTA 6 will spawn plenty more theories and Easter eggs, whether they're a continuation of the Chiliad mystery or something entirely new. It'll also likely be the biggest video game of all time, whether it includes a decade-long mystery or not. But the longevity of the Chiliad mystery makes one thing clear: Rockstar is the champion of this type of lore, and including something similar, where the game never truly feels complete without it being solved, will keep a huge portion of the community occupied for years to come.

#3516. Forget Rush Hour 4, Jackie Chan's Sequel To Hit 142-Minute Thriller Confirms His Best New Action Franchise

Jackie Chan is one of the most beloved martial arts movie stars, and his filmography is remarkable because it transcends genres. Chan is a talented martial artist, but he's also a stuntman. His action scenes are often as much about how he uses the environment as they are about trading blows.

Jackie Chan also has multigenerational appeal and has been a mainstay in action cinema for decades. Fans of 70s kung fu movies may know him best as Wong Fei-Hung in Drunken Master. Chan played Keung in Rumble in the Bronx, and even casual moviegoers know him as Chief Inspector Lee in Rush Hour.

The Rush Hour films are adored for many reasons. Chan teams up with Carter (Chris Tucker), an unpredictable LAPD detective, and the pair have incredible on-screen chemistry. The franchise also stands out among similar series because it's lighthearted and laugh-out-loud funny. Fans of Jackie Chan's stunt work won't be disappointed, and the movies are accomplished comedy action films even if you're less interested in the physical feats.

It's no surprise that Rush Hour fans are waiting for news about its fourth installment. However, the actor has also worked on numerous projects in China, and one of those recent Jackie Chan movies is set to become a franchise itself. It may be grittier and more violent than audiences familiar with Rush Hour are used to. Still, it remains an exceptional action movie, with jaw-dropping parkour, and Chan is as charismatic as ever.

The Shadow's Edge was released in 2025, with a sequel reportedly in the works. The movie introduces us to a skilled group of young thieves. They use a combination of high-flying martial arts and parkour, but they also have far more high-tech tools at their disposal. One member of the group is a professional hacker who uses the police force's own technology against them.

The authorities decide to call in a retired expert officer, Wong Tak-chung (Jackie Chan), to help bring the group down. He assembles a young task force, teaching them surveillance and fieldwork without relying so heavily on technology that could expose them. Tak-chung also discovers that the group has links to a mysterious criminal mastermind known as The Shadow (Tony Leung Ka-fai), who has eluded the police for years.

Jackie Chan's character is a great mentor, but he can still fight, and he's the highlight of several incredible action scenes. One particular brawl in a claustrophobic apartment is a big highlight. Leung's action scenes are also incredible as almost futuristic technology clashes with old-school training.

Without delving into spoilers, The Shadow's Edge does have a satisfying conclusion, but it leaves the door wide open for a sequel. It's too early to say when The Shadow's Edge 2 will release, but production officially began in October 2026.

Jackie Chan has been involved in several newer Western releases, including Karate Kid: Legends. He also starred alongside John Cena in Hidden Strike, which premiered in 2023. Several of Chan's latest movies have debuted in China. We've already covered The Shadow's Edge, and it's arguably a must-watch for fans of Jackie Chan movies, even if you don't enjoy subtitles.

Many of Chan's recent Chinese movies are quite different from what some Western fans may be used to. A Legend premiered in 2024 and deserves a special mention because it's a sequel to The Myth, which was released in 2005. Professor Fang (Jackie Chan) is an archaeologist. Ancient relics are discovered during a glacier excavation, and they are significant because Fang has seen them in his dreams.

A Legend tells a story in the present day and another in Ancient China as Fang learns more about the artifacts. Some action scenes set in Ancient China are particularly impressive, with stylish, large-scale battles and personal sword fights. Jackie Chan also starred in Unexpected Family in 2026. It's a charming comedy, though it's also very different from what general audiences may be used to, as it doesn't feature any martial arts.

#3515. Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Clipfarming, influencer screenings, and meme-bait popcorn buckets: promoting a movie in the internet age is often a full-court offensive to get noticed. In that spirit, why not just get down to business and resort to modern civilization’s oldest method for seeking attention: dangling some money in people’s faces?

That’s what the marketing teams behind “How to Rob a Bank,” from Amazon MGM Studios, and “Ebenezer,” from Skydance’s Paramount Pictures, have tried in the weeks leading up to their shared November 13 release to North American theaters.

For the former ensemble heist thriller, a branded ATM was moved between multiplexes throughout the Los Angeles area over the course of four days. Those who learned of the campaign on the film‘s social media channels could gain clues about the machine’s location and a specified PIN number, which would spark payouts of a single one-hundred-dollar bill to those who bothered to seek out (or stumble upon) it. Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

“Ebenezer” took a more cheeky, trifling approach, promoting an official Venmo account for Johnny Depp’s Christmas crab apple that users could request funds from. Those who scrolled through the account’s transactions would see it shares the character’s penny-pinching spirit: the only completed transactions were those giving away one single cent. The Venmo account was only active for a few hours, though a Paramount Instagram post from last week teases followers to “check back” as “Ebenezer might be feeling generous on @venmo again.”

Several film news aggregation accounts like Culture Crave and DiscussingFilm reported that the account “crashed” due an overwhelming amount of requests, though Paramount declined to comment on if such a description was accurate. Venmo did not respond to a request asking if the company partnered with the studio on the sponsorship.

Much like that line, there is also a tackiness du jour to both money-mindset stunts, especially in a world where awards shows, professional sports and geopolitical events can hardly be watched without outlets asking you to bet — erh, predict — on them. A video posted to Paramount’s socials opens with a Venmo request for $500, asking Scrooge to help pay off a user’s student loans.

Not to mention the real inadvertent quirk: the account has been able to receive payments from users. Considering the scant number of one-cent payouts from the account and the number of influxes, it is almost certain that Paramount could have made money on the stunt, though an individual with knowledge of the account shared that all received funds were sent back to users via private transactions.

Krystyna Ursta, a 27-year-old actress, video editor, and Depp fan in Los Angeles, shared that she gave about $30 to the account and received a full refund a few days later — plus an extra penny and an invitation to a special screening of the film in New York on Monday. She will be attending a local press screening instead. Ursta also posted a video of herself reacting to the account, one of many fan responses that flooded in on social media.

“I kind of figured that they will probably return it,” Ursta wrote over text after being reached through her Instagram handle, which she included in her Venmo transactions. “I’m such a big fan. I was happy to support the film.”

The rather gimmick-less gimmick of waving around money also helps capture the attention of people that aren’t necessarily interested in seeing the movie, but are going through the average modern experience of thinking about one’s financial situation. Aggregation accounts were quick to post graphics reporting on both stunts, with captions like “HOW TO ROB A BANK ATM’S ARE BEING SET UP AROUND LOS ANGELES AND GIVING PEOPLE FREE MONEY AND IT COULDN’T HAPPEN AT A BETTER TIME” and “EBENEZER SCROOGE WILL SEND YOU REAL MONEY ON VENMO BUT THERE’S A CATCH SWIPE FOR MORE.”

There’s also people like Scott, a 35-year-old based out of Atlanta that couldn’t help but engage with the “Ebenezer” Venmo account after seeing it on X. He sent a penny, then received one in return. (A disclaimer: six Venmo users were reached for interview about their Ebenezer experience by sending them $0.01 with this reporter’s contact information in the caption; Scott was the only response that timed out before publication.)

“Seeing Ebenezer is now on Venmo was too funny and stupid to not engage with,” he wrote over text. “There’s something very boring dystopia about it: the idea of a fictional character from a 200-year-old Christmas story being commercialized on Venmo just shows how dumb Hollywood can. … It’s like McDonald’s Monopoly: take our slop and we might give your money.”

Also helpful for the studios is how little dangling the potential of money actually costs. Sans staffing fees, producing the “Ebenezer” Venmo account and its activity used a sum less than the coins between the couch cushions on the Paramount lot. Per the “How to Rob a Bank” promo’s website, each location’s prize pool gave away ten one-hundred-dollar bills and twenty twenty-dollar-bills ($1,400 total), plus some theater-supplied prizes like gift cards. An employee at the Regal Sherman Oaks that worked on the day of the on-site promotion said the ATM seemed to deal out the rewards in a random order, as opposed to $100 dollar bills for the first finders. Amazon MGM declined to comment, while Stellar Agency Inc., which sponsored and administered the promotion, did not respond to a request.

Both had much smaller overheads than a “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” promotion than ran in April 2025. To launch the magician threequel’s first trailer, Lionsgate reportedly gave away roughly $250,000 to those that texted a mysterious phone number displaying in Times Square in the hours up to the drop. Like “Ebenezer” and “How to Rob a Bank,” it was a promotion that sparked a viral moment with plenty of user-generated content, each sharing the widely desired fantasy of receiving free money.

Neon handed out basic resources for an “I Love Boosters” promotion in May, where stars KeKe Palmer and LaKeith Stanfield took over a Shell gas station in West Pico to give out complimentary refills to the first 70 cars that arrived. The stunt played on then-peaking fuel prices, which had skyrocketed in the wake of the U.S.’ initial bombing of Iran in February and the subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In the months since, President Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retains control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump announced the idea, his approval rating was at a dismal 35 percent, per a CNN aggregate of various polls. Though the offer is unprecedented and dubious on its face, it has been covered extensively — and it cost nothing to float it.
