#3495. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3494. Everything Coming to Prime Video in November 2026

Sports fans can catch the four Friday night doubleheaders from November 6 through 27 featuring Emirates NBA Cup 2026 Group Play action, as well as Thursday Night Football. If you want sports with some added drama and fun acting, look out for Nicolas Cage as John Madden when the Madden biopic makes its way to the streaming platform this month. And finally, the most-anticipated sci-fi event of the year that Prime Video and fans have been waiting for, Blade Runner 2099 will surely take your breath away. There’s a lot to look forward to, so here’s your guide to everything coming to Prime Video in November 2026.

The first-ever television production in The Lord of the Rings franchise, The Rings of Power serves as a prequel to The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings film trilogy and is adapted from J.R.R. Tolkien’s extensive history of Middle-earth, drawn from the appendices of The Lord of the Rings. Set during a time of relative peace, the series covers major events from Middle-earth’s Second Age, including the forging of the legendary rings and Sauron’s rise to power as the new Dark Lord. Morfydd Clark, Robert Aramayo, Benjamin Walker, Ismael Cruz Córdova, and Daniel Weyman reprise their roles for Season 3, with Jamie Campbell Bower, Eddie Marsan, and Simon Pegg as new characters.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has thrilled fans with its opulent production ever since its premiere in 2022. The first and second seasons were highly praised for their earnest tribute to Tolkien’s universe and the innovative expansion of the history of Middle-earth. Rings of Power Season 3 is set five years after the fall of Eregion during the War of the Elves and Sauron, when Sauron secretly begins to craft his weapon of ultimate power that would give him final victory over all Middle-earth.

Inspired by the life and work of American football coach and commentator John Madden, Madden is an all-new biographical sports drama directed and co-produced by David O. Russell. Starring Nicolas Cage as the titular legend, the film chronicles his journey from a Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Oakland Raiders to becoming football's most recognizable voice and building the worldwide Madden NFL video game series. Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, John Mulaney, Sienna Miller, and Shane Gillis star as other real-life personalities.

Described officially as “a celebration of a brilliant mind whose once-in-a-century spirit and personality, partnership with his daring wife Virginia, lifelong friendships, and infectious love of people and football transcended the world of sports,” Madden is a must-watch for sports fans. The Pro Football Hall of Fame NFL coach and sports commentator is one of the most recognizable figures in football history and a beloved icon who famously never had a losing season and has won 16 Sports Emmy Awards. Madden will make its streaming premiere on Prime Video on November 18, following its theatrical release on November 11, 2026.

Created by Ben Watkins and produced by Lonnie Ali and Michael B. Jordan, The Greatest is the first-ever authorized scripted series about Muhammad Ali, presenting an intimate exploration of his phenomenal life as a boxer, humanitarian, and global icon. Jaleen Best stars as the titular legend (who fans might recognize from All American: Homecoming), while showrunner Watkins is best known for creating shows like Hand of God and Cross. The series also stars Omari Hardwick, Dana Gourrier, Kai Parham, and Amin Joseph as main characters, with Michael Ealy and Giovanni Ribisi in recurring roles.

Since his landmark gold medal win at the 1960 Olympics, Muhammad Ali has been the subject of several feature films, TV shows, animated TV series, and over a dozen major documentary films and TV specials. But the Prime Video original is special for touching upon his personal life and candid moments. The eight-episode limited series not only traces his journey from Cassius Clay to Muhammad Ali, but also looks at his life beyond the fame and fortune and depicts him as a son, brother, husband, and father.

The latest installment in the Blade Runner franchise, Blade Runner 2099 is a direct sequel to Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 and Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner, all of which are based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?. The miniseries is set 50 years after the events of the 2017 film and focuses on Olwen, an aging Replicant Blade Runner, and her mysterious partner, Cora, a human pretending to be a replicant, who are tasked with hunting down a gang of rogue Replicants. Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen and Hunter Schafer plays Cora, with Dimitri Abold and Lewis Gribben as other main characters.

Between 1982 and now, Blade Runner has grown into a robust cyberpunk media franchise that includes two feature films, three shorts, an animated series, and several games. Created by Silka Luisa and produced by Ridley Scott, Blade Runner 2099 is one of the most anticipated sci-fi shows of 2026 and the second TV series in the titular franchise following 2021’s Blade Runner: Black Lotus. As revealed in the trailer, the upcoming miniseries shares the core atmosphere, textures, and grungy world-building established by Ridley Scott in the 1982 film but features higher stakes and a major shift in the power dynamic between humans and replicants.

Directed by Nanette Burstein, The Boy Who Stole Billions? is a deep-dive documentary series about Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of his $32 billion cryptocurrency empire, FTX. The three-part series delves into one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history with unprecedented access and exclusive firsthand accounts from Sam Bankman-Fried himself, provided during his prison sentence. The documentary also features never-before-seen interviews with various other figures involved with Bankman in his personal life and business, including his co-CEO and former girlfriend, Caroline Ellison.

Founded in 2019 by Bankman-Fried and Gary Wang, FTX became a major crypto exchange in its short-lived existence before collapsing in 2022 due to a major financial fraud. Bankman-Fried and his fintech empire have also been the subject of Ben MacKenzie’s 2025 documentary Everyone Is Lying to You for Money and a segment on 60 Minutes. A close-up look at the rise and fall of the poster boy of cryptocurrency, The Boy Who Stole Billions? has been described as “a series that will surprise many, bringing audiences closer to the people behind the headlines and opening up Sam's world in ways it has never been seen before.”

#3493. Apple TV’s new crime thriller series ‘Nocturne’ is now streaming

The first two episodes for Apple TV’s latest crime thriller, “Nocturne,” are now available to stream. Watch the trailer below.

Starring Liev Schreiber (Ray Donovan), Zazie Beetz (They Will Kill Yuo), and Stephen Graham (Adolescence), Nocturne is based on the bestselling crime novels “Lazarus” and “The Sandman,” by Lars Kepler.

When the desperate search for Jurek’s last missing victim forces Jonah to send his surrogate daughter, FBI Agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), up against Jurek, how far will Jonah go?

With the first two episodes now streaming on Apple TV, new episodes will air every Friday through December 25.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#3492. AI data centers are on the ballot in 10 states tomorrow — here's what's at stake for your community

There's something new on the ballot this time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI data centers are powering everything from ChatGPT to Google's Gemini, but the enormous facilities that make these tools possible are facing growing resistance across the country.

On Tuesday, November 3, voters in 10 states will decide on 41 local ballot measures involving data centers, according to Ballotpedia. Twenty-eight measures would restrict development if approved, while 13 would make it easier for projects to move forward.

The votes come as Americans face rising electricity costs and questions about how much power AI infrastructure should consume, who pays for new energy infrastructure and whether communities benefit enough from having these facilities nearby.

For households already struggling with higher utility bills, the debate has become about more than where technology companies build their next server farms.

Data centers are essential to the AI boom. They power cloud storage, streaming services, internet applications and the sophisticated AI systems used by millions of people every day.

But they also require enormous amounts of electricity to operate servers and cooling systems around the clock. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with projections ranging from 9.5% to 15.3%.

That growing demand is putting pressure on utilities to expand generating capacity, transmission lines and other infrastructure.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

And consumers are growing concerned about whether they'll be asked to help pay for those upgrades.

According to Reuters, residential electricity prices have increased more than 10% nationally since 2024, with increases exceeding 20% in Ohio.

Not every increase can be attributed to data centers. Rising fuel costs, aging infrastructure and other factors also contribute. But rapid growth in electricity demand is raising questions about how utilities allocate costs between large commercial customers and existing households.

Ohio is at the center of the debate. According to Ballotpedia, the state accounts for 21 of the 41 measures appearing on November 3 ballots.

Several communities, including Sunbury, Defiance and Oregon, will vote on proposals to prohibit data centers that consume more than 25 megawatts of electricity.

In Sunbury, the restrictions could affect a proposed $2 billion Amazon data center project, according to Reuters. But the issue goes well beyond Ohio. California, voters in Alhambra will decide whether to prohibit data centers within city limits. In Edgewater, Florida, residents will consider an amendment restricting new data center development and expansion.

Several Maine communities will vote on temporary moratoriums, potentially pausing projects while local officials establish development rules.

In Illinois, some voters will will weigh advisory questions about whether their communities should support or restrict data center construction.

And in New Jersey, residents of Downe Township will answer a straightforward question: Do they support data centers in their community? The New Jersey vote is advisory, meaning it measures public sentiment rather than directly authorizing or prohibiting construction.

The measures across the country differ significantly. Some establish outright bans, others would restrict only the largest facilities, and some would impose additional approval requirements. The common thread for all is that more communities want a greater say in how AI infrastructure is built.

Electricity markets operate across large regions, meaning power demand in one community can affect costs well beyond its borders. The PJM regional electricity market, for example, serves New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia and other states. According to a recent FactCheck.org analysis, PJM's independent market monitor has identified data centers as a primary driver of higher capacity market prices.

The monitor estimates that data center demand will add billions of dollars in capacity market charges over the current and following delivery years.

Those charges are shared across the regional electricity market, although the impact on individual household bills varies. Even if a community blocks a new facility, demand from AI companies could shift to another location. Existing infrastructure costs and broader electricity-market conditions would remain.

Likewise, approving a project doesn't automatically mean household bills will increase. The outcome depends partly on whether utilities and regulators require developers to cover the infrastructure costs their facilities create.

Technology companies and development supporters argue that data centers create construction jobs, generate tax revenue and attract investment.Amazon, which has major expansion plans in Ohio, has emphasized the employment opportunities, economic benefits and technology services associated with its facilities.

Supporters also argue that data centers are necessary to support the digital services that households and businesses depend on, including AI tools that are rapidly becoming part of everyday life.

Restrictions, they warn, could move those investments to communities with more favorable development policies.

Opponents raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, noise, land use and the possibility of households subsidizing infrastructure built primarily for large technology companies. The issue crosses traditional political lines, with local opposition emerging in communities across the country.

Tomorrow's election results could affect where major technology companies build new data centers, how local governments regulate them and the conditions developers must meet before construction begins.

For consumers in the U.S., tomorrow may determine how communities and utility regulators will manage the growing electricity and infrastructure demands of AI without placing unnecessary costs on existing customers.

#3491. Apple’s best MacBook Pro decision this week had nothing to do with touch

Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro brings plenty of welcome upgrades, but one of the best things about this week’s launch is what the company decided not to change.

Was I aching for a touchscreen Mac? Not particularly. But I can see how useful it might be for a great deal of users, and I’m happy that their day has finally come. Or will come, starting November 6.

But I’ve been aching for a new Mac. Though my 2023 M2 Pro 16-inch MacBook Pro is still a great machine, its 16GB of RAM is starting to feel a bit cramped. Past me knew this was a mistake.

With the prospect of a revamped MacBook Pro just around the corner, I spent the past few weeks excited about the possibility of biting the bullet and splurging for a new one, even though there had been very conflicting rumors about which chips it would pack.

Although in my heart of hearts I had acquiesced to the idea that the new touchscreen MacBook Pro would get the same chips as the current non-touchscreen line, I was also holding on to the hope that Apple would throw in some performance gains to sweeten the rumored $400 premium deal it would carry.

Performance-wise, the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is identical to the non-touchscreen models, though there is a case to be made that its redesigned thermal system could make it run faster despite using the same chip, though the changes appear to be aimed more at keeping the display cool than improving heat dissipation. Time, and reviews, will tell.

Which makes Apple’s decision to keep the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro for sale all that more welcome and unexpected.

Even when Apple introduced the Touch Bar back in 2016, the only non-Touch Bar option left was the entry-level 13-inch MacBook Pro. If you wanted a more powerful Mac or a 15-inch model, you had to get with the program and pony up the extra $300 for the 13-inch model with Touch Bar, or $400 for the redesigned 15-inch model.

Yes, there is plenty new with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Tandem OLED display, improved thermal performance, thinner, lighter design, slimmer bezels, redesigned audio system, Dynamic Island (debatable for some, I know), and even the return of the glowing Apple logo (woo!) on the lid are all welcome additions. Oh yeah, and “it has touch as well.”

Put all of that together, and the $400 premium is arguably not that unreasonable.

But if, like me, these improvements feel secondary to the performance boost you’re prioritizing for this particular upgrade, getting those same specs for effectively $400 less (or using those $400 for better specs!) feels like a pretty great deal for all parties involved, future me included.

Will future me have preferred that I wait for the M7 generation? Possibly. But then again, waiting for the perfect moment to upgrade is what got me into this situation in the first place, recent price hikes and all.

#3490. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3489. Dave Bautista’s Insane Kratos Transformation For God Of War Silences Skeptics

For years, Dave Bautista was widely fancast as God of War's Kratos. Surprisingly, when he finally landed the part in Prime Video's live-action God of War, many questioned whether he was the right fit. The skepticism came in the wake of Dave Bautista losing a lot of weight and deciding to move away from physically demanding roles like Drax in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Dave Bautista was not the first choice to play Kratos in Prime Video's God of War. Before him, Ryan Hurst was cast for the role. He seemed almost perfect for the part because he had previously voiced Thor in God of War Ragnarök. Unfortunately, an injury forced Hurst to step back from the role, paving the way for Bautista to lead the show's roster.

While many defended Dave Bautista's casting and labeled him as the perfect choice for the part, others believed he had lost too much muscle over the years to accurately embody Kratos. Just a few months after his casting, Dave Bautista has already silenced all doubters with his impressive transformation.

Soon after his casting, Dave Bautista revealed he was training again and focusing on putting on muscle before the filming of Prime Video's God of War ensues. A few months into his training, Bautista has now revealed he has already gained 20 pounds of muscle for the part. He even posted a video to show his transformation, and it is hard not to notice how he already looks like Kratos from God of War's Norse saga:

This is the second update the former WWE star has given on his physique while preparing to play Kratos in God of War. The first update came just two weeks after he started training for the part (via Instagram), where he already seemed prepared for the role. After the 20-pound gain, Dave Bautista now closely resembles Kratos from the games' Norse Saga.

The actor's shaved head and overgrown beard further add to the resemblance, and it seems likely he will gain a few more pounds before the show's filming ensues. Now that his transformation has already silenced all skeptics, it is hard not to wait for the show's behind-the-scenes stills that will reveal him in Kratos' full Spartan armor.

Prime Video's God of War is cleverly skipping the games' Greek mythology arc and jumping ahead to the Norse Saga, which is more dense and poignant in terms of storytelling. It features Kratos as a transformed, grief-ridden man who works on his relationship with his son. Owing to the emotional heft of the source material, the Prime Video series needed someone with a good acting range to play Kratos.

At the same time, since the original game franchise's core appeal lies in its action and larger-than-life godly characters, someone with a towering frame had to be cast for the part. After his transformation, Bautista not only seems to perfectly convey Kratos' immense physical presence but also has the acting chops to capture the emotional weight of his story.

The live-action God of War adaptation has experienced a few early production setbacks, which have delayed its filming. However, Dave Bautista's casting as Kratos has seemingly turned out to be a blessing for the Prime Video series. If everything else falls into place for the upcoming video game adaptation, it will easily find its place among the greatest fantasy shows of our time.

Adapted from the PlayStation video game franchise, God of War is an action-adventure drama series in development under Amazon. The series will center on series protagonist Kratos, but no other information on the series has been divulged.

#3488. Apple acquires Ascend․io, an agentic AI engineering startup

Apple recently struck a deal to acquire Ascend.io, a company focused on agentic data engineering technology.

Under the Digital Markets Act, Apple must now publicly report acquisitions above a certain size. This has given us new insight into the company’s acquisition strategy, including glimpses at its future goals.

The latest update to the EU’s “List of Acquisitions” website reveals a deal between Apple and Ascension Labs, Inc., perhaps better known as Ascend.io.

This is a typical acquihire situation, with Apple’s update saying it “will have the right to make employment offers to and hire certain employees” of Ascension Labs. The deal also includes a “non-exclusive license to Ascend’s intellectual property rights.” Apple will also be able to “be assigned certain patents” owned by the company.

Ascend.io describes itself as “the first Agentic Data Engineering platform,” with AI agents that “automatically handle all the tedious stuff” associated with data engineering. The company was founded in 2015.

Ascend.io’s website has also been updated with the following note:

For the past ten years we pursued a singular mission: Make Data Engineering Delightful. We introduced the industry’s first declarative data pipeline technology. We launched a unified platform that brought all of ingest, transform, and orchestration together. We invented DataAware automation. And most recently we pioneered Agentic Data Engineering — where agents work alongside teams across the entire data engineering lifecycle. Each chapter was different, but the goal the same: make life better for data engineers.

Earlier this month, Apple also struck a deal with an AI startup that lets musicians rework recorded music.
